AGENCY:
Coast Guard, Department of Homeland Security.
ACTION:
Temporary final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary safety zone for certain navigable waters on the Pasquotank River, at Elizabeth City, NC. The safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with an over-the-water drone display. The entry of vessels or persons into this zone is prohibited unless specifically authorized by the Captain of the Port, Sector North Carolina, or their designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective from 7 p.m. to 8 p.m. on November 27, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
To view available documents go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and search for USCG-2026-1411.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have questions about this rule, contact MST1 Eric Gordon, Sector North Carolina Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone 571-608-8783, or email
d05-smb-secnc-marineevents@uscg.mil
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations

II. Background and Authority
On November 9, 2026, the Coast Guard was notified that a drone show will occur on November 27, 2026 over the Pasquotank River, at Elizabeth City, NC. The Captain of the Port, North Carolina (COTP) has determined that potential hazards associated with the drone show, such as being hit by a falling drone, will be a safety concern for anyone beneath the drones in flight and that a safety zone is needed to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment in the navigable waters within the safety zone. The COTP is issuing this rule under authority in
46 U.S.C. 70034
.
The Coast Guard is issuing this rule without prior notice and comment. As is authorized by
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, the Coast Guard finds that good cause exists for not publishing a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) with respect to this rule because it is impracticable. The Coast Guard does not have enough time to solicit and respond to comments if it is to establish this safety zone by November 27, 2026, the date it must be in place to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment.
For the same reason, the Coast Guard finds that under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
, good cause exists for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
.
III. Discussion of the Rule
This rule establishes a safety zone from 7 p.m. until 8 p.m. on November 27, 2026. The safety zone will cover all navigable waters within a 350 foot by 1,500 foot designated area near the Pasquotank River Harbor waterfront. No vessel or person will be permitted to enter the safety zone without obtaining permission from the COTP or their designated representative.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The regulatory flexibility analysis provisions of the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980,
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, do not apply to rules that are not subject to notice and comment. Because the Coast Guard has, for good cause, waived the notice and comment requirement that would otherwise apply to this rulemaking, the Regulatory Flexibility Act's flexibility analysis provisions do not apply here.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-121
), if this rule will affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section.
The National Ombudsman resolves concerns of uneven or excessive federal regulatory enforcement. Reviews are confidential and do not waive the right to pursue administrative appeals or any other legal action. Contact 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247) or
Ombudsman@SBA.gov
.
B. Collection of Information
This rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this rule under
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under
Executive Order 13175
, Consultation and Coordination with Indian Tribal Governments, because it does not have a substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
As required by The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531-1538
), the Coast Guard certifies that this rule will not result in an annual expenditure of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted for inflation) by a State, local, or tribal government, in the aggregate, or by the private sector.
E. Environment
We have analyzed this rule under Department of Homeland Security Directive 023-01, Rev. 1, associated implementing instructions, and Environmental Planning COMDTINST 5090.1 (series), which guide the Coast Guard in complying with the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
), and have determined that this action is one of a category of actions that do not individually or cumulatively have a significant effect on the human environment.
This rule is a safety zone. It is categorically excluded from further review under paragraph L60(a) of Appendix A, Table 1 of DHS Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01, Rev. 1. A Record of Environmental Consideration supporting this determination is available in the docket.

§ 165.T05-1411
Safety Zone; Pasquotank River Harbor, Elizabeth City, NC.
(a)
Location.
The following area is a safety zone: All waters of the Pasquotank River from surface to bottom, encompassed by a line connecting the following points beginning at 36°18.058′ N, 076°13.069′ W, thence to 36°18.057′ N, 076°13.000′ W, thence to 36°17.810′ N, 076°13.000′ W, thence to 36°17.810′ N, 076°13.070′ W and along the shoreline back to the beginning point. These coordinates are based on the World Geodetic System (WGS 84).
(b)
Definitions.
As used in this section,
designated representative
means a Coast Guard Patrol Commander, including a Coast Guard coxswain, petty officer, or other officer operating a Coast Guard vessel and a Federal, State, and local officer designated by or assisting the Captain of the Port Sector North Carolina (COTP) in the enforcement of the safety zone.
(c)
Regulations.
(1) Under the general safety zone regulations in subpart C of this part, you may not enter the safety zone described in paragraph (a) of this section unless authorized by the COTP or the COTP's designated representative.
(2) To seek permission to enter, contact the COTP or the COTP's representative by calling the Sector North Carolina Command Center at 833-732-8628. Those in the safety zone must comply with all lawful orders or directions given to them by the COTP or the COTP's designated representative.
(d)
Enforcement period.
This section will be enforced from 7 p.m. to 8 p.m. on November 27, 2026.

AGENCY:
Securities and Exchange Commission.
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
Although the consolidated audit trail (the “CAT”) continues to be a necessary regulatory tool, its decentralized governance has presented certain challenges to administering the CAT. To address those shortcomings, the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission” or the “SEC”) proposes to assume direct control of the CAT. Specifically, the Commission is proposing amendments to Regulation NMS under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”) that would rescind Rule 613, which obligates the national securities exchanges and national securities associations (collectively, the “SROs”) to act jointly to develop a national market system plan to develop, implement, and maintain the CAT (the “CAT NMS Plan”). The Commission is simultaneously proposing new Rule 17a-26, which would require the SROs and broker-dealers to record and electronically report to a central repository substantially the same information that was previously required to be recorded and reported pursuant to Rule 613, the CAT NMS Plan, related SRO compliance rules, and related exemptive relief previously issued by the Commission.

X. Statutory Authority
I. Introduction
The CAT is an integral part of the Commission's toolkit for overseeing the U.S. securities markets. Among other things, it provides efficient access to market data in a manner that facilitates more effective surveillance, investigation, and enforcement, and provides an unparalleled ability to reconstruct market activity and conduct market analysis. In these ways, the CAT supports regulatory efforts to administer and enforce the federal securities laws. Without it, or some effective substitute, the ability of the Commission and the SROs to protect investors and to maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets would be significantly diminished.
The Commission adopted Rule 613 of Regulation NMS in 2012.
[
1
]
Rule 613 required the SROs to jointly develop and submit to the Commission a national market system plan to create, implement, and maintain a consolidated audit trail to collect specified data from the SROs and their members and to provide access to such data to each SRO and the Commission “for the purpose of performing . . . regulatory and oversight responsibilities pursuant to the federal securities laws, rules, and regulations.”
[
2
]
The national market system plan submitted by participating SROs (or the “Participants”) to fulfill the requirements of Rule 613 was approved by the Commission in 2016.
[
3
]
By its nature, a national market system plan is jointly administered by the SROs and governed collectively. However, in the context of administering a complex and expensive market-wide audit trail system, the decentralized governance structure established by an NMS Plan across 29 Participant-owners, and with many changes of the required specifications along the way, has presented certain challenges to administering the CAT and warrants revisiting.
[
4
]
The Commission therefore proposes herein to rescind Rule 613. Because the CAT is operational, and it would require a significant investment of time and resources to create a new audit trail that could replace it, the Commission has determined that it would not make economic or operational sense to eliminate or retire the CAT, even if aspects of the CAT could be improved or refined. For this reason, the Commission simultaneously proposes new Rule 17a-26, which would require the SROs and broker-dealers to record and electronically report substantially the same information that is currently required to be recorded and reported pursuant to Rule 613, the CAT NMS Plan, related SRO compliance rules, and related exemptive relief previously issued by the Commission. Proposed Rule 17a-26 would require that data to be reported to the Commission or its designee instead of to a CAT system independently administered by the Participants under a national market system plan.
The Commission also anticipates that additional steps would be needed to fully transition the CAT to the Commission's direct control, including: the sale and transfer of CAT assets and the establishment of new contractual arrangements to ensure operational continuity; the use of Congressionally appropriated funds to support the operation of the CAT; and the establishment of new advisory committees and/or working groups, as appropriate, to obtain feedback from market participants regarding the CAT.
The approach proposed herein is designed to address the inefficiencies in the current governance structure for the CAT and to allow the Commission to assume direct control of the CAT, while ensuring the CAT's continued operation with minimal disruption.
II. Background
The Exchange Act, as amended,
[
5
]
tasks the Commission with overseeing the U.S. securities markets, including supervising certain market participants such as broker-dealers, national securities exchanges, and national securities associations.
[
6
]
The Exchange Act further provides that specified entities, including national securities exchanges and registered securities associations, fall within the definition of an SRO.
[
7
]
As an SRO, each national securities exchange and national securities association must comply, and enforce compliance by its members and associated persons, with the Exchange Act, the Commission's rules and regulations thereunder, and the SRO's own rules.
[
8
]
Effective market oversight by the Commission and SROs relies on, among other things, access by regulatory users at the Commission and the SROs to sufficiently accurate, timely, and complete market data. Because the vast majority of securities transactions in modern markets occur electronically, at high speeds and volumes and across trading venues, cross-market audit trails and related data sources have come to play an important role in the oversight of securities markets. Such audit trails and related data sources aid regulators in conducting robust cross-market market surveillance, investigations, enforcement activities, and engaging in cross-market reconstructions and analyses, as appropriate.
Prior to the implementation of the CAT, the Commission and the SROs had to cobble together disparate market data from various audit trails and related data sources, including the Electronic Blue Sheet (or “EBS”) system,
[
9
]
manual requests to market participants, daily reports produced by clearing agencies that provide aggregated information to the SROs and the Commission, market-specific matching engines and/or order
(
printed page 76036)
book feeds, market-specific audit trails, precursor cross-market audit trails like the now-retired Order Audit Trail System (“OATS”) and the Consolidated Options Audit Trail System (“COATS”),
[
10
]
trade reporting facilities, proprietary data feeds made available by SROs and/or off-exchange trading venues, and publicly-available consolidated data feeds provided by securities information processors. Each of these audit trails and related data sources was useful, but each was also limited in its scope and effectiveness.
[
11
]
Assembling a consolidated cross-market audit trail from these audit trails and related data sources was a cumbersome, complex, and time-consuming process that was prone to error.
[
12
]
A. Rule 613 and the CAT NMS Plan
To improve the accuracy, completeness, accessibility, and timeliness of the data available to regulators, in 2012, the Commission adopted Rule 613 of Regulation NMS.
[
13
]
Rule 613 requires the SROs to jointly develop and submit to the Commission a national market system plan to create, implement, and maintain a consolidated audit trail to collect specified data from the SROs and their members and to provide access to such data to each SRO and the Commission “for the purpose of performing . . . regulatory and oversight responsibilities pursuant to the federal securities laws, rules, and regulations.”
[
14
]
The rule further requires that each SRO be a sponsor of this national market system plan
[
15
]
and that the national market system plan “include a governance structure to ensure fair representation of the plan sponsors, and administration of the central repository, including the selection of the plan processor.”
[
16
]
The national market system plan submitted by the Participants to fulfill the requirements of Rule 613—the CAT NMS Plan—was approved by the Commission in 2016.
[
17
]
The CAT is intended to furnish both the Commission and the SROs with timely access to a comprehensive, uniform, accurate, and linked set of trading data that allows them to efficiently retrieve relevant information about the full lifecycle of all orders in NMS and OTC Equity Securities
[
18
]
across the markets and trading centers that compose the national market system.
[
19
]
The core functionality of the CAT includes collecting data from both SROs and Industry Members
[
20
]
about the original receipt or origination of an order, the routing of an order and the receipt of an order that has been routed, executions, modifications, and cancellations.
[
21
]
The Plan Processor,
[
22
]
FINRA CAT, LLC (“FINRA CAT”), uses this data to “link and create the order lifecycle” using a “daisy chain approach,” in which “a series of unique order identifiers, assigned to all order events handled by CAT Reporters[,] are linked together by the Central Repository[
[
23
]
] and assigned a single CAT generated CAT-Order-ID that is associated with each individual order event and used to create the complete lifecycle of an order.”
[
24
]
In addition to this linked data, the CAT is required to provide regulators with SIP Data.
[
25
]
Although the CAT no longer collects customer and account-level information pursuant to recent amendments to the CAT NMS Plan approved by the Commission,
[
26
]
the CAT's architecture of identifiers and lifecycle linkage enables regulators with a specific regulatory purpose to analyze a particular customer's trading activity for Eligible Securities
[
27
]
across markets, brokers, and/or accounts through generation of a CAT Customer ID (“CCID”).
[
28
]
This transactional data may only be associated with customer and account-level information if such information is obtained separately from Industry Members.
[
29
]
B. Feedback Received in Response to the Concept Release
On April 16, 2026, the Commission issued a Concept Release on Consolidated Audit Trail and Other Audit Trails and Data Sources (the “Concept Release”) describing various
(
printed page 76037)
developments with respect to the CAT since the Commission's approval of the CAT NMS Plan in 2016. The Concept Release sought feedback regarding whether changes should be made to the CAT's structure, scope, functionality, and security, including changes that would strike a different balance between privacy considerations and regulatory need.
[
30
]
1. Necessity of the CAT
The Concept Release asked commenters to consider whether the CAT is necessary to enable the Commission and the SROs to fulfill their statutory obligations and/or whether any other audit trails and related data sources are sufficient for those purposes.
[
31
]
In response, the SROs stated that continued access to the data provided by the CAT is essential to their regulatory programs and should be maintained, at least in some form.
[
32
]
One SRO commenter in particular stated that “the need for a consolidated audit trail to facilitate cross-market oversight by regulators has never been more acute,” given the “unprecedented speed and complexity” of today's U.S. securities markets—which now include 29 registered national securities exchanges, more than 40 alternative trading systems, and hundreds of broker-dealers that provide liquidity in the over-the-counter market by executing customer orders out of their own inventory.
[
33
]
Another SRO commenter stated that it uses the CAT to “identify potential fraud, market manipulation, or other violative behaviors that harm investors or disrupt the fair and orderly operation and integrity of the securities markets.”
[
34
]
Another SRO commenter specified that it uses CAT Data
[
35
]
to oversee the covered markets for “market manipulation, fraud, or other proscribed, illicit trading activities, including potential layering, spoofing, insider trading, front running, or cross-product manipulation and to ensure compliance with best execution rules,” as well as to “guide risk scoping and examinations of member firms, reducing the amount of data that [it] has to request from firms and making the process more efficient for [it] and its members.”
[
36
]
A third SRO commenter stated that it uses CAT Data for disciplinary actions related to “disclosure failures, unauthorized trading in client accounts, violation of Commission and SRO anti-manipulation rules, failing to supervise reasonably for manipulative trading, failing to comply with SRO anti-money laundering rules, best execution failures, and a host of other conduct that threatens investors and the integrity of U.S. capital markets.”
[
37
]
Multiple SRO commenters also stated that the CAT increases the efficiency of their regulatory programs, because CAT Data enables more targeted surveillance and/or examinations of their members and reduces the number and scope of informational requests that would otherwise be necessary, thus decreasing compliance burdens on broker-dealer members.
[
38
]
Moreover, SRO commenters stated that there is no realistic or viable replacement for the CAT, because the SROs “decommissioned other systems”—like OATS—that “allowed for regulatory access and use of order and trade data that was not otherwise available,” in reliance on the existence of the CAT.
[
39
]
Although other data sources are still available to regulators, SRO commenters indicated that these data sources should not be considered true replacements for the CAT. As one SRO commenter stated, “legacy audit trails and data sources, whether individually or collectively, do not provide the same cross-market, order-level lifecycle reconstruction functionality as the CAT,” and “reconstructing trading activity from disaggregated systems has historically been time-consuming, error-prone, and operationally inefficient.”
[
40
]
One SRO
(
printed page 76038)
commenter further stated that maintaining the CAT would be a better outcome than creating a new reporting regime to replace the CAT, given the expense and delay associated with that alternative.
[
41
]
Many other commenters made similar arguments in favor of the CAT. Noting the complexity and fragmentation of modern U.S. securities markets, these commenters stated that regulators “need a comprehensive, accurate, and timely audit trail to reconstruct market events, investigate misconduct, detect manipulation, and enforce securities laws.”
[
42
]
These commenters stressed the regulatory benefits provided by the CAT. One commenter, for example, stated that:
The continued operation of the CAT is particularly important for protecting retail investors. Individual investors often lack the resources and market access available to institutional participants and therefore rely on regulators to ensure markets operate fairly. CAT enhances regulators' ability to detect and investigate practices such as market manipulation, spoofing, layering, insider trading, and other abusive conduct that can harm investors and erode confidence in the markets. CAT also serves as an indispensable investigative and enforcement tool. By allowing regulators to reconstruct market events with precision, it significantly improves the speed and effectiveness of examinations, surveillance, and enforcement actions.
[
43
]
Such commenters expressed concern that eliminating the CAT would create gaps in market surveillance or otherwise compromise regulation of the U.S. securities markets, despite the existence of other audit trails and related data sources.
[
44
]
Accordingly, these commenters encouraged the Commission to “retain CAT, continue improving its effectiveness, and ensure regulators have access to the data necessary to protect investors and maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets.”
[
45
]

The CAT enables the Commission and the SROs to protect investors and to maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets by making it possible for regulators to conduct market oversight, including cross-market surveillance, investigations, and enforcement activities, as well as cross-market reconstructions and analyses where appropriate. Examples of Commission use cases include, but are not limited, to:
Surveilling and investigating various forms of abusive, fraudulent, and manipulative trading activity, including insider trading, front-running, cherry-picking, and manipulative trading;
Identifying potential unsuitable sales activity;
Evaluating tips and complaints;
Facilitating risk-based reviews of SEC registrants and targeting potentially higher-risk activity during examinations—for example, by establishing baselines and standard trading behavior of SEC registrants and by identifying anomalous activity that may warrant further examination, such as atypical liquidation patterns, concentrations of daily trading volume, abnormal trading imbalances, unusual profit and loss patterns, or irregular transaction pricing;
Testing and validating representations made by SEC registrants;
Identifying and measuring costs to market participants affected by a market disruption;
Conducting studies of market structure, market activities, usage of order types, and/or behavior of market participants;
Assessing the impact of potential and implemented regulatory changes—for example, by performing data analyses using CAT Data in support of rulemaking to inform both policy decisions and economic analyses; and
Investigating or analyzing current market events.

Access to CAT Data improves regulators' ability to perform reconstruction of market events and to conduct market analysis and research to inform policy decisions, as well as to perform other regulatory activities, in particular market surveillance, examinations, investigations, and enforcement functions. The CAT allows the Commission to link suspicious trading activity to unique market participants and to more efficiently identify and investigate violative behavior in the markets. It is an integral part of the Commission's toolkit for overseeing the U.S. securities markets, facilitating more effective surveillance, investigation, enforcement, and market analysis and thereby reducing potential harm to investors. Without it, the ability of the Commission to protect investors and to maintain fair, orderly, and efficient markets would be significantly diminished.
[

The Commission therefore has determined that it would not make sense to eliminate or retire the CAT, even if aspects of the CAT could be improved or refined.

C. Proposal To Restructure the Governance and Funding of the CAT
The Commission proposes to implement several changes to the current governance and funding structure of the CAT, including the two rulemaking changes proposed herein: (1) the rescission of Rule 613; and (2) the implementation of new Rule 17a-26, which would substantially maintain current CAT data reporting requirements, except that data would be reported to the Commission or its designee (the “Proposal”).
To fully enable a transition to the new governance and funding structure, the Commission further anticipates additional steps would be needed outside the context of the rulemaking proposed herein, including: (3) the rescission of the CAT NMS Plan and related SRO compliance rules; (4) the sale and transfer of CAT LLC and/or FINRA CAT assets and the establishment of a contract between the Commission and its designee (the “Designee”) for the maintenance and operation of the CAT System; (5) the use of Congressionally appropriated funds to support the operation of CAT;
[
79
]
and (6) the establishment of advisory committees and/or working groups, as appropriate, to obtain feedback from market participants regarding the ongoing operation of the CAT System (collectively, with the Proposal, the “Implementation Steps”).
The Commission is proposing these changes because it believes that, as compared to the CAT's current governance and funding structure, there are a number of policy benefits to providing the Commission with direct control of the CAT and using appropriated funds to support its maintenance and operation. Rescinding Rule 613 would enable the Participants to eliminate the diffuse ownership structure required by the CAT NMS Plan and thereby address the inefficiencies in the current governance structure. The Proposal would further give the Commission direct control over CAT reporting requirements through proposed Rule 17a-26. In addition, the Implementation Steps would give the Commission direct control over CAT performance requirements. Decision-making authority would be significantly more concentrated than it is today, which would address inefficiencies relating to administration of a complex market-wide evolving technology system like the CAT through a decentralized governance structure. Moreover, the proposed use of appropriated funds to support the operation of CAT would establish a permanent and defined funding solution for the CAT, further incentivize cost management discipline, and help to avoid the recurrence of certain long-standing disputes amongst the Participants and Industry Members in the future.
To ensure that there are no disruptions or gaps with respect to ongoing CAT reporting by Participants and Industry Members or to ongoing usage of CAT Data by regulators, the Commission further anticipates that the above-described changes would be implemented in a manner that aligns the effective dates for the rescission of Rule 613 and the rescission of the CAT NMS Plan and any related SRO compliance rules with the effective dates for Rule 17a-26, the completed transfer of CAT LLC and/or FINRA CAT assets, and any contract between the Commission and the Designee for the operation of the CAT.
In developing this Proposal, the Commission carefully considered the comments received on the Concept Release. Each aspect of the Implementation Steps is discussed further below, including issues that would need to be resolved before the Implementation Steps could be taken. The Commission solicits comment on each aspect of the Implementation Steps through a number of general and specific questions, and the Commission also welcomes comments on any other aspects of the Implementation Steps, particularly on any costs, burdens, or benefits that may result from the Implementation Steps.

IV. Proposed Rule 17a-26
Overview of Proposed Rule 17a-26
Currently, the CAT is implemented through the CAT NMS Plan, as required by Rule 613. The CAT System is owned by the Participants and operated on their behalf by FINRA CAT, pursuant to a contractual arrangement. Participant reporting requirements are imposed by the CAT NMS Plan and reporting requirements for Industry Members are imposed through rules adopted by each Participant (“SRO CAT Compliance Rules”).
[
159
]
Under proposed Rule 17a-26, national securities exchanges, national securities associations, and broker-dealers would be required to maintain and report certain information to the Commission or the Designee, and such information would be ingested, processed, and made available for regulatory purposes. If the proposed rule were adopted, the CAT NMS Plan and SRO CAT Compliance Rules would no longer be necessary to impose reporting obligations.
As proposed, Rule 17a-26 is based on relevant elements of the CAT NMS Plan and SRO CAT Compliance Rules, in a manner generally designed to maintain reporting requirements for the SROs and Industry Members for the CAT as they exist today. As noted above, this general approach is supported by comments received on the Concept Release, which explicitly urged the Commission to eliminate the CAT NMS Plan in favor of promulgating its own reporting rule that leveraged existing requirements from Rule 613 and/or the CAT NMS Plan.
[
160
]
The intent of replicating current requirements found in the CAT NMS Plan and SRO CAT Compliance Rules is minimizing disruptions in the reporting of information to the CAT during the
(
printed page 76049)
transition to a new governance and funding model. For example, the Commission anticipates that, if Rule 17a-26 is adopted as proposed, both the Participants and Industry Members that currently report pursuant to the CAT NMS Plan and SRO Compliance Rules could maintain the same reporting format under the same technical specifications as they do today. Proposed Rule 17a-26 would not implement new substantive reporting requirements; it would also incorporate previously-granted exemptive relief, as discussed in greater detail below in Part IV.L.
This design avoids costs associated with creating new systems or technology development costs related to meeting new reporting standards, consistent with suggestions made by commenters on the Concept Release. For example, one commenter noted that “SROs and industry members have expended substantial resources to report consistent with current CAT specifications.”
[
161
]
CAT LLC similarly stated that, “[g]iven the time and investment required to fully implement the CAT and to revamp Industry Member and Participant systems to comply with it, it would not be sensible or cost-effective to eliminate the CAT in favor of developing a different audit trail from scratch.”
[
162
]
Maintaining current reporting requirements in a new rule, including incorporating exemptive relief, “would avoid unnecessary cost and potential confusion that could result from introducing entirely new requirements regarding core reporting.”
[
163
]
Maintaining current CAT reporting requirements would also benefit regulatory users of CAT Data and regulators who have developed systems to utilize CAT Data as it exists today.
[
164
]
Because it is maintaining current CAT reporting requirements, the Commission is not proposing to alter reporting requirements in the proposed rule at this time. Nevertheless, the Commission acknowledges concerns regarding the elements reportable to the CAT presented by commenters to the Concept Release
[
165
]
and welcomes specific comments on the proposal to maintain CAT reporting requirements in proposed Rule 17a-26.
There are some differences in what is required today of CAT Reporters pursuant to the CAT NMS Plan and SRO CAT Compliance Rules and what would be required pursuant to the proposed rule, but these differences are not directly related to the specific elements required to be reported to the CAT. The proposed rule would expand clock synchronization and Business Clock requirements that are currently imposed on just Industry Members to all CAT Reporters (
see, infra,
Part IV.C below), take a different approach to errors and error corrections than is currently contemplated in the CAT NMS Plan, without modifying existing timeframes for initial corrections (
see, infra,
Part IV.J below), and incorporate existing exemptive relief relating to reporting that is technically not part of or pursuant to the CAT NMS Plan (
see, infra,
Part IV.L below). But these and other differences from existing requirements, as described more fully below, are not designed or anticipated to impact the day-to-day requirements of reporting transaction information to the Commission or the Designee, as compared to existing requirements under Rule 613, the CAT NMS Plan, and SRO CAT Compliance Rules.
Preamble to Proposed Rule 17a-26
Proposed Rule 17a-26 includes a preamble describing the purpose of the proposed Rule 17a-26 and limitations on the use of information submitted to the Commission or the Designee pursuant to the proposed rule. Specifically, proposed Rule 17a-26 states that national securities exchanges, national securities associations, and broker-dealers are required to report certain information to the Commission or the Designee, to allow for the maintenance of a consolidated audit trail to be used for regulatory purposes only. It would state that the information reported pursuant to this section may only be accessed and used by authorized regulatory staff of the Commission, national securities exchanges, and national securities associations to support regulatory purposes, such as market reconstruction and analyses, surveilling, examining, investigating, or enforcing compliance by its members and their associated persons with federal securities laws, the Commission's rules and regulations thereunder, and a national securities exchange or national securities association's own rules.
These limitations on the access and use in the proposed preamble are consistent with and build upon existing limitations for CAT Data. Rule 613 and the CAT NMS Plan limit the use of CAT Data to solely surveillance and regulatory purposes.
[
166
]
The CAT NMS
(
printed page 76050)
Plan also provides that the Plan Processor must provide Participants' regulatory staff and the Commission with access to CAT Data for regulatory purposes only.
[
167
]
Examples of functions for which Participants' regulatory staff and the SEC can currently use CAT Data include economic analysis, market structure analyses, market reconstructions, market surveillance, investigations, and examinations.
[
168
]
In their comments on the Concept Release, Cboe and Nasdaq supported efforts to “further reinforce or enhance these restrictions on how CAT Data can be used.”
[
169
]
The Commission agrees that current restrictions on CAT Data access and use could be further clarified in proposed Rule 17a-26.
The proposal to limit access and use of the consolidated audit trail to authorized regulatory staff of the Commission, national securities exchanges, and national securities associations to support regulatory purposes only is designed to continue to prevent such information from being directly accessed by non-regulatory staff, or used for commercial purposes or other non-regulatory purposes, as such usage would be inconsistent with the purposes of CAT, which was designed to be a regulatory tool.
[
170
]
CAT data is intended to be used by regulators for regulatory purposes, not for non-regulatory purposes such as by private litigants seeking to obtain such data for civil lawsuits, which is a concern that has been raised by commenters on the Concept Release.
[
171
]
For example, usage of such information that does not serve solely regulatory purposes, such as economic analyses or market structure analyses in support of SRO rule filings with both a regulatory and commercial purpose, would be inconsistent with the proposed rule. In contrast, the definition would not prohibit the use of such information by a national securities exchange to support a rule filing with a solely regulatory purpose. The Commission declines at this time to specify what actions that would constitute “regulatory use” or otherwise explicitly limit or impose terms on the use of CAT Data when it is used for regulatory purposes, as suggested by a commenter on the Concept Release.
[
172
]
The delineation suggested by this commenter could chill or prohibit otherwise appropriate regulatory use. However, the proposed rule provides examples of appropriate regulatory purposes, including market reconstruction and analyses, surveilling, examining, investigating, or enforcing compliance by its members and their associated persons with federal securities laws, the Commission's rules and regulations thereunder, and a national securities exchange or national securities association's own rules.
The CAT System is currently subject to a comprehensive information security program that subjects the SROs to various security and confidentiality requirements designed to appropriately constrain the use of CAT data, and the Commission intends to substantially maintain this program under the Proposal.
[
173
]
The access and use restrictions set forth in proposed Rule 17a-26 would therefore acknowledge the regulatory need for such data while maintaining security and confidentiality protections for such data consistent with existing requirements.

In addition, the proposed rules would differ insofar as synchronization logs would be allowed to be preserved for a shorter time period (three years instead of five years), certification of satisfaction of the synchronization requirements will be explicitly required to be made to the Commission or the Designee annually (rather than “in accordance with the certification schedule established by the Operating Committee”), and violation reporting would not be “pursuant to thresholds set by the Operating Committee pursuant to the CAT NMS Plan.”

Tolerances for CAT Reporters
Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(1) would specify that for purposes of reporting to the Central Repository, each national securities exchange and national securities association must synchronize its Business Clocks at a minimum to within 100 microseconds of the time maintained by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (“NIST”), consistent with industry standards, and each Industry Member must synchronize their respective Business Clocks at a minimum to within fifty (50) milliseconds of the time maintained by the NIST, and maintain such a synchronization. The provision would state that the tolerance provided for in proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(1) includes all of the following: the difference between the NIST atomic clock and the CAT Reporter's Business Clock, the transmission delay from the source, and the amount of drift of the CAT Reporter's Business Clock.
Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(1) is consistent with current requirements and is designed to help ensure that clocks are synchronized within a specific level of granularity and that time drift does not exceed a defined level of deviation. The majority of trading of NMS Securities is done electronically, and computers necessarily have some rate of deviation when keeping time. Proposed Rule 17a-26(c) is designed to strike an appropriate balance between the need for accurately timestamped reported events and the burden of maintaining clock synchronization and the amount of deviation allowed in timekeeping. Effective clock synchronization is essential to maintaining an accurately time-sequenced audit trail, particularly one where time stamps will be in millisecond increments or less, especially in the modern market where order events occur within microseconds. The ability to sequence market events is crucial to the efficacy of detecting and investigating some types of manipulation, particularly those involving high frequency trading. Any drift of such a system's clock relative to the clocks of other systems may of course hinder the time-sequencing of cross-system events, but any drift between Business Clocks would not preclude the ability of regulators from performing a detailed, accurate time-sequenced analysis of all the orders, cancellations, modifications, and executions performed by a specific system of interest.
The proposed clock synchronization standards of 50 milliseconds for broker-dealers and the finer 100 microsecond standard for national securities exchanges and national securities associations are based on current requirements in the CAT NMS Plan and SRO CAT Compliance Rules. In approving the CAT NMS Plan, the Commission noted that the Participants considered various clock synchronization options, ranging from microseconds to one second, before settling on a 50 millisecond standard, which the Participants believed represented the then current industry standard for Industry Members.
[
261
]
The Participants stated that, based on their analysis, imposing a finer clock synchronization standard for Industry Members as part of the initial implementation of the CAT would significantly increase the cost of compliance for some segments of the Industry.
[
262
]
With respect to the national securities exchanges and national securities associations themselves, the Participants represented that they all operated pursuant to a clock synchronization standard that is within 100 microseconds of the time maintained by NIST.
[
263
]
One commenter on the Concept Release objected to the 50 millisecond standard for Industry Members, stating that the tolerance “makes the CAT data useless,” and that “[a] wide latency tolerance mussed up data that one cannot roll the data forward and backward to see which trade message came in first, second, third, or a hundred thousandth,” and “[i]n turn, [the CAT] is not suitable for Best Ex, surveillance, or regulatory market
(
printed page 76060)
monitoring purposes.”
[
264
]
The Commission disagrees that the clock synchronization requirements have made the CAT useless. While a reduced tolerance may lead to a greater ability to confidently sequence otherwise unlinked order events in perfect sequence, the existing requirements are sufficient for regulatory needs and strike an appropriate balance between precision and the risks of transition to a significantly less tolerant synchronization standard at this time.
Tolerances for Manual Order Events and Allocation Reports
Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(1)(A) would establish different clock synchronization requirements for Manual Order Events and Allocation Reports. Specifically, notwithstanding the requirements of proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(1), proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(1)(A) would state that each national securities exchange, national securities association, and Industry Member must synchronize their Business Clocks used solely for Manual Order Events and Business Clocks used solely for the time of allocation on Allocation Reports to within one second of the time maintained by the NIST atomic clock, consistent with industry standards, and maintain such synchronization.
Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(1)(A) is consistent with the CAT NMS Plan and SRO CAT Compliance Rules, which also allow for the reporting of Manual Order Events and Allocation Reports to a one-second clock synchronization standard. For manual systems and manual events, the timing is inherently less precise and a one-second clock synchronization standard is reasonable. For Allocation Reports, a one-second clock synchronization standard is reasonable because the regulatory benefit of the timing of an allocation does not require millisecond precision, and unlike other CAT order events that require linkage, allocations are not time-critical. Maintaining these clock synchronization standards, as well as the standards in Rule 17a-26(c)(1), will mean that CAT Reporters can continue to synch clocks as they do now and will avoid having to make systems or reporting changes to meet new standards.
As discussed above, certain requirements that are only imposed on Industry Members by SRO CAT Compliance Rules today would be extended to apply to national securities exchanges and national securities associations as well. Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(1)(B) would require that Business Clocks be synchronized every business day before market open to ensure that timestamps for Reportable Events are accurate, and that to maintain clock synchronization, Business Clocks must be checked against the NIST atomic clock and resynchronized, as necessary, throughout the day. While the CAT NMS Plan requires Participants to synchronize its Business Clocks at a minimum to within 100 microseconds of the time maintained by NIST, it does not explicitly require Participants to synchronize their Business Clocks every business day before market open or resynchronize those clocks, as necessary, throughout the day.
[
265
]
Requiring all CAT Reporters to regularly resynchronize their Business Clocks should help ensure that they are in compliance with the standards in Rule 17a-26(c)(1) both at the start of each trading day and throughout each trading day, which is essential in ensuring that the timestamps applied to reportable events are accurate and within synchronization requirements, as Business Clocks could drift or become less consistent with the time maintained by NIST overnight or over a trading day.
Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(2) would impose documentation requirements related to clock synchronization and Business Clocks, consistent with existing requirements in SRO CAT Compliance Rules for Industry Members, except for shortening the required period logs are to be maintained from five years to three years, and proposing to apply these documentation requirements to all CAT Reporters. Specifically, proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(2) would require national securities exchanges, national securities associations, and Industry Members to document and maintain their synchronization procedures for Business Clocks, including keeping a log of the times when they synchronize their Business Clocks and the results of the synchronization process. Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(2) would specify that the log should include notice of any time a Business Clock drifts more than the applicable tolerance specified in proposed Rule 17a-26(c) and that such log must include results for a period of not less than three years ending on the then current date, or for the entire period for which the national securities exchange, national securities association, or Industry Member has been required to comply with Rule 17a-26 if less than three years. Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(3) would require each national securities exchange, national securities association, and Industry Member subject to proposed Rule 17a-26 to certify that its Business Clocks satisfy the synchronization requirements set forth in proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(1) on an annual basis. Consistent with the existing requirements in SRO CAT Compliance Rules for Industry Members, pursuant to the proposal, CAT Reporters would maintain the certification as part of their books and records.
The proposed requirement that all CAT Reporters maintain documentation for their synchronization procedures for Business Clocks, including a log of the times when they synchronize their Business Clocks and the results of the synchronization process should help ensure that all CAT Reporters maintain a record of clock synchronization should review be required. As noted above, this is currently imposed on only Industry Members pursuant to SRO CAT Compliance Rules.
[
266
]
Requiring such log to document synchronization times and results for a period of up to three years is appropriate because it is consistent with the amount of time CAT Data is currently required to be stored by the Plan Processor pursuant to the CAT NMS Plan. The three year requirement differs from the current five year requirement imposed on Industry Members pursuant to SRO CAT Compliance Rules, and does not foreclose the ability of Industry Members to maintain that amount of logs if they choose to do so.
Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(3) will require certification from each national securities exchange, national securities association and broker-dealer subject to Rule 17a-26 that its Business Clocks satisfy the synchronization
(
printed page 76061)
requirements set forth in Rule 17a-26(c)(1) on an annual basis. Currently, Industry Members are required to complete an annual clock synchronization certification form, certifying that the Industry Member satisfies the synchronization requirements of the SRO CAT Compliance Rules for the prior calendar year.
[

Consistent with those existing requirements, CAT Reporters would maintain the certification required by proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(3) as part of their books and records. Requiring an annual certification from all CAT Reporters should help ensure that each CAT Reporter is maintaining Business Clocks with synchronization consistent with Rule 17a-26(c)(1).
Proposed Rule 17a-26(c) would also include violation reporting requirements for clock synchronization and Business Clocks, based in part on existing requirements in SRO CAT Compliance Rules. Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(4) would require national securities exchanges, national securities associations, and Industry Members with Business Clocks to report to the Commission or the Designee violations of paragraph (1) of proposed Rule 17a-26(c). Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(4) would also state that a national securities exchange, national securities association, or Industry Member that engages in a pattern or practice of reporting Reportable Events outside of the required clock synchronization time period as set forth in Rule 17a-26(c)(1) without reasonable justification or exceptional circumstances may be considered in violation of this section. Currently, the SRO CAT Compliance Rules require violation reporting by Industry Members “pursuant to the thresholds set by the Operating Committee pursuant to the CAT NMS Plan,” but proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(4) has no similar language. In addition, this proposed provision would extend the violation reporting requirements and pattern or practice provision that is currently in SRO CAT Compliance Rules to apply to all CAT Reporters and not just Industry Members. Proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(4) should continue to help ensure that CAT Reporters take great care in maintaining accurate Business Clocks and that the responsible party is made aware of any deviations from the requirements of proposed Rule 17a-26(c)(1).

D. Timestamps
Proposed Rule 17a-26(d) would impose requirements regarding timestamps for reporting to the Central Repository. Specifically, Rule 17a-26(d) would require each CAT Reporter to record and report to the Central Repository with time stamps in milliseconds. Rule 17a-26(d)(1) would state that to the extent that a CAT Reporter's order handling or execution systems utilize time stamps in increments finer than milliseconds, such CAT Reporter shall record and report to the Central Repository with time stamps in such finer increment up to nanoseconds; provided, that CAT Reporters that capture timestamps in increments more granular than nanoseconds must truncate the timestamps after the nanosecond level for submission to Central Repository, rather than rounding such timestamps up or down. Proposed Rule 17a-26(d)(2) would provide for different timestamp requirements for Manual Order Events and Allocation Reports. Specifically, national securities exchanges, national securities associations, and Industry Members would be permitted to record and report: (i) Manual Order Events to the Central Repository in increments up to and including one second, provided that CAT Reporters shall be required to record and report the time when a Manual Order Event has been captured electronically in an order handling and execution system of such CAT Reporter in milliseconds; and (ii) the time of allocation on Allocation Reports in increments up to and including one second.
The proposed requirements regarding timestamps are designed to be substantively identical to existing reporting requirements for CAT Reporters, pursuant to the CAT NMS Plan, SRO CAT Compliance Rules, and exemptive relief granted by the Commission. Rule 613 required the CAT NMS Plan to impose granularity requirements that reflect current industry standards and be at least to the millisecond.

H. Recording and Reporting National Securities Exchanges and National Securities Associations Data
Proposed Rule 17a-26(h) would describe the recording and reporting obligations for national securities exchanges and national securities associations for each order and each Reportable Event, as applicable. The reporting requirements of proposed Rule 17a-26(h) are based on the reporting requirements for Participants in the CAT NMS Plan, in particular Section 6.3, and are designed to require the reporting of the same elements for orders and Reportable Events as is currently required today.
Proposed Rule 17a-26(h) would state that national securities exchanges and national securities associations are required to record and report data to the Central Repository as required by this section in a manner that ensures the timeliness, accuracy, integrity, and completeness of such data, sufficient for an accurate, time-sequenced record of orders beginning with the receipt or origination of an order by a member of a national securities exchange or national securities association and further documenting the life of the order through the process of routing, modification, cancellation, and execution (in whole or in part) of the order. This language is designed to ensure, in conjunction with the rest of proposed Rule 17a-26(h), that the rule requires the reporting of information for each order and each Reportable Event, as applicable, in a manner consistent with existing reporting requirements and sufficient to maintain current processing and linkage procedures and provide regulators useful data.
1. Details of Orders and Reportable Events
Proposed Rule 17a-26(h)(1), which is based on current Section 6.3(d) of the CAT NMS Plan, would describe the elements required to be reported by national securities exchanges and national securities associations for the various parts of an order lifecycle consistent with what is currently required by the CAT NMS Plan. Proposed Rule 17a-26(h)(1) would state that each national securities exchange and national securities association shall record and electronically report to the Central Repository certain details for each order and each Reportable Event, as applicable, in the manner prescribed
(
printed page 76065)
by the Technical Specifications, for the following Reportable Events: (i) the original receipt or origination of an order; (ii) the routing of an order; (iii) the receipt of an order that has been routed; (iv) if an order is modified or cancelled; and (v) if the order is executed, in whole or in part.
Original Receipt or Origination of an Order
For the original receipt or origination of an order, proposed Rule 17a-26(h)(1)(i) would require the reporting of: (A) Firm Designated ID(s) for each Customer; (B) CAT-Order-ID; (C) SRO-Assigned Market Participant Identifier of the Industry Member receiving or originating the order; (D) date of order receipt or origination; (E) time of order receipt or origination (using timestamps pursuant to Rule 17a-26(d)); and (F) Material Terms of the Order. For the routing of an order, proposed Rule 17a-26(h)(1)(ii) would require the reporting of: (A) CAT-Order-ID; (B) date on which the order is routed; (C) time at which the order is routed (using timestamps pursuant to Rule 17a-26(d)); (D) SRO-Assigned Market Participant Identifier of the Industry Member, national securities exchange, or national securities association routing the order; (E) SRO-Assigned Market Participant Identifier of the Industry Member, national securities exchange, or national securities association to which the order is being routed; (F) if routed internally at the Industry Member, the identity and nature of the department or desk to which the order is routed; and (G) Material Terms of the Order.
Receipt of an Order That Has Been Routed
For the receipt of an order that has been routed, proposed Rule 17a-26(h)(1)(iii) would require the following information: (A) CAT-Order-ID; (B) date on which the order is received; (C) time at which the order is received (using timestamps pursuant to Rule 17a-26(d)); (D) SRO-Assigned Market Participant Identifier of the Industry Member, national securities exchange, or national securities association receiving the order; (E) SRO-Assigned Market Participant Identifier of the Industry Member, national securities exchange, or national securities association routing the order; and (F) Material Terms of the Order.
Order Modification or Cancellation
If an order is modified or cancelled, proposed Rule 17a-26(h)(1)(iv) would require: (A) CAT-Order-ID; (B) date the modification or cancellation is received or originated; (C) time at which the modification or cancellation is received or originated (using timestamps pursuant to Rule 17a-26(d)); (D) price and remaining size of the order, if modified; (E) other changes in the Material Terms of the Order, if modified; and (F) whether the modification or cancellation instruction was given by the Customer or was initiated by the Industry Member, national securities exchange, or national securities association.

Proposed Rule 17a-26(h)(1) generally mirrors existing CAT NMS Plan provisions and proposed Rule 17a-26(h)(1)(vi) would codify into the rule the requirement that information or events be reported as prescribed in the Technical Specifications. Maintaining existing obligations and timelines for error correction would allow the Commission or the Designee to, at minimum, maintain current processing and feedback practices with respect to errors, while maintaining the ability to make system changes to provide more feedback or make other changes to improve and facilitate the error correction process for CAT Reporters in the future.
Proposed Rule 17a-26(j) would differ in some respects from existing requirements with respect to error rates and error correction. Currently the CAT NMS Plan imposes a system error rate,
[
323
]
and the Participants have Industry Member-specific metrics established pursuant to SRO CAT Compliance Rules.
[
324
]
In contrast, proposed Rule 17a-26 will not have any specific compliance thresholds within the proposed rule. Instead, proposed Rule 17a-26(j) is designed to impose obligations to report accurate information to the CAT, and an obligation to correct any errors discovered after submission, while requiring the establishment, maintenance, and enforcement of written policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure compliance with these obligations.
Proposed Rule 17a-26(j) states that CAT Reporters must report data to the CAT in a manner that ensures the timeliness, accuracy, integrity, and completeness of such data because erroneous CAT Data limits the regulatory value of the information and regulatory utility of the CAT. Similarly, the proposed rule imposes an obligation on CAT Reporters to correct errors in previously reported information so that the accuracy, integrity, and completeness of such information is maintained. If CAT submissions are substantially late, inaccurate, unreliable, or incomplete, the regulatory benefits of collecting such information could be substantially diminished or eliminated. Timely information allows for more effective processing of such information and the ability for regulators to review information on a timely basis. Accuracy refers to the need for CAT data to accurately reflect the reportable event—if CAT data is inaccurate it does not accurately reflect the relevant order or order event and could lead to many different issues, including misleading or incorrect analysis by regulators. Integrity of CAT submissions and data is essential in ensuring that such information has not been altered and remains reliable. Finally, completeness is necessary for processing of CAT submissions and for regulatory purposes, as incomplete records could frustrate the ability of the CAT to process and link records and reduce the regulatory utility of the CAT.
The proposed rule maintains a deadline of reporting corrections for identified errors by 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time on T+3, which is consistent with existing requirements under the CAT NMS Plan. Even with a CAT Reporter's best efforts, initial submissions to the CAT could be “erroneous” and require correction. For example, proposed Rule 17a-26 imposes deadlines for initial CAT reporting that are similar to what is currently required, and a CAT Reporter may not have all of the information required for a fully complete and accurate submission by that deadline, or be informed after such deadline that there needs to be a correction or modification to the submission. The Commission anticipates that, like today, CAT submissions would be processed and validated with issues identified and relevant CAT Reporter(s) informed of what the error or issue is with the submission files.
Proposed Rule 17a-26(j)(2) would require the development of written policies and procedures by CAT Reporters that are reasonably designed to ensure that it complies with any obligations to report information pursuant to this section, which should help ensure that CAT Reporters are reporting in a consistent manner and in a way designed to help ensure the timeliness, accuracy, integrity and completeness of reporting. The proposed rule would require that such written policies and procedures be reasonably designed, which means that such policies and procedures may differ amongst CAT Reporters, as there are CAT Reporters of different sizes, different business practices, and other differences that would make any one specific approach to written policies and procedures impractical. Requiring that each CAT Reporter review and update these policies and procedures at least annually, and maintain a record of such review, should help ensure that such policies and procedures remain reasonably designed for complying with obligations to report information pursuant to proposed Rule 17a-26.

K. Reference Data Reporting
Proposed Rule 17a-26(k) would define what and how certain information regarding accounts and Customers (“Reference Data”) would be reported to the CAT, in a manner consistent with current requirements of the CAT NMS Plan. The provisions of proposed Rule 17a-26(k) are designed to capture the existing reporting requirements relating to Reference Data under the current CAT NMS Plan, including exemptive relief and Plan amendments previously approved by the Commission.
At the inception of CAT, customer information was required to be reported and maintained in CAT to enable regulators to more quickly and reliably identify the customers associated with potentially unlawful trading activity and to facilitate the reconstruction of important market events.
[
325
]
At the same time, the Commission has sought to balance these benefits against the risks associated with collecting and storing personally identifiable investor information. From the start, for example, personal customer information in CAT was stored separately from transaction data. In addition, due to exemptive relief and amendments to the CAT NMS Plan, certain sensitive PII, such as SSNs, has never been required to be reported to the CAT.
In 2020, in light of concerns raised by market participants, industry representatives and the Participants, the Commission granted exemptive relief that limited the personal customer information that must be reported to the CAT to name, address, and birth year (“CCID Exemption Order”).
[
326
]
The CCID Exemption Order also permitted the Participants to implement the CCID alternative or CCID process. Under the CCID alternative, the Plan Processor generates a unique CAT Customer-ID, or CCID, using a two-phase transformation process that avoids having SSNs/ITINs reported to or stored in the CAT. In the first transformation phase, a CAT Reporter transforms the SSN/ITIN into an interim transformed value. This transformed value, and not the SSN/ITIN, is submitted to a separate system within the CAT (“CCID Subsystem”), keeping it apart from other customer and account information. The CCID Subsystem then performs a second transformation to create the globally unique CCID for each Customer that is unknown to, and not shared with, the original CAT Reporter. The CCID is then sent to the customer and account information system (“CAIS”) of the CAT, where it is linked with the other customer and account information. The CCID may then be used by the Participants' regulatory staff and Commission staff in queries and analysis of CAT data.
The CCID approach was developed by the Participants in collaboration with Industry Members.
[
327
]
The ability to generate CCIDs preserves a core regulatory purpose of the CAT by allowing for the tracking of a specific order of a Customer throughout its entire lifecycle without the reporting or storage of social security numbers and other personally identifiable information in the CAT. The ability to link information about order events throughout the national market system to a unique customer identifier is one of the core regulatory advances of the CAT over the fragmented regulatory data sources that preceded it.
In February 2025, the Commission provided an exemption from the requirement to report other personal customer information not covered by the CCID Exemption Order, specifically names, addresses, and years of birth (collectively, “Name, Address, and YOB”) for natural persons with SSNs or ITINs (the “CAIS Exemption Order”).
[
328
]
The CAIS Exemption Order did not extend this relief to the reporting of customer information of foreign natural persons and legal entities. The Commission explained that it weighed the benefits of maintaining certain PII in the CAT differently in light of both the heightened security risks posed by the increased sophistication of bad actors and the prospect of relatively efficient indirect access to customer information.
[
329
]
The Commission concluded that the regulatory benefit of collecting the names, addresses and years of birth for natural persons reported with transformed SSNs no longer justified the associated risks.
[
330
]
The Commission emphasized, however, that the system of generating reliable CCIDs—the anonymized, unique customer identifiers contained in the CAT that are linked to each order event captured in the transaction database—would not be impacted.
[
331
]
Thus, if a regulator needs to determine the identity of the individual behind a particular CCID, the regulator would be able to use one or more of the Firm Designated IDs (“FDIDs”) associated with the CCID and contact the broker-dealer(s) who reported the FDID(s) and request the name, address and/or year of birth for the individual Customer.
[
332
]
The Commission later approved an amendment to the CAT NMS Plan that eliminated all CAT NMS Plan requirements to report Names, Addresses, YOBs, SSNs/ITINs, and EINs to the CAT and to remove such previously reported customer information stored in the CAT,

as well as codified the Participants' current method of generating anonymized customer identifiers without requiring the receipt or storage of individual SSNs/ITINs in the CAT.

On March 27, 2026, the Commission approved an amendment to the CAT NMS Plan that: (i) eliminated both the requirement to report Account Reference Data and Customer Reference Data to the CAT; (ii) eliminated CAIS from the CAT and instead established the “Reference Database”; (iii) and allowed for the implementation of the “Reference Data Approach,” which utilizes a revised approach for the generation of CCIDs that minimizes the data needed for its creation.

2. Updates and Error Correction for Reference Data
Proposed Rule 17a-26(k)(2), (3), and (4) would define requirements relating to updates and error correction for Reference Data required by proposed Rule 17a-26(k)(1). Specifically, Rule 17a-26(k)(2) would require the submission of any updates, additions, or other changes to the information required by paragraph (k)(1) of this section, for each of its Customers with an Active Account on a daily basis. The provision would state that Industry Members submitting new or modified Reference Data must provide it to the Central Repository no later than 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time on T+1.
Proposed Rule 17a-26(k)(3) would require periodic updates to Reference Data. The provision would state that, on a periodic basis as designated by the Commission or the Designee, each Industry Member shall submit to the Central Repository a complete set of Firm Designated IDs, the Transformed Identifier, and other information required by paragraph (k)(1) of this section for each of its Customers with an Active Account.
Proposed Rule 17a-26(k)(4) addresses error correction requirements for Reference Data. It would state that CAT Reporters must report data to the Central Repository in a manner that ensures the timeliness, accuracy, integrity, and completeness of such data, and that any CAT Reporter having an obligation to report under this section that discovers an error in information previously reported pursuant to paragraph (k)(1) of this section shall correct such error(s). The provision would also state that for each Industry Member for which errors in the information required by paragraph (k)(1) of this section, for each of its Customers with an Active Account submitted to the Central Repository have been identified by the Commission, the Designee, or otherwise, such Industry Member shall submit corrected data to the Central Repository by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on T+3.
The requirements for daily and periodic updates, as well as error correction of Reference Data, are based in part on existing obligations imposed on Industry Members through SRO CAT Compliance Rules, which require daily updates, periodic updates, and error correction of customer information.

However, as compared to current SRO CAT Compliance Rules, these provisions have been modified for the Reference Data Approach, specifically so that Industry Members submitting new or modified Reference Data must provide it to the Central Repository no later than 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time on T+1. This timeline for Reference Data reporting is required by the CAT NMS
(
printed page 76076)
Plan but is not currently reflected in SRO CAT Compliance Rules.
[

The requirements for daily updates, periodic updates, and error correction of Reference Data are designed to help ensure that the elements required to be reported pursuant to proposed Rule 17a-26(k)(1) are reported with timeliness, accuracy, integrity, and completeness, which is essential for the ability of regulators to reliably use such information for regulatory purposes. The proposed requirement would be consistent with the CAT NMS Plan and current practice, and would help ensure that CAT Reporters have an obligation to correct errors that are discovered in previously reported Reference Data as well as provide a deadline for such corrections.

V. Economic Analysis
A. Introduction
Section 3(f) of the Exchange Act requires the Commission, whenever it engages in rulemaking and is required to consider or determine whether an action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, to consider, in addition to the protection of investors, whether the action would promote efficiency, competition, and capital formation.
[
401
]
In addition, Section 23(a)(2) of the Exchange Act requires the Commission, when making rules under the Exchange Act, to consider the impact such rules would have on competition.
[
402
]
Exchange Act Section 23(a)(2) prohibits the Commission from adopting any rule that would impose a burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Exchange Act. The discussion below addresses the likely economic effects of the proposed rule, including the likely effect of the proposed rule on efficiency, competition, and capital formation.
Effective oversight of the national market system requires regulators to be able to reconstruct the lifecycle of an order across the disparate trading centers and broker-dealers that may interact with the order as it is filled. The information needed to do so is generated by and dispersed across numerous market participants, such as national securities exchanges, alternative trading systems, and broker-dealers trading directly with customers. This dispersion gives rise to two problems that limit both the incentive and the practical ability of any group of market participants to assemble such a record without regulatory intervention.
First, even if a group of market participants coordinated to assemble their own order and trade data into a consolidated record, they would capture only a portion of the benefits of doing so. This is because many of those benefits, such as improved detection and deterrence of cross-market manipulation, insider trading, and other misconduct, extend broadly to other market participants and investors who would not contribute to the cost of producing that record. Because these surveillance benefits extend broadly to market participants and investors who did not contribute to building the
(
printed page 76082)
record, and the venues and broker-dealers producing it cannot withhold those benefits from non-contributors, no single participant or group of participants will generally have an incentive to invest in building a consolidated audit trail sized to its full market-wide value, and a purely private market is therefore likely to underproduce such a record relative to the socially optimal level.
Second, even if market participants recognized the collective value of a consolidated record, they would also face substantial coordination costs in establishing common reporting standards and assembling data across competing venues with different systems, formats, and commercial incentives, making it unlikely that such an outcome would emerge voluntarily. As a result, without being required by regulation, consolidated cross-market order data is likely to be independently produced by market participants at a level below the amount warranted by its broader regulatory and market-wide benefits.
Regulators attempted to address this problem before the adoption of the CAT by requiring market participants to report order and trade information through various mandatory audit trails and data sources. These earlier regulatory efforts, however, were fragmented, incomplete, and difficult to use in combination with one another, leaving regulators without the comprehensive, cross-market view needed for effective oversight of modern markets. Before the CAT, regulators relied on a patchwork of sources to reconstruct activity across markets, including OATS, COATS, the Electronic Blue Sheet system, trade reporting facilities, and requests to individual market participants, among others. Although each source provided useful information, none provided a complete cross-market record, and combining information across these sources could be cumbersome, time-consuming, prone to error, and may have, at times, prevented regulators from identifying violative activity by a customer trading through multiple broker-dealers.
[
403
]
The Commission adopted Rule 613 in 2012 to improve the accuracy, completeness, accessibility, and timeliness of cross-market audit trail data by requiring the creation of the CAT.
[
404
]
Rule 613 set up the CAT through a structure in which the responsibility for operating the CAT, the responsibility for funding it, and the use of its data are divided among different entities.
For example, under the current structure, the Participants have ended up in disputes over the funding model for the CAT, both among themselves and with market participants, resulting in uncertainty, litigation, and distraction.
The Proposal would rescind Rule 613 and replace it with proposed Rule 17a-26, use appropriated funds to support the CAT,
[
405
]
and maintain substantially the same reporting requirements that exist today. These changes would resolve certain recurring disputes surrounding CAT cost allocation described above, by removing a point of contention among market participants, namely, how to fund the CAT under the CAT NMS Plan.
The proposed joint rescission of Rule 613 and implementation of Rule 17a-26 are designed to leave reporting obligations substantially unchanged. The Commission's goal with this Proposal is to address concerns regarding CAT governance and funding while preserving the regulatory benefits of the CAT described above.
Several components of the restructuring described in Part II.C would occur outside this rulemaking, including rescission of the CAT NMS Plan and related SRO compliance rules, the transfer of CAT assets, the use of Congressionally appropriated funds, and any agreement with a designee. To the extent the economic effects of the proposed rule depend on those actions, the analysis below identifies the assumptions on which the analysis relies. The Commission also identifies areas in which available information does not permit an effect to be quantified and requests comment and data that could inform those estimates.
B. Baseline

The economic analysis appropriately considers existing regulatory requirements, including recently approved amendments and exemptive reliefs, as part of its economic baseline against which the costs and benefits of the proposed rule are measured.
