Office of the Secretary
AGENCY:
Department of Defense (DoD).
ACTION:
Renewal of Federal advisory committee.
SUMMARY:
The DoD is publishing this notice to announce it is renewing the Department of Defense Wage Committee (“the DoD Wage Committee”) as a discretionary Federal advisory committee.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jim Freeman, Advisory Committee Management Officer for the Department of War (DoW), 703-692-5952.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The DoW is renewing the DoD Wage Committee in accordance with
chapter 10 of title 5 U.S.C.
(commonly known as the “Federal Advisory Committee Act” or “FACA”), and 41 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) part 102-3, “Federal Advisory Committee Management,” [
90 FR 58417
; December 16, 2025], and DoW policies and procedures. The
(
printed page 75836)
public or interested organizations may submit written statements about the DoD Wage Committee mission and functions. Written statements may be submitted at any time or in response to the stated agenda of planned meetings of the DoD Wage Committee. All written statements shall be submitted to the DoD Wage Committee's Designated Federal Officer (DFO), and this individual will ensure that all written statements are provided to the membership for their consideration. The DoD Wage Committee's DFO is Mr. Karl Fendt, and he may be contacted at (571) 372-1618, or
karl.h.fendt.civ@mail.mil
.
Consistent with
41 CFR 102-3.65(a)
, the DoW is publishing the DoD Wage Committee's Public Interest Determination.
Pursuant to
41 CFR 102-3.60(a)
, to establish, renew, reestablish, or merge a discretionary (agency discretion) advisory committee, an agency must first consult with the General Services Administration's Committee Management Secretariat (the Secretariat) and, as part of the consultation, provide a written public interest determination approved by the head of the agency to the Secretariat with a copy to the Office of Management and Budget. In addition, pursuant to
41 CFR 102-3.35
, an agency shall follow the same consultation process and document in writing the same determination of need before creating a subcommittee under a discretionary committee that is not made up entirely of members of a parent advisory committee.
Information on the following factors for the DoD Wage Committee is provided to the Secretariat to demonstrate that renewing the DoD Wage Committee is in the public interest:
1.
Annual Budget:
The Department of War (DoW) estimates annual operating costs to support the DoD Wage Committee are $54,896.54, which includes personnel travel, meetings, and contract support.
a.
Federal personnel on a full-time equivalent (FTE) basis:
The estimated annual personnel costs to the DoW are 0.3 full-time equivalent at $47,160.87, which includes basic pay with cost of living allowance (COLA).
b.
Other Federal internal costs:
Program element to support DoD Wage Committee contract costs are $5,592.00.
c.
Proposed payments to members:
Consistent with
10 U.S.C. 173
, members of the DoD Wage Committee are not compensated for their services, except for travel and per diem reimbursement for official DoD Wage Committee related business.
d.
Proposed number of members:
The DoD Wage Committee will be comprised of not more than 5 members with the chairperson and two members designated by the Secretary of War (SecWar).
e.
Reimbursable costs:
The estimated reimbursement costs, to include travel, for DoD Wage Committee staff and members are $2,143.67.
2.
If applicable, the total dollar value of grants expected to be recommended during the fiscal year:
Not applicable
3.
Criteria for selecting members to ensure the committee has the necessary expertise and fairly balanced membership:
As described in its proposed charter and membership balance plan, the DoD Wage Committee, pursuant to
5 CFR 532.227(b)
consists of five members, with the chair and two members designated by the SecWar. Of the remaining two members, pursuant to
5 CFR 532.227(b)(1)
, one member shall be designated by each of two labor organizations having the largest number of wage employees covered by exclusive recognition in the DoW.
Those individuals representing the labor organizations are each selected by their home labor organization to provide the DoD Wage Committee with the points of view of nongovernment entities or a recognizable group of persons that have interests in the subject matter under consideration by the DoD Wage Committee. The DoW in evaluating the other three candidates for DoD Wage Committee membership, considers each candidate's educational and professional experience concerning the subject matters tasked to the DoD Wage Committee through statute and regulations.
The DoW has found that viewing the complex issues facing the DoW through the lens of a multidisciplinary advisory committee provides the DoW and, more importantly, the American public with a broader understanding of the issues on which subsequent policy decisions are based. Membership shall be fairly balanced in terms of points of view represented and the functions to be performed by the DoD Wage Committee. The DoD Wage Committee's membership balance is not static, and the DoW Appointing Authority may change the membership based upon work assigned to the DoD Wage Committee.
4.
List of all other DoW Federal Advisory Committees:
A complete listing of DoW Federal advisory committees can be located at:
https://www.facadatabase.gov/​FACA/​s/​account/​001t000000DCAooAAH/​department-of-defense
.
5.
Justification that the information or advice provided by the Federal advisory committee or subcommittee is not available from another Federal advisory committee, another Federal Government source, or any other more cost-effective and less burdensome source:
The DoD Wage Committee is a Federal advisory committee that provides independent advice and recommendations on matters relating to the conduct of wage surveys and the establishment of wage schedules for all appropriated fund and non-appropriated fund wage areas of blue-collar employees within the Federal wage system. Members receive only travel and per diem reimbursement for official committee-related business.
6. If the consultation is a committee renewal, a summary of the previous accomplishments of the committee and the reasons it needs to continue:
The DoD Wage Committee meets bi-weekly to approve wage survey matters and pay schedule adjustments for 131 Appropriated Fund and 118 Nonappropriated Fund wage areas, with a population of over 240,000 crafts and trades employees. In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 5343(a)(3)
, a lead agency, DoD in this case, “shall conduct wage surveys, analyze wage survey data, and develop and establish appropriate wage schedules and rates for prevailing rate employees.”
Title 5 CFR
532.227(a) provides greater details of the requirement for a committee when it states, “shall establish an agency wage committee for the purpose of considering matters relating to the conduct of wage surveys, the establishment of wage schedules and making recommendations thereon to the lead agency.” The regulation then requires the lead agency to submit to the wage committee its data and analysis for the committee's consideration and recommendations. The Defense Civilian Personnel Advisory Service (DCPAS) also cannot commence wage change surveys without the DoD Wage Committee because
5 CFR 532.247(g)(2)
requires DoD to “consult with the agency wage committee” before it does so and then to consider “all of the information, analysis, and recommendations made available to it pursuant to this subpart.”
Title 5 CFR
532.245(a). Once approved, the pay schedule adjustments are then administered by DCPAS and distributed each pay period for use at all Federal agencies, not only DoD. Another provision at
5 CFR 532.307(c)
, requires the lead agency to submit survey matters to the wage committee to gain the committee's recommendations before ordering a full-scale survey
(
printed page 75837)
related to the determination of a dominant industry, which is used to ensure DoD is capturing relevant data compared to the workforce itself.
7.
Explanation of why the committee/subcommittee is essential to the conduct of agency business:
The DoD Wage Committee's work is directed by
5 CFR 532.209
,
532.227
,
532.231(e)
, and
532.243
and the Office of Personnel Management Operating Manual, Federal Wage System, Appropriated and Nonappropriated Funds, S3-2 Agency Level. The DoD Wage Committee shall: (a) consider and make recommendations to the DoD on any matter involved in developing specifications for a wage survey on which the DoD proposes not to accept the recommendations of a local wage survey committee and any matters on which a minority report has been filed; (b) consider the survey data, upon completion of a wage survey, of the local wage survey committee's report and recommendations, and the statistical analyses and proposed pay schedules derived from them, as well as any other data or recommendations pertinent to the survey, and recommends wage schedules to the pay-fixing authority; and (c) have a majority of the DoD Wage Committee to constitute a decision and recommendation of the DoD Wage Committee, but a member of the minority may file a report with the DoD Wage Committee's recommendations. Meetings are scheduled to be held approximately 24 times a year on a bi-weekly schedule to receive, review, and consider wage survey specifications; wage survey data; local wage survey committee reports and recommendations; and to approve wage schedule adjustments. Schedules are then issued on the same schedule throughout the year. The Committee is also critical in guaranteeing labor-management involvement in determining the wage schedules. Without these committee meetings, wage surveys would not occur and pay schedule adjustments would cease for the entire Federal Wage System (FWS) population.
Dated: November 20, 2026.

Alternate OSD Federal Register Liaison Officer, Department of Defense.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines on a country-wide basis that imports of certain corrosion-resistant steel products (CORE) completed in Indonesia using cold-rolled steel (CRS) manufactured in the Socialist Republic of Vietnam (Vietnam) are not circumventing the antidumping duty (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) orders on CORE from Vietnam. The period of inquiry is January 1, 2025, through December 31, 2025. Interested parties are invited to comment on this preliminary determination.
DATES:
Applicable November 24, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Natalie Jersa at (202) 482-6353 or Mark Ross at (202) 482-4794, Office of Policy, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On December 19, 2025, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the AD and CVD orders on CORE from Vietnam.
[
1
]
On March 25, 2026, Commerce initiated a country-wide circumvention inquiry pursuant to section 781(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), to determine whether imports of CORE completed in Indonesia using CRS manufactured in Vietnam are circumventing the
Orders,
and, accordingly, should be covered by the scope of the
Orders.
[
2
]
On April 9, 2026, Commerce issued quantity and value (Q&V) questionnaires to PT. AMNS (AMNS), PT. Sunrise Steel (Sunrise), and PT. Tata Metal Lestari (TML).
[
3
]
Between April 22 and 23, 2026, Commerce received timely responses from all three companies, in addition to one voluntary response from PT Aluminium Extrusion Indonesia (PT Alex Indo).
[
4
]
On July 28, 2026, Commerce extended the deadline to issue its preliminary determination by 60 days.
[
5
]
On October 9, 2026, Commerce extended the deadline to issue its preliminary determination by an additional 30 days.
[
6
]
Accordingly, the deadline for this preliminary determination is now November 20, 2026.
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this circumvention inquiry,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
7
]
The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS), which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov
.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/​frnotices
.
Scope of the Orders
The products covered by these
Orders
are certain flat-rolled steel products, either clad, plated, or coated with corrosion-resistant metals such as zinc, aluminum, or zinc-, aluminum-, nickel- or iron-based alloys, whether or not corrugated or painted, varnished, laminated, or coated with plastics or other non-metallic substances in addition to the metallic coating. For a full description of the scope of the
Orders, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
8
]
Merchandise Subject to the Circumvention Inquiry
This circumvention inquiry covers CORE completed in Indonesia using Vietnamese-origin CRS that is subsequently exported from Indonesia and imported into the United States (inquiry merchandise).
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this circumvention inquiry in accordance with section 781(b) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.226
. For a complete description of the methodology underlying the preliminary determination,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum. A list of topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is included in the appendix to this notice.
Preliminary Determination
As detailed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum, Commerce preliminarily determines that CORE completed in Indonesia using Vietnamese-origin CRS that is subsequently exported from Indonesia to the United States is not circumventing the
Orders
on a country-wide basis. Accordingly, in accordance with section 781(b) of the Act, Commerce is making a negative preliminary determination of circumvention of the
Orders.
Verification
As provided in 19 CFR 351.307, Commerce intends to verify information relied upon in making its final determination.
Public Comment
Because Commerce intends to conduct verification, a timeline for the submission of case briefs and written comments will be provided to interested parties at a later date regarding the deadline for submitting case briefs.
[
9
]
Rebuttal briefs, limited to issues raised in case briefs, may be submitted no later than seven days after the deadline for
(
printed page 75831)
case briefs.
[
10
]
Parties who submit case or rebuttal briefs in this proceeding are encouraged to submit with each argument: (1) a statement of the issue; (2) a brief summary of the argument; and (3) a table of authorities.
[
11
]
As provided under
19 CFR 351.309(c)(2)
and
(d)(2)
, we request that interested parties provide at the beginning of their briefs a public, executive summary for each issue raised in their briefs.
[
12
]
Further, we request that interested parties limit their executive summary of each issue to no more than 450 words, not including citations. We intend to use the executive summaries as the basis of the comment summaries included in the issues and decision memorandum that will accompany the final determination in this proceeding. We request that interested parties include footnotes for relevant citations in the executive summary of each issue. Note that Commerce has amended certain of its requirements pertaining to the service of documents in
19 CFR 351.303(f)
.
[
13
]
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.310(c)
, interested parties who wish to request a hearing must submit a written request to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance, U.S. Department of Commerce, within 30 days after the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
, filed electronically via ACCESS. Hearing requests should contain: (1) the party's name, address, and telephone number; (2) the number of participants and whether any participant is a foreign national; and (3) a list of the issues to be discussed. Issues raised in the hearing will be limited to issues raised in the respective comments.
[
14
]
If a request for a hearing is made, Commerce intends to hold the hearing at a date and time to be determined and will notify the parties through ACCESS.
[
15
]
Parties should confirm the date, time, and location of the hearing two days before the scheduled date.
All submissions, including affirmative and rebuttal comments, as well as hearing requests, should be filed using ACCESS. An electronically-filed document must be received successfully in its entirety by ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the established deadline.
Notification to Interested Parties
This determination is issued and published in accordance with section 781(b) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.226(g)(1)
.

[A-570-082; C-570-083]
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that imports of certain steel wheels (steel wheels), completed in the Socialist Republic of Vietnam (Vietnam) using hot-rolled steel (HRS) produced in the People's Republic of China (China), are circumventing the antidumping duty (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) orders on steel wheels from China. Interested parties are invited to comment on this preliminary determination.
DATES:
Applicable November 24, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Jacob Saude, AD/CVD Operations, Office VII, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-0981.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On May 24, 2019, Commerce published the AD and CVD orders on steel wheels from China.
[
1
]
On March 19, 2026, Commerce initiated a country-wide circumvention inquiry pursuant to section 781(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), to determine whether imports of steel wheels completed in Vietnam using HRS manufactured in China are circumventing the
Orders.
[
2
]
On August 10, 2026, Commerce selected NCC Vietnam Co., Ltd. (NCC Vietnam) as the mandatory respondent in this circumvention inquiry.
[
3
]
On August 14, 2026, pursuant to section 351.226(e)(1), Commerce extended the deadline for the preliminary determination by 83 days until November 9, 2026.
[
4
]
On November 6, pursuant to section 351.226(e)(1), Commerce extended the deadline for the preliminary determination by 7 days until November 16, 2026.
[
5
]
Accordingly, the deadline for this preliminary determination is now November 16, 2026.
For a detailed description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
6
]
A list of topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is attached as an appendix to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is available via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS), which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov
.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/​frnotices
.
Scope of the Orders
The merchandise subject to the
Orders
is certain steel wheels produced primarily from hot-rolled steel. For a complete description of the scope of the
Orders, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
7
]
Merchandise Subject to the Circumvention Inquiry
This circumvention inquiry covers steel wheels assembled and completed in Vietnam using Chinese-origin hot-rolled steel, that is subsequently exported from Vietnam to the United States (inquiry merchandise).
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this circumvention inquiry in accordance with section 781(b) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.226
. For a complete description of the methodology underlying the preliminary determination,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum. A list of topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is included as the appendix to this notice.
Preliminary Circumvention Determination
As detailed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum, Commerce preliminarily determines that steel wheels completed in Vietnam using Chinese-origin HRS and subsequently exported from Vietnam to the United States is circumventing the
Orders
on a country-wide basis. As a result, in accordance with section 781(b) of the Act, we preliminarily determine that this merchandise should be included within the scope of the
Orders. See
the “Suspension of Liquidation and Cash Deposit Requirements” section below for details regarding suspension of liquidation and cash deposit requirements.
Suspension of Liquidation and Cash Deposit Requirements
Based on the preliminary affirmative country-wide determination of circumvention with respect to Vietnam, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.226(l)(2), Commerce will direct U.S.
(
printed page 75829)
Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to suspend liquidation and to require a cash deposit of estimated duties on unliquidated entries of inquiry merchandise that were entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption, on or after March 19, 2026,
[
8
]
the date of initiation.
Steel wheels completed in Vietnam from HRS that are not of Chinese origin is not subject to this inquiry. Therefore, cash deposits are not required for such merchandise under the
China Orders.
However, Commerce preliminarily finds that steel wheels completed in Vietnam using China-origin HRS is circumventing the AD and CVD orders on steel wheels from China. Imports of steel wheels completed in Vietnam are subject to certification requirements, and cash deposits may be required.
Certifications
Considering our affirmative country-wide preliminary circumvention determination, Commerce preliminarily determines that no Vietnamese company, including NCC Vietnam, is currently ineligible to certify that individual entries of steel wheels are not subject to the collection of cash deposits. If any company, including NCC Vietnam, wishes to certify that its individual entries of steel wheels are not subject to the
Orders,
it must demonstrate to Commerce its eligibility and capability in a certification review. Upon reviewing any selected respondent in a future administrative review segment, or upon a company's request for a certification review within the context of the administrative review segment, Commerce will evaluate each individual company's certification eligibility, which may be subject to verification. This requirement will allow Commerce to better administer the country-wide circumvention determination and ensure accuracy of certifications following the publication of the
Final Determination
of this inquiry.
Public Comment
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.226(f)(4)
, case briefs or other written comments should be submitted to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance no later than 14 days after the date of the publication of this notice.
[
9
]
Rebuttal briefs, limited to issues raised in case briefs, may be submitted no later than seven days after the deadline for case briefs.
[
10
]
Parties who submit case or rebuttal briefs in this proceeding are encouraged to submit with each argument: (1) a statement of the issue; (2) a brief summary of the argument; and (3) a table of authorities. As provided under
19 CFR 351.309(c)(2)
and
(d)(2)
, we request that interested parties provide at the beginning of their briefs a public, executive summary for each issue raised in their briefs.
[
11
]
Further, we request that interested parties limit their executive summary of each issue to no more than 450 words, not including citations. We intend to use the executive summaries as the basis of the comment summaries included in the issues and decision memorandum that will accompany the final determination in this proceeding. We request that interested parties include footnotes for relevant citations in the executive summary of each issue. Note that Commerce has amended certain of its requirements pertaining to the service of documents in
19 CFR 351.303(f)
.
[
12
]
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.310(c)
, interested parties who wish to request a hearing must submit a written request to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance, U.S. Department of Commerce, within 30 days after the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
, filed electronically via ACCESS. Hearing requests should contain: (1) the party's name, address, and telephone number; (2) the number of participants and whether any participant is a foreign national; and (3) a list of the issues to be discussed. Issues raised in the hearing will be limited to issues raised in the respective comments.
[
13
]
If a request for a hearing is made, Commerce intends to hold the hearing at a date and time to be determined and will notify the parties through ACCESS.
[
14
]
Parties should confirm the date, time, and location of the hearing two days before the scheduled date.
All submissions, including affirmative and rebuttal comments, as well as hearing requests, should be filed using ACCESS. An electronically-filed document must be received successfully in its entirety by ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the established deadline.
U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) Notification
Consistent with section 781(e) of the Act, Commerce will notify the ITC of this preliminary determination to include the merchandise subject to this circumvention inquiry within the
Orders.
Pursuant to section 781(e) of the Act, the ITC may request consultations concerning Commerce's proposed inclusion of the inquiry merchandise. If, after consultations, the ITC believes that a significant injury issue is presented by the proposed inclusion, it will have 60 days from the date of notification by Commerce to provide written advice.
Notification to Interested Parties
This determination is issued and published in accordance with section 781(b) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.226(g)(1)
.
Dated: November 16, 2026.
Kasey O'Connor,
Deputy General Counsel, performing the non-exclusive functions and duties of the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines on a country-wide basis that imports of certain corrosion-resistant steel products (CORE) completed in Indonesia using hot-rolled steel (HRS) or cold-rolled steel (CRS) manufactured in the People's Republic of China (China) are not circumventing the antidumping duty (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) orders on CORE from China. The period of inquiry is January 1, 2021, through December 31, 2025. Interested parties are invited to comment on this preliminary determination.
DATES:
Applicable November 24, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Cassie Graham or Garrison Goetsch, Office of Policy, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-2159 or (202) 482-1606, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On July 25, 2016, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the AD and CVD orders on CORE from China.
[
1
]
On March 25, 2026, Commerce initiated a country-wide circumvention inquiry pursuant to section 781(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), to determine whether imports of CORE completed in Indonesia using HRS or CRS manufactured in China are circumventing the
Orders,
and, accordingly, should be covered by the scope of the
Orders.
[
2
]
On April 9, 2026, Commerce issued quantity and value (Q&V) questionnaires to PT. AMNS (AMNS), NS BlueScope Indonesia (NS BlueScope), PT. Sunrise Steel (Sunrise), and PT. Tata Metal Lestari (TML).
[
3
]
Between April 21 and 23, 2026, Commerce received timely responses to the Q&V questionnaire from all four companies, in addition to one voluntary response from PT Aluminium Extrusion Indonesia (PT Alex Indo).
[
4
]
On July 28,
(
printed page 75825)
2026, Commerce extended the deadline to issue its preliminary determination by 60 days.
[
5
]
On October 9, 2026, Commerce extended the deadline to issue its preliminary determination by an additional 30 days.
[
6
]
Accordingly, the deadline for this preliminary determination is now November 20, 2026.
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this circumvention inquiry,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
7
]
The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS), which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov
.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/​frnotices
.
Scope of the Orders
The products covered by these
Orders
are certain flat-rolled steel products, either clad, plated, or coated with corrosion-resistant metals such as zinc, aluminum, or zinc-, aluminum-, nickel- or iron-based alloys, whether or not corrugated or painted, varnished, laminated, or coated with plastics or other non-metallic substances in addition to the metallic coating. For a full description of the scope of the
Orders, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
8
]
Merchandise Subject to the Circumvention Inquiry
This circumvention inquiry covers CORE completed in Indonesia using Chinese-origin HRS or CRS that is subsequently exported from Indonesia and imported into the United States (inquiry merchandise).
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this circumvention inquiry in accordance with section 781(b) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.226
. For a complete description of the methodology underlying the preliminary determination,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum. A list of topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is included in the appendix to this notice.
Preliminary Determination
As detailed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum, Commerce preliminarily determines that CORE completed in Indonesia using Chinese-origin HRS or CRS that is subsequently exported from Indonesia to the United States is not circumventing the
Orders
on a country-wide basis. Accordingly, Commerce is making a negative preliminary finding of circumvention of the
Orders.
Verification
As provided in 19 CFR 351.307, Commerce intends to verify information relied upon in making its final determination.
Public Comment
Because Commerce intends to conduct verification, a timeline for the submission of case briefs and written comments will be provided to interested parties at a later date.
[
9
]
Rebuttal briefs, limited to issues raised in case briefs, may be submitted no later than seven days after the deadline for case briefs.
[
10
]
Parties who submit case or rebuttal briefs in this proceeding are encouraged to submit with each argument: (1) a statement of the issue; (2) a brief summary of the argument; and (3) a table of authorities.
[
11
]
As provided under
19 CFR 351.309(c)(2)(iii)
and
(d)(2)(iii)
, we request that interested parties provide at the beginning of their briefs a public executive summary for each issue raised in their briefs.
[
12
]
Further, we request that interested parties limit their executive summary of each issue to no more than 450 words, not including citations. We intend to use the executive summaries as the basis of the comment summaries included in the issues and decision memorandum that will accompany the final results in this administrative review. We request that interested parties include footnotes for relevant citations in the executive summary of each issue. Note that Commerce has amended certain of its requirements pertaining to the service of documents in
19 CFR 351.303(f)
.
[
13
]
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.310(c)
, interested parties who wish to request a hearing must submit a written request to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance, U.S. Department of Commerce, within 30 days after the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
, filed electronically via ACCESS. Hearing requests should contain: (1) the party's name, address, and telephone number; (2) the number of participants and whether any participant is a foreign national; and (3) a list of the issues to be discussed. Issues raised in the hearing will be limited to issues raised in the respective comments.
[
14
]
If a request for a hearing is made, Commerce intends to hold the hearing at a time and date to be determined and will notify the parties through ACCESS.
[
15
]
Parties should confirm the date, time, and location of the hearing two days before the scheduled date.
All submissions, including affirmative and rebuttal comments, as well as hearing requests, should be filed using ACCESS. An electronically-filed document must be received successfully in its entirety by ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the established deadline.
Notification to Interested Parties
This determination is issued and published in accordance with section 781(b) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.226(g)(1)
.
Dated: November 19, 2026.

AGENCY:

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) determines that producers/exporters subject to this review made sales of subject merchandise at less than normal value during the period of review (POR) August 1, 2024, through July 31, 2025.
DATES:
Applicable November 24, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Caroline Carroll, AD/CVD Operations, Office IX, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-4948.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On July 17, 2026, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the preliminary results of the 2024-2025 administrative review of the antidumping duty order on hydrofluorocarbon (HFC) blends from the People's Republic of China (China) and invited interested parties to comment.
[
1
]
We received no comments from interested parties on the
Preliminary Results.
Therefore, we made no changes from the
Preliminary Results,
and accordingly, there is no decision memorandum accompanying this notice. Commerce conducted this administrative review in accordance with section 751 of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).
Scope of the Order
[
2
]
The products covered by the
Order
are HFC blends from China. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the
Preliminary Results.
Final Results of Review
For the final results, we continue to find that, because the 12 companies listed in the appendix to this notice failed to establish their eligibility for a separate rate,
[
3
]
they are part of the China-wide entity. Because no party requested a review of the China-wide entity, the entity is not under review, and the entity's rate (
i.e.,
216.37 percent)
[
4
]
is not subject to change.
Disclosure
Normally, Commerce discloses to interested parties the calculations of the final results of an administrative review within five days of a public announcement or, if there is no public announcement, within five days of the date of publication of the final results in the
Federal Register
, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.224(b). However, because Commerce has not performed any calculations in this review, there are no calculations to disclose for these final results.
Assessment Rates
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.212(b)
, Commerce will determine, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate entries of subject merchandise in accordance with the final results of this review. Specifically, we will instruct CBP to liquidate entries all entries of subject merchandise exported by the companies listed in the Appendix to this notice during the POR at the rate for the China-wide entity (
i.e.,
216.37 percent).
Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of the final results in the
Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (
i.e.,
within 90 days of publication).
Cash Deposit Requirements

title: Loyalty and the Exclusive Purpose Rule in Selecting Plan Investments and Exercising Shareholder Rights
abstract: In this proposed rule, the Department of Labor (Department) clarifies the fiduciary duty of loyalty under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA). The proposed rule affirms that ERISA's duty of loyalty requires fiduciaries to act with the exclusive purpose of ensuring retirement security and providing promised benefits to plan participants and their beneficiaries. The amendments clarify the neutral application of ERISA's fiduciary duties of prudence and loyalty to selecting investments and investment courses of action, and to exercising shareholder rights, including proxy voting, the use of written proxy voting policies and guidelines, and shareholder engagement activities. The amendments would enhance the regulation by adding an affirmative expression of the duty of loyalty that is more consistent with the statute, and removing the tiebreaker test and participant preference provisions, which do not comport with the best reading of the statute and are susceptible to abuse, including use by a fiduciary as pretext to employ plan assets to pursue personal preferences or objectives unrelated to financial benefits under the plan. In the Department's view, the best reading of ERISA's exclusive purpose provision is and has always been that a plan fiduciary may not start with an ulterior motive or consider any factors collateral to plan participants' financial interests during any part of the process of making investment-selection decisions. The proposal would strengthen the fiduciary standards of pension and retirement plans covered by ERISA as instructed in President Trump's Executive Order 14366, Protecting American Investors from Foreign-Owned and Politically Motivated Proxy Advisors.
dates: Comments on the proposal must be submitted on or before January 25, 2027.

SUMMARY:
In this proposed rule, the Department of Labor (Department) clarifies the fiduciary duty of loyalty under the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA). The proposed rule affirms that ERISA's duty of loyalty requires fiduciaries to act with the exclusive purpose of ensuring retirement security and providing promised benefits to plan participants and their beneficiaries. The amendments clarify the neutral application of ERISA's fiduciary duties of prudence and loyalty to selecting investments and investment courses of action, and to exercising shareholder rights, including proxy voting, the use of written proxy voting policies and guidelines, and shareholder engagement activities. The amendments would enhance the regulation by adding an affirmative expression of the duty of loyalty that is more consistent with the statute, and removing the tiebreaker test and participant preference provisions, which do not comport with the best reading of the statute and are susceptible to abuse, including use by a fiduciary as pretext to employ plan assets to pursue personal preferences or objectives unrelated to financial benefits under the plan. In the Department's view, the best reading of ERISA's exclusive purpose provision is and has always been that a plan fiduciary may not start with an ulterior motive or consider any factors collateral to plan participants' financial interests during any part of the process of making investment-selection decisions. The proposal would strengthen the fiduciary standards of pension and retirement plans covered by ERISA as instructed in President Trump's
Executive Order 14366
,
Protecting American Investors from Foreign-Owned and Politically Motivated Proxy Advisors.

A. Executive Summary

The Department has addressed these standards previously in regulatory and sub-regulatory guidance, including the Department's Investment Duties regulation at
29 CFR 2550.404a-1
(Investment Duties regulation), which has been amended several times in recent years. The Department believes that further amendments are needed to ensure that the regulation is based on the best reading of the ERISA statute and is consistent with the statute's purposes.
The proposal would restore neutrality to the Investment Duties regulation by removing terminology associated with environmental, social and governance (ESG) issues, which has become the subject of substantial public controversy and political attention. By clarifying that ERISA neither favors nor disfavors any investment objective or investment strategy, the proposal would depoliticize ESG issues under ERISA, add long-term stability to the regulation, and bolster confidence of plan fiduciaries in the conduct of their ERISA-regulated activities. The proposal also would enhance the protectiveness
(
printed page 75987)
of the regulation by adding an affirmative expression of the duty of loyalty that is more consistent with ERISA's plain language, and by removing provisions that are susceptible to abuse and may be employed by a fiduciary as pretext to use plan assets in pursuit of personal preferences or objectives unrelated to financial benefits under the plan. In addition, the proposal supplements the notice of proposed rulemaking entitled Fiduciary Duties in Selecting Designated Investment Alternatives (“Investment Selection NPRM”), published on March 31, 2026, which addressed a fiduciary's duty of prudence under ERISA in selecting investment options for a participant-directed individual account plan.
[
2
]
The preamble to the Investment Selection NPRM stated that “nothing in [that proposal] excuses a fiduciary from complying with its obligations to act loyally or avoid prohibited conflicts of interest under sections 404(a)(1)(A) or 406 of ERISA respectively.”
[
3
]
This proposal would clarify ERISA's fiduciary duty of loyalty. Finally, consistent with
Executive Order 14366
,
Protecting American Investors from Foreign-Owned and Politically Motivated Proxy Advisors,
the proposal would more clearly articulate that ERISA's fiduciary duties apply broadly to the exercise of shareholder rights including both proxy voting and shareholder engagement activities.
[
4
]
B. Background and Purpose of Regulatory Action
1. General
Title I of ERISA establishes minimum standards that govern the operation of private-sector employee benefit plans, including fiduciary responsibilities. Section 404 of ERISA requires that plan fiduciaries act prudently and diversify plan investments so as to minimize the risk of large losses, unless under the circumstances it is clearly prudent not to do so.
[
5
]
Sections 403(c) and 404(a) also require fiduciaries to act solely in the interest of the plan's participants and beneficiaries, and for the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to participants and beneficiaries and defraying reasonable expenses of administering the plan.
[
6
]
2. Sub-regulatory Guidance.
2.1. Collateral Effects and Interests in Investment Decisions
Over the years the Department has issued sub-regulatory guidance, such as interpretive bulletins, advisory opinions, information and other letters, to assist plan fiduciaries in understanding their obligations under ERISA with respect to investment decisions involving interests apart from investment return. The sub-regulatory guidance has articulated broad principles governing a fiduciary's ability to consider effects collateral to investment return in making pension plan investments. The Department's guidance generally concluded that ERISA's duty of loyalty does not categorically prohibit consideration of collateral interests in a fiduciary's evaluation of a particular investment opportunity, but the existence of such collateral interests can be considered in evaluating the investment only if the fiduciary determines that the investment is appropriate for the plan, taking into account the role the particular investment plays in the plan's investment portfolio, and is expected to provide an investment return to the plan commensurate to other available investments having similar risks.
[
7
]
In 1994, the Department published Interpretive Bulletin 94-1 (IB 94-1), which addressed economically targeted investments (ETIs) selected, in part, for collateral interests apart from the investment return to the plan investor.
[
8
]
The Department's objective in issuing IB 94-1 was to state that ETIs
[
9
]
are not inherently incompatible with ERISA's fiduciary obligations. The preamble to IB 94-1 explained that the requirements of sections 403 and 404 of ERISA do not prevent plan fiduciaries from investing plan assets in ETIs if the investment has an expected rate of return at least commensurate to rates of return of available alternative investments, and if the ETI is otherwise an appropriate investment for the plan in terms of such factors as diversification and the investment policy of the plan. Some commentators have referred to this as the “all things being equal” test or the “tiebreaker” standard. The Department stated in the preamble to IB 94-1 that when competing investments serve the plan's economic interests to an equivalent degree, plan fiduciaries can use such collateral considerations as the deciding factor for an investment decision.
In 2008, Interpretive Bulletin 2008-01 (IB 2008-01) superseded IB 94-1,
[
10
]
and then, in 2015, Interpretive Bulletin 2015-01 (IB 2015-01) superseded IB 2008-01.
[
11
]
Although the Interpretive Bulletins differed in tone and framing, each included the “all things being equal” test, while also stressing that the focus of plan fiduciaries on the plan's financial returns and on providing promised benefits to participants and beneficiaries may never be subordinated to collateral interests. Each Interpretive Bulletin also cautioned that fiduciaries violate ERISA if they accept reduced risk-adjusted returns in pursuing social, environmental, or other policy goals or any other collateral interests.
The preamble to IB 2015-01 additionally explained that if a fiduciary prudently determines that an investment is appropriate based solely on economic considerations, including those that may derive from ESG factors, the fiduciary may make the investment without regard to any collateral interests the investment may also promote. In Field Assistance Bulletin 2018-01 (FAB 2018-01), the Department indicated that IB 2015-01 had recognized that there could be instances when ESG issues present business risks or opportunities to companies that officers and directors need to manage as part of the company's
(
printed page 75988)
business plan, and that qualified investment professionals would treat the issues as significant economic considerations under generally accepted investment theories.
[
12
]
The FAB further stated that when they are appropriate economic considerations, such ESG issues should be considered by a prudent fiduciary along with other relevant economic factors to evaluate the risk and return profiles of alternative investments. In other words, in these instances, the Department viewed these factors not as “tiebreakers,” but “risk-return” factors affecting the economic merits of the investment.
FAB 2018-01 cautioned, however, that “[t]o the extent ESG factors, in fact, involve business risks or opportunities that are properly treated as economic considerations themselves in evaluating alternative investments, the weight given to those factors should also be appropriate to the relative level of risk and return involved compared to other relevant economic factors.”
[
13
]
FAB 2018-01 also emphasized that fiduciaries “must not too readily treat ESG factors as economically relevant to the particular investment choices at issue when making a decision,” as “[i]t does not ineluctably follow from the fact that an investment promotes ESG factors, or that it arguably promotes positive general market trends or industry growth, that the investment is a prudent choice for retirement or other investors.” Rather, ERISA fiduciaries must always put first the economic interests of the plan in providing retirement benefits, and “[a] fiduciary's evaluation of the economics of an investment should be focused on financial factors that have a material effect on the return and risk of an investment based on appropriate investment horizons consistent with the plan's articulated funding and investment objectives.”
[
14
]
FAB 2018-01 also explained that in the case of an investment platform that allows participants and beneficiaries an opportunity to choose from a range of investment alternatives, a prudently selected, well managed, and properly diversified ESG-themed investment alternative could be added to the available investment options on the 401(k) platform without requiring the plan to remove or forgo adding other non-ESG-themed investment options to the platform.
[
15
]
As stated in the FAB, however, the selection of an investment fund as a qualified default investment alternative (QDIA)
[
16
]
is not analogous to a fiduciary's decision to offer participants an additional investment alternative as part of a prudently constructed lineup of investment alternatives from which participants may choose. The FAB expressed concern that the decision to favor the fiduciary's own policy preferences in selecting an ESG-themed investment option as a QDIA for a 401(k)-type plan without regard to possibly different or competing views of plan participants and beneficiaries would raise questions about the fiduciary's compliance with ERISA's duty of loyalty.
[
17
]
In addition the FAB stated that, even if consideration of such factors could be shown to be appropriate in the selection of a QDIA for a particular plan population, the plan's fiduciaries would have to ensure compliance with the previous guidance in IB 2015-01. For example, the selection of an ESG-themed target date fund as a QDIA would not be prudent if the fund would provide a lower expected rate of return than available non-ESG alternative target date funds with commensurate degrees of risk, or if the fund would be riskier than available non-ESG alternative target date funds with commensurate rates of return.
2.2. Proxy Voting
The Department's past sub-regulatory guidance has consistently recognized that the fiduciary act of managing employee benefit plan assets includes the management of voting rights, as well as other shareholder rights connected to shares of stock, and that management of those rights, and shareholder engagement activities, is subject to ERISA's prudence and loyalty requirements.
The Department first issued sub-regulatory guidance on proxy voting and the exercise of shareholder rights in the 1980s. For example, in 1988, the Department issued an opinion letter to Avon Products, Inc. (the Avon Letter), in which the Department took the position that the fiduciary act of managing plan assets that are shares of corporate stock includes the voting of proxies appurtenant to those shares, and that the named fiduciary of a plan has a duty to monitor decisions made and actions taken by investment managers with regard to proxy voting.
[
18
]
In 1994, the Department issued its first interpretive bulletin on proxy voting, Interpretive Bulletin 94-2 (IB 94-2).
[
19
]
IB 94-2 recognized that fiduciaries may engage in shareholder activities intended to monitor or influence corporate management if the responsible fiduciary concludes that, after taking into account the costs involved, there is a reasonable expectation that such shareholder activities (by the plan alone or together with other shareholders) will enhance the value of the plan's investment in the corporation. The Department also reiterated its view that ERISA does not permit fiduciaries, in voting proxies or engaging in other shareholder activities, such as “monitoring or communication” with corporate management (now commonly known as corporate engagement or shareholder engagement, whether such engagement activities are limited to corporate management or extend to other shareholders, advisors, or third persons), to subordinate the economic interests of participants and beneficiaries to unrelated objectives.
In October 2008, the Department replaced IB 94-2 with Interpretive Bulletin 2008-02 (IB 2008-02).
[
20
]
The Department's intent was to update the guidance in IB 94-2 and to reflect interpretive positions issued by the Department after 1994 on shareholder engagement and socially directed proxy voting initiatives. IB 2008-02 stated that fiduciaries' responsibility for managing proxies includes both deciding to vote and deciding not to vote.
[
21
]
It further stated that the fiduciary duties described at ERISA sections 404(a)(1)(A) and (B) require that in voting proxies the responsible fiduciary shall consider only those factors that relate to the economic value of the plan's investment and shall not subordinate the interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income to unrelated objectives. In addition, IB 2008-02 stated that votes shall be cast only in accordance with a plan's economic
(
printed page 75989)
interests, and further
[
22
]
explained that if the responsible fiduciary reasonably determines that the cost of voting (including the cost of research, if necessary, to determine how to vote) is likely to exceed the expected economic benefits of voting, the fiduciary has an obligation to refrain from voting. The Department warned that “[p]lan fiduciaries risk violating the exclusive purpose rule when they exercise their fiduciary authority in an attempt to further legislative, regulatory or public policy issues through the proxy process.”
[
23
]
The Department reiterated in IB 2008-02 that any use of plan assets by a plan fiduciary to further political or social causes “that have no connection to enhancing the economic value of the plan's investment” through proxy voting or shareholder activism is a violation of ERISA's exclusive purpose and prudence requirements.
[
24
]
In 2016, the Department issued Interpretive Bulletin 2016-01 (IB 2016-01), which reinstated the language of IB 94-2 with certain modifications.
[
25
]
IB 2016-01 reiterated and confirmed that “in voting proxies, the responsible fiduciary [must] consider those factors that may affect the value of the plan's investment and not subordinate the interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income to unrelated objectives.”
[
26
]
In its guidance, the Department has also stated that it rejects a construction of ERISA that would render the statute's tight limits on the use of plan assets illusory and that would permit plan fiduciaries to expend trust assets to promote myriad personal public policy preferences at the expense of participants' economic interests, including through shareholder engagement activities, voting proxies, or other investment policies.
[
27
]
3. Regulatory Guidance
The Department's Investment Duties regulation at
29 CFR 2550.404a-1
was originally adopted in 1979 to provide guidance on ERISA's fiduciary duty of prudence under ERISA section 404(a)(1)(B) with respect to investments and investment courses of action.
[
28
]
3.1. 2020 Final Rules
In 2020, the Department published two final rules (2020 final rules) that amended the Investment Duties regulation. The Department's objective was to address perceived confusion about the implications of its non-regulatory guidance with respect to ESG considerations, shareholder rights, and proxy voting.
[
29
]
The Department noted, for instance, that confusion with respect to ESG investing issues appeared to persist, potentially generated in part by the different iterations of the sub-regulatory guidance. The Department also expressed concern that current ESG trends suggested that plan fiduciaries may make investment decisions for purposes distinct from the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to participants and beneficiaries and defraying reasonable expenses of administering the plan, in violation of their fiduciary duty of loyalty. The Department further noted that marketers may be inappropriately targeting 401(k)-type plans covered by ERISA for investment products represented to promote perceived interests and goals unrelated to financial performance, and, as a result, participants may be offered funds that accept lower returns or higher investment risks to pursue ESG objectives.
In a final rule published in November 2020, the Department amended the Investment Duties regulation to generally require plan fiduciaries to select investments and investment courses of action based solely on consideration of “pecuniary factors.”
[
30
]
The final rule also added a specific requirement for fiduciaries to consider reasonably available alternatives to meet their prudence duties under ERISA with respect to an investment or investment course of action. It furthermore added regulatory text setting forth required investment analysis and documentation requirements for those circumstances in which plan fiduciaries may use non-pecuniary factors when choosing between or among investments that the fiduciary is unable to distinguish on the basis of pecuniary factors alone (
i.e.,
there is a “tie”). It added a provision expressly providing that, in the case of selecting or retaining designated investment alternatives for an individual account plan that allows plan participants and beneficiaries to choose from a broad range of investment alternatives, a fiduciary would not be prohibited from considering or including an investment alternative solely because it promotes, seeks, or supports one or more non-pecuniary goals. However, the provision prohibited plans from adding or retaining any investment as a QDIA, or as a component of such a QDIA, if the investment includes, considers, or indicates the use of one or more non-pecuniary objectives in its investment objectives or goals or its principal investment strategies.
In December 2020, the Department published a final rule that further amended the Investment Duties regulation by adding provisions that address the duties of ERISA fiduciaries with respect to the exercise of shareholder rights (including shareholder engagement and proxy voting), adoption of proxy voting policies and guidelines, and the selection and monitoring of proxy advisory firms.
[
31
]
The preamble to the final rule indicated a concern that there was a misunderstanding that fiduciaries must vote all proxies.
[
32
]
Accordingly, the final rule included specific language indicating that fiduciaries are not required to vote every proxy. It also included a “safe harbor” provision pursuant to which plan fiduciaries could adopt proxy voting policies and parameters prudently designed to serve the plan's economic interest that provide optional means for satisfying their fiduciary duties of loyalty under ERISA.
3.2. 2022 Final Rule
Following publication of the 2020 final rules, the Department heard from a variety of stakeholders who voiced questions and concerns about the 2020 final rules. In October 2021, the Department published a proposed rule to amend the Investment Duties regulation in response to some of those concerns.
[
33
]
In December 2022, the Department published a final rule amending the Investment Duties regulation (2022 final rule).
[
34
]
The 2022 final rule kept in place the longstanding principles that the duties of prudence and loyalty require ERISA plan fiduciaries to focus on relevant risk-return factors and not subordinate the interests of participants and beneficiaries to objectives unrelated to the provision of benefits under the plan such as by sacrificing investment returns or taking on additional investment risks. It also retained the core principle that when a plan's assets include shares of stock, the fiduciary duty to manage plan assets includes the management of shareholder rights
(
printed page 75990)
related to those shares, such as the right to vote proxies.
The 2022 final rule, however, also effectively rescinded or modified certain amendments that were adopted by the 2020 final rules. Among other things, the 2022 final rule:
Removed the “pecuniary/non-pecuniary” terminology and added language providing that a fiduciary's determination with respect to an investment or investment course of action must be based on factors that the fiduciary reasonably determines are relevant to a risk and return analysis, and also added that such factors may include the economic effects of climate change and other environmental, social, or governance factors on the particular investment or investment course of action.
Removed the stricter rules for QDIAs, so that the same standards apply to QDIAs as to investments generally.
Amended the “tiebreaker” test with a restated standard that required the fiduciary to conclude prudently that competing investments, or competing investment courses of action, equally serve the financial interests of the plan over the appropriate time horizon and provided that the fiduciary is not prohibited from selecting the investment, or investment course of action, based on collateral interests other than investment returns, and removed the special documentation requirements.
Added a provision stating that fiduciaries do not violate their duty of loyalty solely because they take participants' preferences into account when constructing a menu of prudent investment options for participant-directed individual account plans.
Eliminated the statement that the fiduciary duty to manage shareholder rights appurtenant to shares of stock does not require the voting of every proxy or the exercise of every shareholder right.
Eliminated specific requirements on maintaining records on proxy voting activities and monitoring obligations when using investment managers or proxy advisory firms.
3.3. Litigation Challenging the 2022 Final Rule
Multiple States and private parties sued the Department in Federal court, challenging the 2022 final rule as arbitrary and capricious under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and contrary to ERISA and the major questions doctrine.
[
35
]
Specifically, the plaintiffs alleged that the 2022 final rule's tiebreaker provision breached ERISA's “exclusive purpose” duty.
[
36 37
]
The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Texas entered summary judgment for the Department, finding that the rule was neither contrary to ERISA nor to the major questions doctrine, and that it was not arbitrary or capricious. In so holding, the court deferred to the Department's interpretation of section 404 as reasonable, under the then-binding
Chevron
deference standard.
[
38
]
Plaintiffs appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. While the appeal was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court issued its decision in
Loper Bright Enterprises
v.
Raimondo,
603 U.S. 369 (2024), which overturned
Chevron's
deference standard. In response, the Fifth Circuit vacated the district court's judgment (which had relied on
Chevron
) and remanded the case, directing the district court to reconsider the plaintiffs' challenge in light of
Loper Bright.
[
39
]
On remand, the court held that
Loper Bright
did not impact its previous reasoning that the 2022 final rule is not arbitrary or capricious or violative of the major questions doctrine. As to the 2022 final rule's tiebreaker standard, the district court, applying
Loper Bright
and exercising its independent judgment, concluded the tiebreaker provision is not contrary to section 404's exclusive purpose duty. The court reasoned, the “2022 Rule does not permit a fiduciary to act for other interests than the beneficiaries' or for other purposes than the beneficiaries' financial benefit.”
[
40
]
The court again granted summary judgment for the Department and upheld the 2022 final rule.
4.
Executive Order 14366
On December 11, 2025, President Trump issued
Executive Order 14366
,
Protecting American Investors from Foreign-Owned and Politically Motivated Proxy Advisors.
[
41
]
E.O. 14366
indicates that two firms control more than 90 percent of the proxy advisor market. The two firms advise their clients about how to vote the enormous numbers of shares their clients hold and manage on behalf of millions of Americans in mutual funds and exchange traded funds. They wield enormous influence over corporate governance matters, including shareholder proposals, board composition, and executive compensation, as well as over the capital markets and the value of Americans' investments more generally, including 401(k)s, IRAs, and other retirement investment vehicles. According to

[
42

instructed the Secretary of Labor, consistent with the Administrative Procedure Act, take steps to revise all regulations and guidance regarding the fiduciary status of individuals who manage, or, like proxy advisors, advise those who manage, the rights appurtenant to shares held by plans covered under ERISA, including proxy votes and corporate engagement, consistent with the policy of the order. It also directed the Secretary of Labor to strengthen ERISA fiduciary rules and increase fiduciaries' transparency regarding their use of proxy advisors, ensuring proxy advisors and plan managers act solely in the financial interest of American workers and retirees.
[
