]
C. Review of Current Regulation and Reasons for Change
The Department believes that, independent of the judgment in the litigation, select portions of the 2022 final rule may be construed as promoting investments with ESG-related investment strategies over other investments, contrary to the best reading of the ERISA statute. In singling out investments with ESG-related investment strategies as particularly appropriate for plans, the Department believes the 2022 final rule contravenes
(
printed page 75991)
ERISA's historical neutrality standard which neither favors nor disfavors specific investment categories or classes. Favoring investments with ESG-related investment strategies in this way impermissibly suggests that nonfinancial factors (
i.e.,
mixed motivations) may be introduced into investment decisions in violation of both the plain meaning of ERISA and the U.S. Supreme Court's interpretation of ERISA, which firmly establish that fiduciaries can consider only the benefits investments provide to plan participants and beneficiaries and plan participants' financial interests when making such decisions.
The Department has also reconsidered the viability of the so-called tiebreaker rule. The best reading of ERISA's duty of loyalty is and has always been that fiduciaries cannot consider issues and interests collateral to plan participants' financial interests and benefits during any part of the process they use to select investments. On its face, the tiebreaker rule permits just that. It therefore does not comport with the best reading of ERISA, and the Department believes that it should be rescinded.
Furthermore, the Department is concerned that the tiebreaker rule has facilitated fiduciaries' ability to conceal disloyal or otherwise suspect investment decisions. To the limited extent that any two proposed investments would possibly present identical risk-adjusted return profiles (
i.e.,
“ties”), which would be the first step before the application of any purported “tiebreaker rule” for fiduciaries to consider collateral interests, investment selection must not operate such that nefarious actors can more easily disguise illegal loyalty breaches. Accordingly, some parties may have manufactured ties that did not exist as a pretext to make investment decisions that are otherwise impermissible under ERISA. Removing the tiebreaker rule will remove the incentive and opportunity for bad actors to engage in such pretextual behavior. The discussion of ESG in the 2022 final rule, when combined with the tiebreaker provision, also may have been interpreted by some persons as suggesting that nonfinancial factors can be introduced into fiduciary investment decisions. Such a construction would, in the Department's view, be in clear conflict with the plain language of the exclusive purpose requirement in ERISA.
Similarly, the Department is also concerned that language stating that a “fiduciary may not subordinate the interests of the participants and beneficiaries” does not capture the plain language or intent of ERISA, which establishes a more rigorous investment standard. A key point underlying the district court's decision, and its analogy to a driver choosing the more scenic of two roads to its destination (discussed further below), is that the duty of loyalty under ERISA requires a fiduciary to start with a proper purpose—the fastest route in that analogy—and as the driver may not conduct the route selection with an eye on their scenic qualities, neither may the ERISA fiduciary keep in mind ulterior motives when making investment decisions. Just like a driver may not choose the fastest of the scenic routes, a fiduciary cannot choose the most financially rewarding of a limited pool of investments assembled because of their social impact. That is an improper purpose. And as ERISA's text makes clear, a fiduciary must begin with and maintain an exclusive focus on participant's financial benefits under the plan throughout the investment selection process. ERISA requires fiduciaries to consider only plan participants' financial interest, not simply that they avoid placing any other interest above it.
[
44
]
Thus, the Department is considering replacing the anti-subordination language with ERISA's more affirmative exclusive purpose construction.
A further concern is that the participant preferences portion of the rule also has sown confusion for plan fiduciaries. The language creates a kind of trap for the unwary to the extent it is taken to suggest that the consideration of participant preferences in the selection of a plan investment menu is an acceptable proxy for a rigorous consideration and determination on the economic merits. In selecting plan investment options, plan fiduciaries must act in participants' best interests even if plan participants might make different choices left to their own devices. The Department is concerned that this provision could be exploited by promotors, consultants, investment providers, and others who may market investments with ESG-related investment strategies to suggest to their plan sponsor clients that such funds with poor financial performance and/or high fees may be selected if enough plan participants want them. While this would be a misinterpretation of the existing regulatory standard, the Department is concerned that this misinterpretation may be widespread, which would be understandable given how the standard is currently articulated. The individual or collective preferences of participants can have no bearing on the fiduciary duties of plan sponsors under ERISA, and cannot determine whether an investment is objectively preferable to another.
D. Discussion of the Proposed Rule
1. Paragraph (b)(4) of the Proposal
The proposal would amend paragraph (b)(4) of the 2022 rule by removing “[r]isk and return factors may include the economic effects of climate change and other environmental, social, or governance factors on the particular investment or investment course of action.” This language was added to the 2022 rule primarily because the Department wanted to clarify that, in some instances, depending upon the individual facts and circumstances, climate change and other environmental, social, or governance factors may be relevant in a risk-return analysis of an investment.
[
45
]
The intent of paragraph (b)(4) of the 2022 rule was to address stakeholders' assertions that the 2020 rule effectively chilled the market with respect to consideration of any climate change and other environmental, social or governance factors irrespective of whether the consideration of climate change and other environmental, social, or governance factors may have been particularly relevant in a risk-return analysis of an investment or investment course of action.
[
46
]
The proposal would remove this language because it may be misconstrued as suggesting that these factors (climate change and other environmental, social, or governance factors) are likely to be risk and return factors in any number of significant cases. While such factors can be relevant in some contexts, for example, where they present investment risks, the Department does not want to give the impression that they are in all or even most investment-selection decisions. Put differently, the Department is concerned that the 2022 clarification—with its explicit mention of these undefined and politically-loaded terms—has or will have had the effect of promoting, endorsing, or even encouraging investment behavior based on social or nonfinancial factors, distinctly independent from the economic merits of the investment at issue. The Department's intent is to restore neutrality and remove any perceived governmental approval of or
(
printed page 75992)
preference for these factors absent economic merit.
The Department is hopeful that, by restoring neutrality through the removal of unnecessary references to ESG, the proposal will depoliticize this topic under ERISA. In this regard, the Department takes notice that ESG considerations have become the subject of substantial public controversy and legislative attention. Congress passed a joint resolution under the Congressional Review Act to disapprove the 2022 rule, which the President vetoed.
[
47
]
Several States have also enacted measures addressing ESG-related investing, ESG-related proxy voting, public pension decisions, or financial relationships with firms deemed to engage in boycotts of certain industries. Although State laws do not control the interpretation of ERISA, these developments underscore the degree to which the regulatory language itself has become contested and may distract from the neutral, unbiased fiduciary principles established by Congress in ERISA.
Likewise, the Department believes that neutral regulatory language would improve administrability. ERISA fiduciaries, service providers, and courts are familiar with the concepts of prudence, loyalty, diversification, and financial materiality. A regulation organized around those concepts may be easier to apply than one that is read through the lens of broader public debates about ESG. In the Department's view, regulatory clarity is especially important in the retirement plan context, where fiduciaries must make decisions on behalf of participants and beneficiaries whose interests are protected by ERISA's exclusive-purpose framework.
The Department further believes that removing ESG-associated language would better highlight ERISA's exclusive-purpose rule. The statutory question is whether fiduciaries are acting to provide benefits to participants and beneficiaries and to defray reasonable expenses of administering the plan. The Department is concerned that continued reference to ESG may, in some circumstances, be interpreted as signaling that collateral social or policy goals are independently relevant under ERISA. The Department does not believe that is the proper reading of the statute. Under the proposal, the regulation would more clearly state that the fiduciary's inquiry must remain tied to the economic interests of the plan participants.
In light of foregoing, the Department believes it is appropriate to propose amendments that remove ESG-associated language from paragraph (b)(4) of the current rule, while preserving fiduciaries' ability to consider all financially relevant information. By removing ESG-associated references, the proposal would clarify that ERISA neither favors nor disfavors any investment label or ideology. Rather, the regulation would focus on the fiduciary process required by statute that looks exclusively to plan participants' financial interests.
The Department stresses, however, that the proposed amendment would not create a categorical prohibition on considering any type of information. Proposed paragraph (b)(4) includes identical language from paragraph (b)(4) of the current regulation providing that a fiduciary's determination with respect to an investment or investment course of action must be based on factors that the fiduciary reasonably determines are relevant to a risk and return analysis, and that whether any particular consideration is a risk-return factor depends on the individual facts and circumstances. Thus, under the proposal, a fiduciary may consider any factor that the fiduciary reasonably determines is relevant to the risk-and-return analysis. The proposal is intended to remove potential distractions, not to prevent fiduciaries from analyzing financially relevant facts. This neutral framework would give a fiduciary flexibility and discretion in engaging in an objective and thorough investment analysis as it encounters new risks and opportunities, and as investments and the investment marketplace change over time. It would not, based on mere labels, impose limits that automatically force a fiduciary to question soundly-reasoned investment approaches taken by other market participants, or to analyze investments differently than how other investors would. Instead, as with all other decisions under ERISA, it would give fiduciaries the flexibility to consider the relevant information under the circumstances to act in plan participants' financial interest. If adopted, plan fiduciaries would be required to comply with this rule for both new and existing investments by using the ongoing investment monitoring that ERISA requires to ensure that both comply with the final rule. To be clear, the proposed rule does not necessarily require fiduciaries to divest or terminate any existing investment, investment course of action, or designated investment alternative. This proposed rule will apply only prospectively. Fiduciaries should do what they must always do under ERISA: continually evaluate their investments for their consistency with plan participants' and beneficiaries' financial interests and the Department's best interpretation of ERISA's duty of loyalty, as set forth in this rule.
At the same time, however, this proposed rule's prospective application does not immunize fiduciaries' actions and investment selections prior to the rule's effectiveness from enforcement actions and potential liability under ERISA provisions, duties, or mandates. Consistent with the relevant statutes of limitation, regulated entities must not construe this rule to reduce the Department's ability to investigate and prosecute fiduciaries for actions that were illegal while the prior rules were in effect. To that end, the Department recognizes the reliance interests that fiduciaries might have had related to how they may have made investment decisions based on any flawed interpretation of the best reading of ERISA's duty of loyalty subsequent to the 2022 final rule. The Department seeks comments regarding these reliance interests associated with the 2022 rule and the interaction of the regulatory text with prior investment decisions.
Relatedly, the Department seeks comments on what has caused the large outflow from ESG funds in recent years, and more specifically, whether this trend is reflected in ERISA plan investments.
2. Paragraph (c)(1) of the Proposal
The proposal would amend paragraph (c)(1) of the 2022 rule by removing the phrase “may not subordinate” and replacing it with “shall discharge his duties with respect to the plan with the exclusive purpose of maximizing.” Thus, in its entirety, paragraph (c)(1) of the proposal would read as follows: “A fiduciary shall discharge his duties with respect to the plan with the exclusive purpose of maximizing the interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan, and may not sacrifice investment return or take on additional investment risk to promote benefits or goals unrelated to financial interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan.”
The intent of these proposed changes is to enhance the protectiveness of the regulation by better aligning it with the text of ERISA. In particular, section 404(a)(1)(A) of ERISA, in relevant part, provides that “a fiduciary shall
(
printed page 75993)
discharge his duties with respect to the plan solely in the interests of the participants and beneficiaries and for the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to participants and their beneficiaries.”
[
48
]
While the more limited anti-subordination language has been the Department's sub-regulatory position for more than 30 years and regulatory position for 6 years, the statutory text of section 404(a)(1)(A) plainly demands a more rigorous, financially-motivated standard when selecting investments than simply “not subordinating” participants' financial interests to nonfinancial objectives.
[
49
]
And although the anti-subordination language has been used as support for the Department's tiebreaker test, as explained below, this proposal would eliminate the tiebreaker test. The new language also reflects the best reading of the statute.
The current regulation's loyalty provision, at paragraph (c)(1), contains two prohibitions: first, against subordination of participants' interests to other objectives; second, against sacrificing return or taking on additional risk to promote goals unrelated to participants and beneficiaries. Because the provision is limited to setting forth prohibitions, it merely identifies conduct that would violate ERISA's loyalty requirement. This prohibition-based formulation may be misconceived as permitting consideration of collateral objectives so long as participants' financial interests are not ultimately subordinated.
The proposed amendment, by contrast, sets forth a more affirmative expression of the duty of loyalty under ERISA. This more affirmative expression of ERISA's duty of loyalty is framed not as an abstract duty to “maximize” returns without regard to other fiduciary constraints, but as a duty to maximize participants' and beneficiaries' financial interests on a risk-adjusted basis, consistent with the plan documents and ERISA's prudence, diversification and expense limitations.
The Supreme Court has explained that ERISA's fiduciary standards have their origins in the common law of trusts,
[
50
]
and the Second Circuit has stated that these standards require fiduciaries to act with an “eye single to the interests of the participants and beneficiaries.”
[
51
]
As the Supreme Court explained when interpreting the National Labor Relations Act's similar duty of loyalty, “[a] fiduciary cannot contend that, although he had conflicting interests, he served his masters equally well or that his primary loyalty was not weakened by the pull of his secondary one.”
[
52
]
They have also held that fiduciaries may not permit “union, employer or self interests” to influence plan administration.
[
53
]
The Supreme Court has likewise emphasized that ERISA incorporates the duty of prudence, again with its origin in trust law, including an ongoing obligation to monitor investments and remove imprudent ones,
[
54
]
and, where materially better financial terms are available to participants, courts have held that fiduciaries must act to secure those advantages.
[
55
]
These authorities support the proposition that ERISA requires fiduciaries to pursue only the course of action that best advances participants' and beneficiaries' financial interests—maximizing expected benefits net of reasonable expenses, and subject to prudent risk management, diversification, and plan terms—rather than merely not subordinating their interests to other objectives.
[
56
]
The text in paragraph (c) of the proposal reflects these principles.
The proposal's reference to “maximizing interests of the participants and beneficiaries . . .
under the plan”
(emphasis added) is to make clear that the “maximizing interests” obligation is to be understood in relation to, and with a focus on the benefits under the plan, rather than an obligation solely to pursue the highest investment return in all cases. For instance, the Department does not intend the “maximizing” language to be interpreted as compelling a fiduciary to make investment decisions focused on maximizing return on plan investments while ignoring prudence, risk, diversification, liquidity, funding obligations, or any other factors required or relevant with regard to providing promised benefits under the plan. Similarly, the Department also does not intend this language to prohibit a defined benefit plan fiduciary from using a liability-driven investment strategy to reduce the risk of underfunding to the plan.
[
57
]
Nor is this “maximizing” obligation violated merely because a counterparty benefits from a transaction with a plan.
[
58
]
3. Removal of the Tiebreaker Provision—Paragraph (c)(2)
In adopting the 2020 final rule, the Department expressed doubt that ties ever occur, but nonetheless included a tie breaker provision. In proposing the rule, the Department set forth the proposition that true ties may theoretically occur, acknowledged that it currently lacked sufficient evidence to say that they do not, and solicited comments on the matter.
[
59
]
The 2020 tiebreaker provision provided that if a fiduciary was unable to distinguish investment alternatives on the basis of pecuniary factors, the fiduciary could then, in effect, break the tie by relying on non-pecuniary factors.
[
60
]
Importantly,
(
printed page 75994)
to safeguard against improperly finding a tie in order to rely on non-pecuniary factors, the 2020 tiebreaker provision included a requirement that fiduciaries adequately document occurrences of ties.
[
61
]
The final rule adopted in 2022 amended the tiebreaker provision by modifying the standard for finding a tie. The 2022 final rule also removed the documentation requirement from the tiebreaker provision.
The Department is proposing to rescind the tiebreaker provision and remove it from the regulation. The best reading of ERISA's exclusive purpose rule requires and has always required that fiduciaries act solely to provide plan participants with benefits, and to look only to their financial interests during the process of making investment-selection decisions.
[
62
]
The tiebreaker rule seems to obviate this principle by letting fiduciaries consider collateral interests when selecting investments, while also facilitating unlawful conduct. At best, assuming a fiduciary started with a proper purpose, the provision merely serves as a mechanism that facilitates choosing between investments that would each equally benefit a plan in terms of anticipated returns on a risk-adjusted basis, and therefore does not appear to provide a plan with any overall financial benefit. This is because the selection of either investment would place the plan in the same economic position.
On the other hand, at its worst, the provision is susceptible to abuse and may be easily employed by a fiduciary as pretext as it uses plan assets to pursue objectives unrelated to the plan and its participants and beneficiaries. In practice, a fiduciary inclined toward a particular collateral objective may have an incentive to characterize competing investments as economically equivalent in order to invoke the tiebreaker provision. Once a tie is found, the regulation expressly permits reliance on collateral benefits, thereby creating a pathway through which nonfinancial considerations may influence an investment decision. This concern is heightened because the current provision singles out collateral interests for special treatment. If two investments equally serve the financial interests of the plan, a fiduciary may choose between them for a variety of reasons. The regulation, however, specifically identifies collateral interests as a permissible basis for selection, which may encourage reliance on considerations unrelated to providing benefits under the plan.
The Department acknowledges that a district court has held that the tiebreaker rule is consistent with the best reading of ERISA's duty of loyalty.
[
63
]
In relevant part, the court stated that when the fiduciary identifies competing investment courses of action that all “equally serve the financial interests of the plan,” then any choice between those actions is in the sole interest of the beneficiary and for the exclusive purpose of maximizing his financial benefits. According to the court, under these circumstances, all options the fiduciary faces accomplish, and do not evade, the fiduciary's duty of loyalty. The district court's opinion included a driving analogy to illustrate its reasoning:
Just as a driver, duty-bound to choose the fastest route to his destination, may choose the most scenic of two routes that each bring him to his destination at the same time, so too can a fiduciary choose a preferable investment option between two that will equally satisfy his duty of loyalty. When the driver takes the most scenic of the two fastest, he does not act for a different purpose than taking the fastest route—he did choose the fastest route. The fact it is also scenic does not mean he employed another purpose at all. If he had chosen the two most scenic routes—and then selected the fastest of the two—he would have acted with an impermissible purpose. He could choose the most scenic of fast routes but could not choose the fastest of scenic routes. The order elucidates his exclusive purpose.
[
64
]
Under the district court's interpretation, ERISA's exclusive purpose rule focuses on results and anti-subordination: so long as a fiduciary never selects a financially inferior investment and never lets collateral interests overtake plan participants' financial interests in making the investment choice, the fiduciary does not violate its duty of loyalty.
The Department believes the district court's analysis is not consistent with the best reading of ERISA's duty of loyalty. The district court ignored that ERISA's duty of loyalty focuses on process and not outcome. It demands that fiduciaries act with an “eye single” towards plan participants' and beneficiaries' financial interests when making fiduciary decisions
[
65
]
for the “exclusive purpose of providing benefits” to them.
[
66
]
Simply put, exclusive means exclusive,
[
67
]
and single means single.
[
68
]
A fiduciary cannot conduct a process to select investments with a “single-minded purpose” toward plan participants' and beneficiaries' financial interests if it considers other interests as it does so, even if only in the limited circumstances the tiebreaker rule permits, and without subordination to financial interests.
[
69
]
Not subordinating those financial interests to collateral interests or avoiding putting them on equal footing also does not suffice; using the district court's analogy, ERISA demands not only that the driver choose the fastest route to his destination, but also extricate all other factors from the process by which he chooses that route. ERISA's duty of loyalty and its exclusive purpose rule give plan participants and beneficiaries more procedural protection than the district court allowed, and the Department therefore disagrees with its holding that the tiebreaker rule is consistent with the best reading of ERISA. The Department is interested in comments regarding whether the tiebreaker rule is consistent with ERISA's duty of loyalty.
The Department acknowledges that it previously expressed confidence in the protectiveness of the 2022 tiebreaker provision based on other requirements under ERISA and the regulation,
[
70
]
but it is re-evaluating that conclusion in light of a recent court decision involving ERISA's loyalty requirement that highlights the potential for business relationships and nonfinancial conflicts involving persons acting in the investment marketplace that may influence a fiduciary's decisions,
[
71
]
as well as other proposed changes to paragraph (c) of the regulation, discussed earlier.
The Department also continues to have doubts as to the existence of ties, and the need for a tiebreaker provision. In explaining the usefulness of the tiebreaker provision in the 2022 rule, the Department stated that “[a]lthough some fiduciaries, by the nature of their arrangements with plans, may apply investment strategies that never require
(
printed page 75995)
them to choose between alternatives that equally serve the plan's needs, other fiduciaries, such as those making investments outside liquid financial markets, may find the tiebreaker test useful for circumstances in which there are equally strong cases for competing investments under a risk-return analysis.”
[
72
]
The Department is interested in comments on fiduciaries' experience in evaluating different types of investments, and on whether the Department's assessment of the types of plan engagements with investment fiduciaries and plan investment opportunities described above is reasonable and reflective of the current environment. Additionally, the Department is interested in comments on whether there have been any changes in the investment marketplace or advances in investment analysis since its earlier non-regulatory guidance on fiduciary consideration of collateral effects and interests (
e.g.,
IB 94-1) that would obviate the need for a plan fiduciary, acting in accordance with its duty of prudence under ERISA, to choose among competing investments.
Irrespective of whether it would be reasonable for a fiduciary to conclude that multiple investments are tied, a tiebreaker provision may not be needed. A tiebreaker provision is only necessary if the fiduciary seeks to break a tie based on a collateral interest other than investment return.
[
73
]
A fiduciary could resolve an ostensible tie by making a non-arbitrary choice between investments' financial and other features that directly benefit plan participants, and indeed that is exactly what would have to be done in that situation by a fiduciary that did not have a focus on collateral interests such as ESG. Doing so comports with ERISA's text, which requires fiduciaries act exclusively to “provide benefits to participants and their beneficiaries.”
[
74
]
Just as any one potential investment may have a certain risk-return profile, so too will it have a variety of other distinguishing benefits for plan participants. These are not merely collateral interests, but instead are additional financial-adjacent benefit or value to participants that may properly serve as a basis for a decision. For instance, a fiduciary could use factors such as the customer service offered to participants by a fund or the fiduciary's assessment of the fund's operations to break an ostensible tie. Moreover, even if it were otherwise permissible to make an investment-related decision based on a collateral interest, fiduciaries would have to remain cognizant of their obligations to ensure they are not engaging in a transaction prohibited by ERISA section 406. For instance, if the collateral interest involves a party in interest to the plan (
e.g.,
an employer whose employees are covered by the plan or a union whose members are covered by the plan), a prohibited transaction may occur.
[
75
]
Because of the Department's serious doubts that it comports with the best reading of ERISA, potential risk to participants' retirement security from its abuse, and the possibility that the provision does not provide any benefit to plans, the Department does not believe the tiebreaker rule should be included in the regulation. The Department is of the preliminary view that the regulation should not contain a provision that encourages reliance on collateral factors instead of financial benefits in fiduciary investment selection, and thus potentially incentivizes fiduciaries to characterize investments as economically equivalent as a pretext for advancing collateral objectives over financial interests. The Department is interested in comments evaluating the tiebreaker provision's legality and consistency with ERISA, as well as comments on whether eliminating the tiebreaker provision will change plan costs or types of investments. The Department requests comment on whether the removal of the tiebreaker provision could lead to greater compliance certainty and related decreases in costs or burdens on plan fiduciaries in evaluating investments or investment courses of action, or could lead to greater uncertainty and related increases in costs or burdens. The Department is also interested in comments on whether eliminating the tiebreaker test will reduce the instances of non-exempt prohibited transactions.
The Department notes that, as discussed above, it is proposing changes to paragraph (c)(1) of the regulation, which addresses ERISA's duty of loyalty, to make clear that a fiduciary must discharge his duties with respect to the plan for the exclusive purpose of maximizing the interests of plan participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan. If the change to paragraph (c)(1) is finalized as proposed, the Department believes that complying with its requirement to maximize the interests of participants and beneficiaries might reduce the likelihood of reaching any ties in evaluating competing investments.
ERISA's plain language does not allow for collateral considerations or mixed motivations. The duty of loyalty mandates that fiduciaries act “solely” and “for the exclusive purpose of” providing “benefits to participants and their beneficiaries.” “Exclusive” means that fiduciaries must act for the “whole, undivided” purpose of securing proper benefits for participants and beneficiaries.
[
76
]
And “solely” is defined as “to the exclusion of all else.”
[
77
]
4. Removal of the Participant Preference Provision—Paragraph (c)(3)
The 2022 final rule added a provision stating that fiduciaries do not violate their duty of loyalty solely because they take participants' preferences into account when constructing a menu of prudent investment options for participant-directed individual account plans.
[
78
]
In adopting the provision, the Department expressed the view that accommodating participants' preferences could lead to greater participation and higher contribution rates, leading to greater retirement security.
[
79
]
However, the Department cautioned that plan fiduciaries may not add imprudent investment options just because participants may request or prefer them.
[
80
]
The Department is proposing to remove this provision to clarify that participant preference, in and of itself, is a not legitimate basis for a fiduciary to select a plan investment option. Despite the caution to plan fiduciaries in the preamble to the 2022 final rule that participant preference would not justify imprudent investment options, the Department is concerned that the provision as articulated in the regulatory text may nevertheless be a trap for the unwary. A fiduciary's duties of prudence and loyalty under ERISA do not change based on participant preferences.
In this regard, the Department is concerned that this provision of the 2022 final rule creates a misperception that it is acceptable to sacrifice investment performance to obtain greater participation in the plan and higher contribution rates. The
(
printed page 75996)
participant preference provision may convey that a fiduciary may select an underperforming or high fee fund merely because some employees want an ESG or other social-themed fund. However, this runs counter to the fundamental principle that, even in a participant-directed plan, plan fiduciaries “must conduct their own independent evaluation to determine which investments may be prudently included in the plan's menu of investment options.”
[
81
]
Greater participation and higher contribution rates are both laudable objectives but a fiduciary may not, consistent with ERISA's duty of loyalty, sacrifice performance to pursue either objective.
The misperception created by the participant preference provision may also be exploited by promotors, consultants, investment providers, and others who may market investments with ESG-related investment strategies to fiduciaries based solely on participant preference. Plan fiduciaries may feel the need, at the very least, to expend plan resources unnecessarily on investigating and evaluating participant preferences and such potential investments that the fiduciary otherwise may determine to be imprudent. On balance, the Department believes the participant preference provision has the potential to undermine compliance with ERISA's high fiduciary standards. In close-call scenarios, for example, this provision presents a significant risk of being misused by decision-makers. Such misuse not only jeopardizes the best interests of plan participants and beneficiaries but also erodes the essential standard of care that fiduciaries are obligated to uphold.
Removing the participant preference provision is consistent with removing the tiebreaker provision as well. As discussed above, the Department is concerned that the tiebreaker provision is susceptible to abuse and may be used easily by a fiduciary as a pretext to use plan assets in pursuit of objectives unrelated to the plan and its participants and beneficiaries. The participant preference provision appears equally susceptible to such abuse. The Department believes eliminating both these provisions will bring the regulation in line with the best reading of ERISA's exclusive purpose requirement. To be clear, removal of the provision is not intended to signal that fiduciaries are prohibited from listening to participant preferences. However, if acting on participant preferences, fiduciaries must do so in accordance with their duties of prudence and loyalty under ERISA. The Department requests comment on whether this should be reflected in the regulation. More generally, the Department is interested in comments on whether there are any situations in which participant preferences with respect to plan investment options could be useful to fiduciaries in meeting their ERISA responsibilities of prudence and loyalty, and that would be facilitated by paragraph (c)(3).

5.1. Modifying Paragraphs (d)(2)(i), and (d)(2)(ii)(C) and (E) With Respect to Exercising Shareholder Rights
The Department is proposing to amend paragraph (d)(2) to include an explicit reference to shareholder engagement to make clear that, like proxy voting, decisions relating to shareholder engagement are subject to ERISA's fiduciary responsibility provisions and the Investment Duties regulation that would be amended by this proposed rule. Each Interpretive Bulletin that addressed ERISA fiduciary responsibilities with respect to exercise of shareholder rights, discussed above, also included provisions related to shareholder engagement.
[
82
]
The Department intended the 2020 and 2022 amendments to the Investment Duties regulation to cover fiduciary responsibilities with respect to shareholder engagement.
[
83

The Department, therefore, is proposing to add specific reference to “shareholder engagement” to the regulatory text in paragraphs (d)(2)(i) and (d)(2)(ii)(E) reflecting this. The Department is also proposing to add to paragraph (d)(2)(i) a reference to any other related investment courses of action because there may be some confusion as to whether the exercise of shareholder rights constitutes an “investment course of action” as defined in the regulation. 2. Need for Regulation
The proposed rule is intended to address a number of general concerns. First, that prior rulemaking regarding the incorporation of nonfinancial factors into a plan's investment policy strayed from the Department's neutrality stance regarding investment categories or classes. Second, that some investment managers managing plan assets are engaging in shareholder activities that are not in the economic interests of plans, participants, and beneficiaries. Third, that managers may be using the prior rulemaking's tiebreaker and participant preference provisions to engage in conduct otherwise not permitted by ERISA's exclusive purpose obligations. Further, by clarifying that ERISA neither favors nor disfavors any investment objective or strategy, the proposal would depoliticize ESG issues under ERISA and bolster confidence of plan fiduciaries in the conduct of their ERISA-regulated activities.
By clarifying the role of nonfinancial factors in the selection of investment options, plan fiduciaries would be less likely to choose investments that do not maximize the interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan. This should prevent
(
printed page 75998)
plan fiduciaries from choosing funds with lower risk-adjusted returns or higher fees simply because their social or nonfinancial factors aligned with the plan fiduciary's or participants' preferences.
Additionally, by clarifying that fiduciaries must act with the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to participants and beneficiaries when deciding whether to engage in shareholder activities and when carrying out those activities (
i.e.,
proxy voting, shareholder engagement, and other related investment actions), the Department believes the proposed rule would preclude resources from being devoted to proxy voting or shareholder activities that do not benefit plans or participants. As a result, the proposed rule's clarifications regarding a fiduciary's duty when selecting investment options and exercising shareholder rights should increase expected financial outcomes for plans and participants.
2.1. Nonfinancial Factors in Selection of Investments
Section 404(a)(1)(A) of ERISA, in relevant part, requires that “a fiduciary shall discharge his duties with respect to the plan solely in the interests of the participants and beneficiaries and for the exclusive purpose of providing benefits to participants and their beneficiaries.”
[
93
]
The Department of Labor states that a fiduciary's primary responsibility is “to run the plan solely in the interest of participants and beneficiaries and for the exclusive purpose of providing benefits and paying plan expenses.”
[
94
]
This proposal would clarify how that statement applies with respect to nonfinancial factors and plan fiduciaries selecting investments. Such clarification is needed because the 2022 rule creates the potential for fiduciaries to abuse the use of nonfinancial factors in investment selection. The issue is of growing importance since data suggests that the use of nonfinancial factors in the selection of investment options in ERISA plans has been expanding in recent years. The share of defined contribution (“DC”) plans with at least one investment with ESG-related investment strategies increased markedly between 2019 and 2024.
[
95
]
It is essential that plan fiduciaries understand that it is permissible to consider only factors that affect an investment's risk and return when making investment selections. The 2022 rulemaking allows for fiduciaries to use nonfinancial factors, such as ESG considerations, in cases where they claim that competing investments equally serve the financial interests of the plan. The existence of authentic ties has been questioned by some parties, arguing that there are always distinctions between investments in terms of their risk and return characteristics and a litany of other factors.
[
96
]
Moreover, plan fiduciaries, in the process of conducting their responsibilities, encounter similar circumstances when comparing available investments to each other, and still make a selection. This implies they can handle situations with similar investments, both those ESG-related and otherwise, in the same manner; a tiebreaker provision is not required.
The Department is concerned that the tiebreaker provision creates an opportunity for misuse. Plan fiduciaries who want to use ESG or other nonfinancial factors when selecting investments may manufacture inauthentic ties in order to justify investment selections that would otherwise be impermissible under ERISA. If plan fiduciaries are manufacturing ties as a pretext in order to pursue ESG investing, then the proposed rule, by removing the tiebreaker provision and affirming that plan fiduciaries must act with the exclusive purpose of maximizing the financial interests of participants and beneficiaries, would lead to plan fiduciaries discontinuing their use of nonfinancial factors in their investment selections.
The 2022 rulemaking also stated that when constructing an investment menu, a fiduciary would not violate its duty of loyalty solely because it considers participants' preferences, including demand for nonfinancial factors, in a manner consistent with its duty of prudence. The Department is concerned that plan fiduciaries may be similarly using the participant preference provision as a pretext to engage in behavior otherwise impermissible under ERISA. They also may be misunderstanding the provision to mean that ERISA's fiduciary duties change because of participant preferences.
Overall, there are several aspects of the proposal that are intended to eliminate nonfinancial selection criteria in ERISA plans, which will ensure that plans instead focus on an investment's risk and return profile. This will in turn lead to better investment performance for ERISA plans and participants in the long run, as described in more detail below in the Benefits section.
2.2. Shareholder Rights
Paragraph (d)(2)(ii) of § 2550.404a-1 requires that “[w]hen deciding whether to exercise shareholder rights and when exercising shareholder rights, plan fiduciaries must [. . . a]ct solely in accordance with the economic interest of the plan and its participants and beneficiaries [and] [c]onsider any costs involved.”
[
97
]
Most plans delegate the management of plan assets to investment managers,
[
98
]
and the Department has consistently maintained that the fiduciary duty to manage plan assets includes the management of shareholder rights of such assets. While many service providers regularly engage in behavior that renders them ERISA fiduciaries (
e.g.,
proxy advisory firms in certain circumstances and investment managers directly managing funds), others, such as investment managers of mutual funds, are not. Plan fiduciaries are required to act with prudence and diligence when selecting and monitoring service providers regardless of the fiduciary status of the service provider, including persons selected to exercise, advise on, or assist with shareholder rights. Prudence would require fiduciaries to monitor any decisions made and actions taken by investment managers (and other fiduciary service providers) with regard to the exercise of shareholder rights.
The Department is concerned that some investment managers managing plan assets continue to exercise plan shareholder rights, utilize plan assets, or devote resources in furtherance of activities that are not focused on the economic interests of participants and beneficiaries. The proposed rule clarifies that fiduciaries, which may include proxy advisory firms in certain circumstances, must act solely to maximize participants' and beneficiaries' financial benefit when deciding to exercise, or exercising, shareholder rights. They must also be prudent and diligent in choosing and
(
printed page 75999)

2.2.1. Trends in Proxy Voting
An investor who owns common stock has certain formal shareholder rights, including the right to participate in annual and special shareholder meetings and vote on major corporate matters. Shareholders vote on such matters either in person at the annual shareholder meeting or by proxy. The proposals may be put forward by either the corporation (management proposals) or shareholders (shareholder proposals). The legal requirements are discussed in greater detail in the Baseline section, below.
The Department is concerned that in recent years, in response to activist investors, some corporations have prioritized integrating ESG policies into management issues, such as the qualifications of corporate boards, without due consideration of the relevance of specific ESG risks or their implications for the long-term financial performance of the corporation. For instance, Whelan (2024) conducted a survey of Fortune 100 companies which found that in 2023, 43 percent of board members had one or more relevant ESG credential, up from only 29 percent in 2018. The same survey found that the composition of boards changed significantly during this time frame.
[
99

ESG has also grown to be more prevalent in executive compensation. In 2024, 77.4 percent of companies in the S&P 500 Index and 46.5 percent of companies in the Russell 3000 Index incorporated ESG metrics in their executive compensation, compared to 66.7 percent of companies in the S&P 500 Index and 39.9 percent of companies in the Russell 3000 Index in 2021. Of the S&P 500 companies using ESG metrics in director compensation in 2024, 90 percent used human capital management metrics (including Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI)), 59 percent used social metrics, and 53 percent used environmental metrics.
[

In 2025, ISS surveyed 159 investors and investor-affiliated organizations on whether incorporating nonfinancial ESG-related metrics into executive compensation is “an appropriate way to incentivize executives.” 52 percent of respondents noted that compensation programs should use ESG metrics only “if the metrics selected are specific and measurable, and their associated targets are communicated to the market transparently” while four percent of respondents indicated that compensation programs should “only use traditional financial performance measures, for transparency and to maintain alignment with shareholders' financial interests.”

2.2.2. Trends in Shareholder Engagement
While proxy voting is a highly visible method of exercising shareholder rights, investment managers may also engage with corporations in less public ways. For example, they might send letters or emails to corporations, call corporate management, or meet with corporate executives.

Further, the authors noted that, “the voting power of the Big Three is actually substantially greater than the number of shares that they hold [. . .] because the Big Three consistently vote the shares they hold, whereas a substantial proportion of other investors do not vote their shares.” Collectively, the Big Three accounted for a median of 27.6 percent of votes cast at annual meetings of S&P 500 companies.

Shareholder engagement is resource intensive for both investment managers and corporations; however, stakeholders have mixed opinions on the effectiveness of engagement. Each year, PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) conducts a series of surveys of institutional investors and corporate directors, which provide insight into the prevalence and effectiveness of shareholder engagement. For example, PwC's 2025 Global Investor Survey found that 46 percent of institutional investors regularly engage with companies they invest in or cover and another 43 percent engage when there's a specific issue or interest. When asked about whether they expect their stewardship activities to have an impact on investment performance, few institutional investors (16 percent) noted that there is no relationship between their stewardship and investment teams, whereas 72 percent expected stewardship to impact investment performance over the next three to four years.

When investment managers engage with company management in a manner that is not consistent with promoting the economic interests of plan participants and beneficiaries, both investment managers and publicly traded corporations with whom they engage may allocate resources to shareholder activities that are not likely to enhance the company's profitability or shareholder value. Such engagement may divert resources from activities more likely to improve investment returns or corporate performance and may impose costs without corresponding financial benefits to shareholders.
2.2.3. The Role of Proxy Advisory Firms
Growth in the number of shareholder proposals has encouraged reliance on proxy advisory firms. Proxy advisory firms offer voting recommendations as well as research on how proposals on the proxy ballot may affect the company, its risk profile, and its financial future. As discussed by Shu (2024) and Matsusaka and Shu (2024), proxy advisory firms offer economies of scale, allowing shareholders to receive information on proxy proposals at a lower cost.
[
134
]
The Department's 2022 regulation encouraged the reliance on “efficient structures,” such as proxy advisory firms, to prudently manage expenses associated with proxy voting.
[
135
]
However, the Department received comments expressing concern over the role and influence of proxy advisory firms in response to both its 2020 and 2022 rules. Today, their influence continues to be a matter of concern, as demonstrated by the House Committee on Financial Service's hearing on the matter held in April 2025.
[
136
]
The Department is concerned that past regulatory guidance has encouraged plans and their fiduciaries to over-rely on proxy advisory services.
The Department requests comments on how often plans or 3(38) investment fiduciaries engage with proxy advisory firms, including how often and for what type of services. The Department would also appreciate comments on the costs associated with these engagements.
2.3. Conclusion
The proposed rule clarifies for fiduciaries and service providers how to consider nonfinancial factors in investment decision making and when exercising shareholder rights. As discussed throughout this analysis, uncertainty around this issue may have contributed to investment choices and shareholder activities that were not undertaken to advance the economic interests of plan participants and beneficiaries. This proposed rule would clarify fiduciaries' duty of loyalty by reaffirming that investment decisions must be based on risk and return factors and that shareholder rights for plan assets should be exercised only when doing so is in the economic interest of participants and beneficiaries.

The baseline for this Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) is current law, comprised by
29 CFR 2550.404a-1
and relevant regulatory actions taken by the SEC and statements made by SEC staff. Each is discussed in greater detail below.
3.1. Investment Duties Under ERISA
29 CFR 2550.404a-1
requires plan fiduciaries to discharge their investment duties in accordance with the prudence
(
printed page 76003)
and loyalty standards.
[
137
]
This proposed rule largely focuses on the loyalty provisions, which prohibit fiduciaries from subordinating participants' and beneficiaries' financial interests to nonfinancial objectives or sacrificing returns to promote unrelated goals. The Department finalized amendments to the
29 CFR 2550.404a-1
in December 2022, which serves as the baseline for this proposed rule.
Under the 2022 rule, a tiebreaker standard under paragraph (c)(2) allowed fiduciaries to consider collateral interests when competing investments “equally serve the financial interests of the plan.” This proposed rule would remove the tiebreaker provision. It would also replace a prohibition against subordination with a requirement that fiduciaries act with the “exclusive purpose of maximizing the interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan.” This proposed rule further removes paragraph (c)(3), which addresses consideration of participants' nonfinancial preferences when selecting plan investments and deletes the statement from paragraph (b)(4) that “risk and return factors may include the economic effects of climate change and other environmental, social, or governance factors on the particular investment or investment course of action.” Finally, the proposed rule amends paragraph (d), adding explicit references to “shareholder engagement,” “all other rights accompanying share ownership,” and “any other related investment courses of action.”
Since 2016, an increasing share of plans have included ESG-related investments in their lineups, leading to an increase in the share of participants that have access to these investments. The Department expects that, absent this proposed rulemaking, plans would continue to utilize ESG-related investments at their current rate and some plan fiduciaries would continue to fail to consider critically the effect of shareholder activities on the economic interests of plan beneficiaries and participants. Under the proposed rule, the Department expects that plans would offer fewer ESG-related investments, restricting them to those funds that are selected based solely on considerations of risk and return. Likewise, the Department expects that entities to which plans delegate shareholder rights would spend fewer resources as they instead limit their activities to those that are in the economic interests of employee benefit plans.

3.2.2. Proxy Voting Responsibilities
In 2003, the SEC adopted a new rule under the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (“Advisers Act”) to require an investment adviser that exercises voting authority over client proxies to adopt policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that the adviser votes proxies in the best interests of its clients, among other requirements.
[
151

This rule was motivated in part by concerns regarding potential material conflicts of interest that may affect the manner in which an adviser votes clients' proxies—including business or personal relationships with participants in proxy contests, corporate directors or candidates for directorships.
Under the final rule, an investment adviser that exercises voting authority over client proxies must adopt policies and procedures reasonably designed to ensure that the adviser votes proxies in the best interests of clients, disclose to clients information about those policies and procedures, and disclose to clients how they may obtain information on how the adviser has voted their proxies. The rule applies to both advisers that have implicit as well as explicit voting authority, including when the advisory contract is silent but the adviser's voting authority is implied by an overall delegation of discretionary authority. The rule does not apply, however, to advisers that provide clients with advice about voting proxies but do not have authority to vote the proxies.

6.1.2. Assumptions for Plans Affected by Changes to Shareholder Rights Policies
To consider how the proposed amendments to paragraph (d) would affect plans, it is helpful to group plans into three general categories:
(1) Plans that invest in securities with voting rights directly or have pass-through shareholder rights from ERISA-covered intermediaries such as master trusts, common trusts, pooled separate accounts, and 103-12 investment entities that pass-through voting rights to the plan. These plans either directly exercise or otherwise manage shareholder rights.
(2) Plans that delegate shareholder rights to a 3(38) investment fiduciary. These plans would work with the investment fiduciary to establish policies on how shareholder rights are exercised.
(3) Plans that invest in or select pooled investment vehicles that in turn invest in securities with shareholder rights. When selecting any such investment, these plans would need to comply with the requirements of paragraph (c), ensuring that the investment decision does not sacrifice investment return or take on additional risk to promote benefits or goals unrelated to financial interests of the participants and beneficiaries.
While the Department lacks comprehensive data on how many plans directly exercise shareholder rights, the Department expects that few plans do due to time and resource constraints. Throughout this analysis, the Department has assumed that most plans delegate the management of shareholder rights for plan assets to investment managers, either 3(38) investment fiduciaries hired by the plan or investment managers managing funds selected by plan fiduciaries, rather than engaging directly with a proxy advisory firm.

7. Benefits
The proposed rule would reinforce the Department's neutrality stance regarding specific investment categories or classes and ensure that fiduciaries discharge their duties with the exclusive purpose of maximizing the interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan. This would clarify for fiduciaries that they cannot use nonfinancial factors in the selection of investments and would affirm that the decisions of fiduciaries regarding shareholder rights should consider the costs and benefits to the participants and beneficiaries. In doing so, the Department anticipates that plan fiduciaries who may have considered nonfinancial factors when making investment or menu selections under the 2022 rulemaking, may revisit these decisions and divest from those investments that cannot be justified on a purely financial basis. By doing so, the proposed rule should improve expected financial outcomes for plans and participants.
The discussion below identifies the major benefits the proposed rule is expected to generate. The Department welcomes comments on the identified benefits, the Department's characterizations of those benefits, and any additional benefits the Department should consider. The Department would also appreciate comments providing additional research, data, and anecdotal discussion of likely responses to the proposal.
7.1. Findings From the Literature on Investment Performance
Recent literature has analyzed the performance of ESG-related funds compared to other funds using various investments, time periods, and methodologies in their comparisons. The body of research has generated a mixture of findings. Taking the totality of the research into consideration, the Department sees suggestive evidence that ESG-related investments underperform other investments, in which case participants and plans would experience financial benefits from avoiding ESG-related investing.
Hornuf and Yuksel (2024) performed a meta-analysis of the literature on ESG-related investment performance.
[
193
]
They assert that on average across the studies, ESG-related investments neither outperform nor underperform other investments. However, they state that the higher quality studies, meaning studies in top tier peer reviewed finance journals, are less likely than other studies to find that ESG-related funds outperform other funds.
Similarly, two detailed financial studies found that ESG-related investments are likely to underperform in the long run and were able to provide possible explanations for why some other studies' methodologies and data might have led to other findings. Pastor, Stambaugh, and Taylor (2022), focusing on the U.S. stock market, assigned “greenness measures” to U.S. stocks between November 2012 and December
(
printed page 76011)
2020. While ESG-related investments outperformed other investments during this period, this pattern reflected an unanticipated increase in environmental concerns.
[
194
]
With further analysis, the authors find that ESG-related investments have lower expected returns than other investments. This finding is supported by both their examination of implied costs of capital and by their analysis of realized returns purged of shocks from climate concerns and earnings.
Van Brakel, Huij, and Kyosev (2025) analyzed active U.S. equity mutual funds from January 1991 to June 2024, comparing the financial performance of ESG-related funds to that of other funds. They find that while ESG-related funds underperform other funds on a buy-and-hold basis by 63 basis points on average, their investors earn higher dollar-weighted returns of 88 basis points on average.
[
195
]
The authors attribute this to investors in ESG-related funds responding more strongly to positive returns without overreacting to negative returns. In other words, investors in ESG-related funds exhibited better timing abilities. Given that the study observes investors who self-selected into their investment holdings, it is to be expected that the investors in ESG-related funds might differ from other investors in important ways, including potentially their financial sophistication, wealth, age, and the financial advice that they received. Indeed, other research shows that retail investors who are interested in pursuing ESG investing tend to be much more likely to seek out financial advice than other investors.
[
196
]
Van Brakel, Huij, and Kyosev (2025) note that their findings have important implications for assessing many other studies in the field. Some studies may have overstated the relative performance of ESG-related funds because their methodology did not take into account how investor timing abilities were influencing the outcomes. Their finding that ESG-related funds had worse financial performance than other funds on a buy-and-hold basis is confirmed by Raghunandan and Rajgopal (2022), who analyzed U.S. mutual funds from 2010 to 2018 that were sponsored by the same asset manager in the same year.
[
197
]
7.2. Estimating the Benefits From Increased Returns
Given significant evidence that ESG-related investments are likely to underperform on average, the Department estimates the benefits from assets being allocated to investments that are not ESG-related rather than ESG-related investments. As the research findings are mixed, the estimate applies a very conservative assumption about the degree of underperformance of only 10 basis points. This assumption is lower than the 63 basis points of underperformance found by Van Brakel, Huij, and Kyosev (2025) because that study only looked at equity mutual funds, while this assumption is also being applied to other retirement plan investments such as bond funds. The Department is aware that some bond funds hold ESG-related investments, but less information is available about their performance. While this estimate is imprecise, it demonstrates the effect of a difference in returns.

Based on estimates of $15.2 trillion in assets held by ERISA-covered pension plans, this amounts to $15.2 billion in plan assets being allocated differently.

7.3 Benefits From Aligning Shareholder Activities With Plan Economic Interests
The proposed amendments to paragraph (d)(2)(ii)(C) of § 2550.404a-1 would replace the requirement that, when deciding whether to exercise shareholder rights or exercising shareholder rights, plan fiduciaries must “not subordinate the interests of the participants and beneficiaries” with the requirement that plan fiduciaries “discharge their duties with respect to the plan with the exclusive purpose of maximizing the interests of the participants and beneficiaries.” As amended, this text would better align with the plain text of ERISA and proposed changes in paragraph (c), and clarify that plan fiduciaries should be exercising shareholder rights only when doing so is in the economic interest of plan participants and beneficiaries. This change mirrors similar language proposed to amend paragraph (c).
The proposed amendments would also amend paragraph (d)(2)(ii)(E) to clarify that plan fiduciaries must exercise prudence and diligence in the selection and monitoring of persons
(
printed page 76012)
designated to exercise, advise on, or assist with exercising all rights accompanying share ownership. This includes research and analysis, recommendations regarding proxy votes, shareholder engagement, administrative services with voting proxies, and recordkeeping and reporting services.
These amendments affirm that plan fiduciaries, and the service providers to which shareholder rights are delegated, should exclusively act in a way that is consistent with the economic interest of the plan. As discussed in the Affected Entities section, the Department expects that most plans delegate the management of shareholder rights for plan assets to investment managers, either investment fiduciaries hired by the plan or by investment managers of investment funds selected by plan fiduciaries. As a result, this analysis focuses primarily on how the proposed rule would affect how investment managers exercise shareholder rights.
With the clarification of the proposed rule, investment managers exercising shareholder rights for plan assets would no longer feel compelled to devote resources to shareholder activities that lack economic justification. This should result in both a reduction of shareholder activities related to ESG topics and an increase in activities on more financially relevant topics.
As discussed below in the Costs section, the Department expects that these investment managers may experience cost savings by devoting fewer resources to researching proxy proposals and conducting shareholder engagements where they determine that the matter is not reasonably expected to advance the economic interest of plan participants and beneficiaries. Under the assumptions explained in the Costs section, the Department estimates that investment managers could save $618.3 million annually by devoting fewer resources to proxy voting and $254.0 million annually by devoting fewer resources to shareholder engagement. Further, the Department assumes that publicly traded corporations could save $240.6 million annually by devoting fewer resources to shareholder engagement.
If investment managers or corporations reinvest these resources into activities that increase shareholder value, it would be a benefit for investors, including plan participants and beneficiaries. The extent to which cost savings are reinvested would depend on whether nonfinancial topics had crowded out more financially relevant issues or had instead driven extra engagement. This analysis does not attempt to estimate the proportion of resources that investment managers would redirect, nor does it attempt to estimate what rate of return such investments might earn. If a significant amount of resources are invested in shareholder activities that increase shareholder value, this would improve investment outcomes for plan participants and beneficiaries.
A study by Heath, Macciocchi, and Ringgenberg (2025) collected information on shareholder engagement from stewardship reports published by 11 institutional investors between 2019 and 2023. Using a discrete choice model that assumes an institutional investor will engage if the expected benefit of shareholder engagement exceeds the expected cost, the study finds, on average, institutional investors' shareholder engagement activity is consistent with the belief that a $10,000 investment in engagement will raise a firm's value by 0.35 basis points.
[
202
]
This finding is not directly applicable to the benefits that might be expected from investment managers reinvesting cost savings into more efficient uses, as it captures an implicit expectation of past behavior of a small sample of large institutional investors and does not capture the variability of expected returns for different types of firms and engagement issues. The Department also would not view the 0.35 basis point increase in firm value estimate as scalable to all engagement activity because investment managers are likely already pursuing the engagement opportunities they expect to generate the highest returns. Accordingly, resources redirected under the proposed rule would not be expected to generate the same return as the engagements observed in the study. To the extent the proposed rule redirects resources away from shareholder activities that are not economically motivated, those resources would likely generate higher marginal returns in alternative, more financially relevant uses.
The Department would appreciate comments, data, and studies that would assist with estimating the potential benefits of investment managers and publicly traded corporations that reinvest cost savings into more efficient uses. The Department is particularly interested in how any such actions would affect shareholder value. The Department also requests descriptions of any other benefits that would result from this proposal.
7.3. Conclusion
The proposed rule could benefit plans, plan participants, and beneficiaries by focusing plan fiduciaries on the exclusive purpose of maximizing the interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan. This focus could lead to assets moving from lower performing ESG-related funds to higher performing other funds leading to higher overall returns. The proposed rule also affirms that plan fiduciaries, and the service providers to which shareholder rights are delegated, should act with the exclusive purpose of maximizing the interests of plan participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan. This could lead to a reduction of resources devoted to shareholder activities that lack economic justification and allow investment managers or corporations to reinvest these resources into activities that increase shareholder value.

8.1. Costs Associated With the Proposal
The Department estimates this rule to have a first-year transition cost of $361.18 million to implement the proposed rule. These costs include reviewing the proposed rule; plans and investment managers updating investment policy statements and written policies governing the exercise of shareholder rights and engagement as needed; and changing investments as needed to comply with the proposed rules requirements.
