The Department conservatively assumes that an ESG-related mutual fund has an excess fee of five basis points and only quantifies the effect for mutual funds. The Federal Reserve reports that private retirement plans hold $5.7 trillion in mutual funds.
[
211
]
As described above in the Affected Entities section, the Department estimates that about 0.1 percent of these assets, or $5.7 billion, would be allocated to an ESG-related fund in the baseline and a fund that is not ESG-related under the proposal.
[
212
]
This means plans, participants, and investment managers would experience an annual cost savings of approximately $2.85 million, absent any compounding appreciation, due to reduced fees.
[
213
]
It is uncertain how these cost savings would be distributed among investors, such as plans and participants, and investment managers. While fees are paid by plans and participants, sometimes an investment manager will issue a waiver to temporarily reduce fees. In such cases, the costs of providing the fund, including research costs, may be partially borne by the investment manager, who would therefore also experience some of the cost savings from reduced ESG investing. Black and Kolbel (2025) found that “ESG funds” are more likely than “conventional funds” to have a waiver that temporarily reduces fees, and that the amounts of the waivers are larger for such ESG funds.
[
214
]
The authors speculate that ESG fund providers may have issued these temporary waivers because they anticipated substantial growth of ESG investing and wanted to use lower fees to compete for early flows.
8.3. Cost Savings Associated With the Proposed Amendments to Paragraph (d)
The Department expects that the proposed amendments to paragraph (d) would result in cost savings by clarifying that shareholder rights should be exercised with the exclusive purpose of maximizing the interests of participants and beneficiaries, regardless of whether those rights are managed directly by a plan or 3(38) investment manager with respect to directly held plan assets, or indirectly by an investment manager of a pooled investment vehicle to whom shareholder rights are delegated.
[
215
]
The discussion below explores the potential cost savings for plans and participants, investment managers, and publicly traded corporations.
8.3.1. Cost Savings for Plans and Participants
As discussed in the Affected Entities section, the Department expects that most plans delegate the management of shareholder activities for plan assets to investment managers, either investment fiduciaries hired by the plan or by investment managers of investment funds selected by plan fiduciaries. To the extent that the proposed amendments result in cost savings for investment managers, as described below, they may lower investment management fees for plans, participants, and beneficiaries. It is uncertain how much of the cost savings would stay with investment managers and how much would be passed on to plans, participants, and beneficiaries. The Department requests comments describing these effects.
8.3.2. Cost Savings for Investment Managers and Publicly Traded Corporations
The proposed rule would preclude investment managers that either manage plan assets directly or a pooled investment vehicle in which a plan invests, from devoting resources to shareholder activities that are not consistent with the economic interests of plan participants. As a stewardship approach that focuses on increasing shareholder value would benefit all shareholders, the Department expects that investment managers would broadly adopt policies focusing exclusively on promoting investors' economic interests, not just for plan assets or funds marketed to plans. This may result in cost savings in three ways:
(
printed page 76017)
(1) Investment managers may spend less time reviewing, researching, and voting on proxy statements that are not consistent with promoting the economic interests of plan participants and beneficiaries;
(2) Investment managers may allocate fewer resources to shareholder engagement that is not consistent with promoting the economic interests of plan participants and beneficiaries; and
(3) To the extent that the proposed rule refocuses investment managers' shareholder activities, publicly traded corporations would devote fewer resources engaging with shareholders.
Below, the Department considers how the proposed rule may affect proxy voting and shareholder engagement behavior and the related cost savings for investment managers and publicly traded corporations. The Department invites comments on its characterization of the actions of investment managers and corporations and on the assumptions used in the analysis below.
8.3.2.1. Proxy Voting
As discussed in the Need for Regulation section, in recent years, ESG themes have become more prevalent in proxy voting, both for management proposals and shareholder proposals. The Department expects that the proposed rule would encourage investment managers to devote fewer resources to researching proposals that are not reasonably expected to affect the economic value of the investment. This would either result in cost savings for the investment manager or, if investment managers redirect resources to activities that increase shareholder value, this would result in a benefit for investors, including plan participants and beneficiaries. This is discussed further in the Benefits section.
The Department received several comments from investment managers on its 2020 NPRM noting that their proxy voting and shareholder engagement are consistent with promoting the long-term economic interests of investors and that large investment managers are able to engage in such activities at a low cost due to economies of scale.
[
216
]
The Department understands that, with economies of scale, the cost of researching and voting proxy votes for large financial institutions may be negligible relative to other costs. However, in aggregate, the Department expects that cost savings could be substantial for investment managers.
The Department does not expect the proposed rule to affect the number of shareholder proposals. Most shareholder proposals have historically been filed by individuals, public pension funds, socially responsible investment funds, or advocacy groups.
[
217
]
Cohen and Hu (2025) found that in 2025, the ten most active shareholders were responsible for 63 percent of total shareholder proposals. Two of these shareholders were individual proponents, four were social investment entities, two were anti-ESG proponents, one was a public pension plan, and one was a union pension plan.
[
218
]
Entities with non-economic motives would likely continue to file shareholder proposals, so the Department does not expect that the proposed rule would have a significant effect on the number of shareholder proposals filed each year. It is possible, however, that the number of shareholder proposals included in proxy statements will evolve in light of recent staff statements.
[
219
]
There is significant uncertainty about how the proposed rule would affect the amount of time investment managers devote to researching proposals. To understand the potential magnitude of cost savings due to decreased time spent reviewing, researching, and voting on proxy statements, the Department assumes that, on average, each investment manager would vote on proxy ballots for the 1,500 companies in the S&P 1500 Index. The Department assumes that on average, the total time that investment professionals spend to review the proxy statement, research, make a voting determination, and vote is equal to twice the time required to read the proxy statement.
The Department is not aware of data on what proportion of time spent voting proxies is devoted to topics without an economic basis. In addition, investment managers often rely on proxy advisory firms for research, voting recommendations, and other services associated with exercising shareholder rights. Many of these services relate to ESG and other nonfinancial matters, and therefore under the proposal, investment managers' demand for proxy advisory firms' services would decrease. The Department would appreciate comments on its assumptions and requests data or anecdotal evidence to inform these estimates. 8.3.2.2. Shareholder Engagement
While often less visible than shareholder proposals, shareholder engagement demands significant resources from investment managers and publicly traded companies. The Department expects that the proposed rule would encourage investment managers to either devote fewer resources to shareholder engagement or
(
printed page 76019)
to redirect resources to activities that are anticipated to provide better returns to shareholders. To the extent that shareholder engagement from investment managers would decrease due to the proposed rule, this would result in cost savings for both investment managers and publicly traded corporations. As discussed in the Affected Entities section, the Department assumes that 1,000 investment managers would be affected by the proposed amendments.
To estimate the number of engagements that each investment manager conducts, the Department considered the analysis by Heath, Macciocchi, and Ringgenberg (2025) of 11 large institutional investors between 2019 and 2023. The analysis found that the institutional investors in the sample engaged, on average, with 320 firms per year. This included letters, emails, phone calls, or in-person or virtual meetings. The authors found that active managers engaged more than passive managers, and engagement was more likely in firms where institutional investors held large dollar stakes. As such, investors were more likely to engage with large-cap firms than with small-cap firms.
[
221

While the study only considered large institutional investors, these account for the majority of shareholder engagements. For example, BlackRock had more than 3,300 engagements with 2,300 companies in 2024.
[

Small and mid-sized investment managers would also be affected by the proposed rule.
While Heath, Macciocchi, and Ringgenberg (2025) considered all forms of engagement, the Department expects that brief correspondence and routine communications constitute a significant portion of total shareholder engagement but require substantially fewer resources per interaction. Accordingly, the Department's cost savings estimates focus on substantive engagement meetings, such as formal meetings and structured discussions that require significant preparation, participation, and follow-up. The Department assumes that 20 percent of total engagements are substantive engagement meetings, or approximately 60 substantive engagement meetings per investment manager, per year on average. Notably, the Department expects investment managers would broadly adopt policies that limit shareholder engagement to those that promote investors' economic interests, not just for plan assets or funds marketed to plans.

8.4. Conclusion
The Department anticipates that the proposal would lead to a significant amount of both costs and cost savings. The Department estimates this proposed rule would have a one-year transition cost of $361.18 million to implement the changes discussed in the preamble. The Department also estimates an annual cost savings of $1,115.79 million from a decrease in shareholder activities due to the rule. The Department would appreciate any information or viewpoints that would allow it to better describe the impact of the proposal on costs and cost savings.
9. Transfers
The Department anticipates that the proposal would result in transfers between parties as assets are moved from ESG-related investments to other investments. It would favor some financial institutions to the detriment of others, and some sectors of the economy to the detriment of others. The expected transfers are discussed in the following subsections.
9.1. Transfers Between Financial Institutions
The Department anticipates that some plans would change their investment lineups in response to the proposed rule. Plans holding ESG-related and other investments that were selected using nonfinancial factors in the baseline of this analysis would shift their lineups to other funds. In aggregate, participants would invest less plan assets in ESG-related funds and more in funds that are not related to ESG. This would constitute a transfer from financial institutions that specialize in sponsoring ESG-related investments to those financial institutions who specialize in other investments. Financial institutions associated with ESG-related investments, including ratings agencies, would experience a decrease in demand for services while financial institutions associated with other investments would experience an increase in demand for services. The Department has not attempted to quantify the potential size of this transfer.
(
printed page 76022)
9.2. Transfers Between Sectors of the Economy
The Department anticipates that some ERISA assets that are held in ESG-related funds in the baseline would instead be held in funds that are not related to ESG under the proposed rule. ESG-related funds tend to invest in certain sectors of the economy but not others. Under the proposal, these ESG-favored sectors would experience reduced investment, likely leading to lower stock values and a higher cost of raising capital. On the other hand, other sectors of the economy would see more investment and tend to prosper. This effect would represent a transfer from ESG-favored sectors to other sectors of the economy. The potential size of this effect is uncertain.
The Department requests comments on the transfers that would result from the proposal, as well as any supplemental information that would allow the Department to better characterize the transfers.
10. Regulatory Alternatives
This proposed rule is a response to prior attempts to extend fiduciary protections to allow for participant preferences or collateral effects to be considered in investment selection. As presented in the preamble to this proposed rule, the Department does not believe the current rule represents the best interpretation of ERISA. This proposed rule makes clear that a plan fiduciary must act in the exclusive financial interest of the plan and its participants, as set forth in ERISA. This proposed rule is meant to remove any uncertainty surrounding the issue of nonfinancial consideration, therefore removing risk exposure to the plan fiduciary. The alternatives considered are described in the subsections below.
10.1. Retaining Elements of the 2022 Rule
The Department considered retaining aspects of the 2022 rule, such as the tiebreaker provision or the consideration of participant preferences when selecting investment alternatives. However, while theoretically possible, the Department has been unable to document actual instances where competing investments equally serve the financial interests of the plan, suggesting that such a provision is either unusable, or vulnerable to abuse. Additionally, the Department was concerned that allowing plan fiduciaries to consider participants preferences could give the impression that plan fiduciaries may subordinate economic returns, resulting in the selection of investments with relatively poor financial performance or high fees. By removing these aspects of the 2022 rule, the Department believes it will prevent abuses that cause financial harm to plan participants.
10.2. Removing Paragraph (d)(2)(ii)(D)
The Department considered removing paragraph (d)(2)(ii)(D), which states that, when exercising or deciding whether to exercise shareholder rights, plan fiduciaries must “[e]valuate relevant facts that form the basis for any particular proxy vote or other exercise of shareholder rights.” The Department considered removing this paragraph due to concerns that this provision may be misunderstood as requiring a plan fiduciary to evaluate every proxy proposal received, without consideration of the benefits or costs of doing so. No such unqualified obligation is imposed by the regulation.
However, the intent of the provision is to ensure that fiduciaries, in making informed proxy voting decisions, consider information that is relevant to a matter that is known or that is available to and reasonably should be known by the fiduciary. For example, as explained in the preamble to the 2020 final rule, if an ERISA-fiduciary client of a proxy advisory firm becomes aware of additional information from an issuer which is the subject of the firm's voting recommendation, under this paragraph the fiduciary would be expected to consider whether such additional information is relevant.
[
225
]
This requirement safeguards against a fiduciary's blind reliance on recommendations provided by an advisor.
The Department believes the intent of this provision is clear, so it does not propose any changes. However, the Department solicits comments on whether changes to paragraph (d)(2)(ii)(D) would be helpful to avoid misinterpretations such as described above, or to better reflect the Department's intended purpose.

1. Need for Regulation
This proposed rule seeks to provide clarity, certainty, and permanency in how it directs plan fiduciaries to select investments and monitor activities related to the exercise of shareholder rights. The proposal deals with two broad topics: fiduciary duties of loyalty in selecting investments and investment courses of action, including selecting qualified default investment alternatives, and exercising shareholder rights, such as proxy voting, the use of written proxy voting policies and guidelines, and shareholder engagement.
The selection of investments and menus by plan fiduciaries is critical to the purpose of pension plans. The 2022 rulemaking allowed, in certain circumstances, for the use of nonfinancial factors, such as ESG considerations or plan participant demand, to be considered as part of the investment selection process. By clarifying the role of nonfinancial factors in the selection of investment options, plan fiduciaries will be less likely to choose investments that do not maximize the economic interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan. As a result, the proposed rule should increase expected financial outcomes for plan participants.
When exercising shareholder rights, plan fiduciaries must act exclusively with the purpose of promoting the economic interest of the plan, participants, and beneficiaries.
[
234
]
The proposed rule clarifies that plan fiduciaries must exercise prudence and diligence in the selection and monitoring of persons designated to exercise shareholder rights or otherwise advise on, or assist with, exercising all rights accompanying share ownership. This includes ensuring that any persons they select to exercise, advise on, or assist with shareholder rights acts in accordance with the economic interest of the plan.
Most plans delegate the management of plan assets to investment managers,
[
235
]
and the Department is concerned that investment managers overseeing plan assets continue to devote resources to shareholder activities that are not focused on the economic interests of participants and beneficiaries. This clarification would preclude such activities. The Department expects that this would either result in cost savings for investment managers and publicly traded corporations or allow investment managers to reinvest these resources into activities that promote firm or shareholder value.
2. Affected Small Entities
The Department estimates the number of affected small plans as all retirement plans that held investments and reported fewer than 100 participants in their 2023 Form 5500 filing. Retirement plans are sponsored by employers in all business types, so this analysis does not discuss impacts by business type. The Department then applies the same assumptions presented in the RIA to estimate the number of small plans affected by each component of the proposed rule.
This proposed rule imposes direct compliance costs on plans to review the rule; update investment policy statements and policies and procedures related to exercising shareholder rights as needed; and change investments to comply with the proposed rule's requirements as needed. Most plans hire investment managers to carry out fiduciary investment management functions. For purposes of this analysis, the Department estimates these compliance costs at the plan level. To the extent service providers perform compliance-related activities on behalf of plans, the Department for its analysis treats those costs as paid by, or passed through to plans.
The proposed rule would also affect small entities responsible for investment decision-making for pooled investment vehicles held by 401(k) plans, such as investment vehicles registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940, CITs, pooled separate accounts, and other pooled investment vehicles. For purposes of this analysis, these entities are referred to as “investment managers.” Small investment managers who act as ERISA fiduciaries would be directly affected by the proposed rule and are considered in this IRFA. However, investment managers that merely offer or manage investment products in which ERISA-covered pension plans may invest, but that do not act as ERISA fiduciaries with respect to plan assets, would not be directly regulated by the proposed rule. Such investment managers may experience indirect effects if plan

[

[

Based on this analysis, the Department estimates that approximately 580 small investment managers would be affected by the proposed rule. The Department believes that this approach overestimates the percent of affected investment managers that are small, as many of the small entities in this industry likely do not provide investment management services to ERISA-covered pension plans. The Department requests comments on this estimate and would appreciate data on the distribution of investment managers.
The Department expects that service providers will pass incremental compliance costs onto plans when possible. The resulting estimates of directly affected entities are presented in the table below.
3. Impact on Small Entities
The discussions below explore how small plans and small investment managers may be affected by the proposed rule.
3.1. Impact on Small Plans
As described in the preamble and the RIA, the proposed rule will impose modest transitional costs on affected small plans, regardless of plan size. The anticipated cost for each plan will differ based on the required actions and whether the plan engages a service provider for help with compliance.
The Department has analyzed the costs for the different combinations of activities in relation to average plan assets for plans with less than 10 participants. These very small plans in terms of participant count also tend to be the smallest in terms of assets. Table 16 presents the results of this analysis. The estimates below reflect plan-level compliance costs and do not net out potential indirect effects on service providers or investment managers, potential pass-through of costs or cost savings through fees, or other indirect market effects.
(
printed page 76028)
As Table 16 shows, most (60 percent) small plans will experience virtually no burden from this proposed rule. Further, only two percent of the affected population will likely experience the full burden associated with the rule, and that impact is estimated to be less than about one quarter of a percent of the average plan assets of plans with less than 10 participants. Impacts on larger plans will be even smaller.
3.2. Impact on Small Investment Managers
Similar to plans, the proposed rule will impose modest transitional costs on affected investment managers who act as ERISA fiduciaries, regardless of size. Directly affected investment managers would incur costs to review the rule, review and update investment policies, and review and update policies pertaining to shareholder rights and engagement. As in the RIA, the Department assumes that roughly two-thirds of investment managers will have cause to review their policies. Of this group of managers, it is further assumed that roughly three-quarters, or half of investment managers, will need to update their policies in order to remain viable investment managers for ERISA-covered pension plan assets. 4. Regulatory Alternatives
Regulatory Flexibility Act analyses typically consider small entity-specific alternatives, such as differing compliance requirements, timetables, specific small entity exemptions, or other scenarios listed in 603(c) of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
[
240
]
The Department has considered whether any such size-differentiated alternatives are available here. Rules that impose new reporting, documentation, or procedural compliance obligations can often be tailored, delayed, or scaled to entity size without undermining the rule's purpose. This proposed rule, by
(
printed page 76030)
contrast, restates and clarifies the fiduciary duty of loyalty that section 404(a)(1)(A) of ERISA already imposes on all plan fiduciaries, regardless of plan size.
The Department does not believe a small entity exemption, delayed timetable, or differing compliance standard would be appropriate or available in this context, because ERISA's duty of loyalty does not vary based on the size of the plan or its fiduciary. A small plan's fiduciary is subject to the same prohibition on subordinating participants' financial interests to collateral objectives as a large plan's fiduciary. Because the standards presented in the proposal are a restatement of those set forth in ERISA, there are no viable size-differentiated alternatives. This proposed rule is meant to remove any uncertainty surrounding the issue of non-financial consideration. The Department requests comment on whether there are size-differentiated alternatives relevant to this rulemaking that the Department has not considered.
5. Duplicate, Overlapping, or Relevant Federal Rules
The Department is issuing this amended rule under sections 404(a)(1)(A) and 404(a)(1)(B) of Title I under ERISA. The Department has sole jurisdiction to interpret these provisions as they apply to plan fiduciaries' consideration in selecting plan investment funds. Therefore, there are no duplicate, overlapping, or relevant Federal rules.
For the requirements relating to proxy voting policies, the Department is monitoring other federal agencies whose statutory and regulatory requirements overlap with ERISA. In particular, the Department is monitoring SEC rules and guidance to avoid creating duplicate or overlapping requirements with respect to proxy voting.
I. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
Title II of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995
[
241
]
requires each Federal agency to prepare a written statement assessing the effects of any Federal mandate in a proposed or final agency rule that may result in an expenditure of $100 million or more (adjusted annually for inflation with the base year 1995) in any one year by State, local, and Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector. This rulemaking is expected to have such an impact on the private sector. For the purposes of this rulemaking, the RIA meets the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act obligations.
J. Federalism Statement
Executive Order 13132
outlines fundamental principles of federalism and requires the adherence to specific criteria by Federal agencies in the process of their formulation and implementation of policies that have “substantial direct effects” on the states, the relationship between the National Government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
[
242
]
Federal agencies promulgating regulations that have federalism implications must consult with state and local officials, and describe the extent of their consultation and the nature of the concerns of state and local officials in the preamble to the proposed amendment.
In the Department's view, when finalized these amendments will not have federalism implications because they will not have direct effects on the states, the relationship between the National Government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among various levels of government. Section 514 of ERISA provides, with certain exceptions specifically enumerated, that the provisions of Titles I and IV of ERISA supersede any and all laws of the states as they relate to any employee benefit plan covered under ERISA. The requirements implemented in the amendments when finalized do not alter the fundamental requirements of the statute with respect to employee benefit plans, and as such have no implications for the states or the relationship or distribution of power between the national government and the states.

(4) A fiduciary's determination with respect to an investment or investment course of action must be based on factors that the fiduciary reasonably determines are relevant to a risk and return analysis, using appropriate investment horizons consistent with the plan's investment objectives and taking into account the funding policy of the plan established pursuant to section 402(b)(1) of ERISA. Investment loyalty duties.
A fiduciary shall discharge his duties with respect to the plan with the exclusive purpose of maximizing the interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan, and may not sacrifice investment return or take on additional investment risk to promote benefits or goals unrelated to financial interests of the participants and beneficiaries in their retirement income or financial benefits under the plan.

AGENCY:
National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Commerce Department.
ACTION:
Notice of public meeting.
SUMMARY:
The New England Fishery Management Council (Council) will hold a 3-day meeting with online webinar participation options to consider actions affecting New England fisheries in the exclusive economic zone (EEZ).
DATES:
The meeting will be held Tuesday, December 8, 2026, through Thursday, December 10, 2026, beginning at 10:30 a.m. EST on the first day and 9 a.m. EST on the last 2 days.
ADDRESSES:
The meeting will be held at Hotel Viking, One Bellevue Avenue, Newport, RI 02848; telephone (844) 806-4895. Webinar registration: Information on how to register and provide public comment via webinar will be posted on the Council's December 2026 meeting web page at:
https://www.nefmc.org/​calendar/​december-2026-council-meeting
.
Register for the webinar at
https://nefmc-org.zoom.us/​webinar/​register/​WN_​qKedpYXjRqutjNtJdQnoAQ#/​registration
.
Address:
New England Fishery Management Council, 50 Water Street, Mill 2, Newburyport, MA 01950; telephone (978) 465-0492;
www.nefmc.org
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Cate O'Keefe, Executive Director, New England Fishery Management Council; telephone: (978) 465-0492, ext. 113.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Agenda
Tuesday, December 8, 2026
The Council will begin the December meeting with a closed session of the Executive Committee at 9 a.m. pursuant to the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act to discuss information about Council resources. Following the closed session, the meeting will open with introductions and announcements by Council Chair Daniel Salerno. The Council will then receive reports on recent activities from the Council Chair and Executive Director; the Greater Atlantic Regional Fisheries Office (GARFO) Regional Administrator; the NOAA Office of the General Counsel; the Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC); the Mid-Atlantic Fishery Management Council (MAFMC); the Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission (ASMFC); the U.S. Coast Guard; NOAA Office of Law Enforcement; and the Highly Migratory Species (HMS) program and International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT). Following a lunch break, NOAA General Counsel will provide a briefing on financial disclosure requirements and voting recusal regulations for regional fishery management council members. The Council will then receive a report from Council staff on the October 2026 Council Coordination Committee (CCC) meeting, followed by a report on the November 2026 Northeast Region Coordinating Council (NRCC) meeting.
The Council will then hold an open period for public comment on issues that are not listed on the agenda. Following public comment, the Council will adjourn to a closed session to discuss appointments to the Scientific and Statistical Committee (SSC), coordinated by Council Chair Daniel Salerno. At 6 p.m., the Council will host a public outreach event at the Hotel Viking to provide an opportunity for informational exchange and foster open
(
printed page 75832)
lines of communication among meeting attendees.
Wednesday, December 9, 2026
The second day of the meeting will begin with Executive Director Cate O'Keefe presenting the Council's 2027 priorities. The Council will take final action on priorities for all fishery management plans and other Council responsibilities. After a lunch break, the Council will receive a report from the Scientific and Statistical Committee (SSC), chaired by Dr. Conor McManus. The report will include the SSC's overfishing limit (OFL) and acceptable biological catch (ABC) recommendations for Atlantic sea scallops, small-mesh multispecies, and several groundfish stocks. Next, the Council will receive a report from the Scallop Committee, chaired by Melanie Griffin, and take final action to set specifications for Atlantic sea scallops for Fishing Years 2027 and 2028, or default specifications if necessary.
Thursday, December 10, 2026
The third day of the meeting will begin with a report from the Small-Mesh Multispecies (Whiting) Committee after which the Council will take final action to set specifications for small-mesh multispecies stocks for Fishing Years 2027-2031 and consider other management measures. The Council will then receive a report from Council staff on the Transboundary Management Guidance Committee (TMGC) and consider approval of recommendations for 2027 total allowable catches (TACs) for shared U.S./Canada groundfish resources on Georges Bank, including Eastern Georges Bank cod and haddock and Georges Bank yellowtail flounder. Next, the Council will receive a report from the Groundfish Committee and take final action on Framework Adjustment 74. The action will establish specifications for several groundfish stocks for Fishing Years 2027-2031, U.S./Canada TACs for 2027, and other management measures. Executive Director Cate O'Keefe will provide updates on Council planning and activities, including fishery management plans, Council priorities, IRA initiatives, and other ongoing efforts. The meeting will conclude with other business and adjourn at approximately 1 p.m.
Special Accommodations
This meeting is physically accessible to people with disabilities. Requests for sign language interpretation or other auxiliary aids should be directed to Executive Director Cate O'Keefe (see
ADDRESSES
) at least 5 days prior to the meeting date.
(Authority
16 U.S.C. 1801
et seq.
)
Dated: November 20, 2026.
Rey Israel Marquez,
Acting Deputy Director, Office of Sustainable Fisheries, National Marine Fisheries Service.

We will consider all comments submitted by the posted deadline and consult as needed with the Federal agency seeking the disposition authority. After considering comments, we may or may not make changes to the proposed records schedule. The schedule is then sent for final approval by the Archivist of the United States. Background
Each year, Federal agencies create billions of records. To control this accumulation, agency records managers prepare schedules proposing retention periods for records and submit these schedules for NARA's approval. Once approved by NARA, records schedules provide mandatory instructions on what happens to records when no longer needed for current Government business. The records schedules authorize agencies to preserve records of continuing value in the National Archives or to destroy, after a specified period, records lacking continuing administrative, legal, research, or other value. Some schedules are comprehensive and cover all the records of an agency or one of its major subdivisions. Most schedules, however, cover records of only one office or program or a few series of records. Many of these update previously approved schedules, and some include records proposed as permanent.
Agencies may not destroy Federal records without the approval of the Archivist of the United States. The Archivist grants this approval only after thorough consideration of the records' administrative use by the agency of origin, the rights of the Government and of private people directly affected by the
(

Government's activities, and whether or not the records have historical or other value. Public review and comment on these records schedules is part of the Archivist's consideration process.

SUMMARY:
The FAA is superseding Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2026-21-08, which applied to certain The Boeing Company Model 737-700, -700C, -800, and -900ER series airplanes. AD 2026-21-08 required a detailed inspection of the left- and right-side form-in-place (FiP) gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for correct sealant installation, a fluid leak test of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panels for any leak, and applicable on-condition actions. Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this AD contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this AD, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Background
The FAA issued AD 2026-21-08, Amendment 39-23497 (
91 FR 67448
, October 27, 2026) (AD 2026-21-08), for certain The Boeing Company Model 737-700, -700C, -800, and -900ER series airplanes. AD 2026-21-08 required a detailed inspection of the left- and right-side FiP gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for correct sealant installation, a fluid leak test of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panels for any leak, and applicable on-condition actions. AD 2026-21-08 was prompted by a leak through the FiP gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel found during a leak check. An investigation found that the fairing requirements of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel caused thin regions of the FiP gasket, which caused the manufacturer to apply non-permitted sealant after the initial FiP gasket had cured, resulting in an uneven sealing surface on the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel and leak. The FAA issued AD 2026-21-08 to address incorrect or missing sealant installation. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in fuel leaking onto the engine exhaust nozzle and a possible fire on the ground.
Actions Since AD 2026-21-08 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2026-21-08, the FAA has determined that there is an error in the compliance time exception specified in paragraph (h) of AD 2026-21-08. The FAA omitted reference to the Revision 1 date of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB in the compliance time exception specified in paragraph (h) of AD 2026-21-08. The FAA has added reference to the Revision 1 date of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB in the compliance time exception specified in paragraph (h) of this AD.
FAA's Determination
The FAA is issuing this AD because the agency has determined the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop in other products of the same type design.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
This AD requires Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, Revision 1, dated June 25, 2026, which the Director of the Federal Register approved for incorporation by reference as of December 1, 2026 (
91 FR 67448
, October 27, 2026). This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
AD Requirements
Although this AD does not explicitly restate the requirements of AD 2026-21-08, this AD retains all of the requirements of AD 2026-21-08. Those requirements are referenced in the material referenced previously, which in turn is referenced in paragraph (g) of this AD.
This AD adds the omitted reference to the compliance time exception specified in paragraph (h) of this AD. This AD requires accomplishing the actions specified in the material already described, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this AD.
Justification for Immediate Adoption and Determination of the Effective Date
Section 553(b) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (
5 U.S.C. 551
et seq.
) authorizes agencies to dispense with notice and comment procedures for rules when the agency, for “good cause,” finds that those procedures are “impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” Under this section, an agency, upon finding good cause, may issue a final rule without providing notice and seeking comment prior to issuance. Further, section 553(d) of the APA authorizes agencies to make rules effective in less than thirty days, upon a finding of good cause.
The FAA is superseding AD 2026-21-08 to correct an error in paragraph (h) of AD 2026-21-08. The FAA omitted reference to the Revision 1 date of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB in the compliance time exception specified in paragraph (h) of AD 2026-21-08. This AD requires using the effective date of this AD, instead of the original issue date or the Revision 1 issue date of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, which provides operators additional time to complete the required actions. The FAA has determined that the change imposes no additional burden on any operator. The FAA has made no other changes to the requirements published in AD 2026-21-08.
Accordingly, notice and opportunity for prior public comment are unnecessary, pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)
. In addition, for the foregoing reason(s), the FAA finds that good cause
(
printed page 75751)
exists pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)
for making this amendment effective in less than 30 days.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The requirements of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) do not apply when an agency finds good cause pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553
to adopt a rule without prior notice and comment. Because the FAA has determined that it has good cause to adopt this rule without notice and comment, RFA analysis is not required.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.

(a) Effective Date
This airworthiness directive (AD) is effective December 1, 2026.
(b) Affected ADs
This AD replaces AD 2026-21-08, Amendment 39-23497 (
91 FR 67448
, October 27, 2026) (AD 2026-21-08).
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to The Boeing Company Model 737-700, -700C, -800, and-900ER series airplanes, certificated in any category, as identified in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, Revision 1, dated June 25, 2026.
(d) Subject
Air Transport Association (ATA) of America Code 57, Wings.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by a leak through the form-in-place (FiP) gasket at the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel found during a leak check. An investigation found that the fairing requirements of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel caused thin regions of the FiP gasket, which caused non-permitted sealant to be applied after the initial FiP gasket had cured, resulting in an uneven sealing surface on the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel and leak. The FAA is issuing this AD to address incorrect or missing sealant installation. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in fuel leaking onto the engine exhaust nozzle and a possible fire on the ground.
(
printed page 75752)
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Required Actions
Except as specified by paragraph (h) of this AD: At the applicable times specified in the “Compliance” paragraph of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, Revision 1, dated June 25, 2026, do all applicable actions identified in, and in accordance with, the Accomplishment Instructions of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, Revision 1, dated June 25, 2026.
Note 1 to paragraph (g):
Guidance for accomplishing the actions required by this AD can be found in Boeing Alert Service Bulletin 737-57A1359, Revision 1, dated June 25, 2026, which is referred to in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, Revision 1, dated June 25, 2026.
(h) Exceptions to Requirements Bulletin Specifications
Where the Compliance Time columns of the tables in the “Compliance” paragraph of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, Revision 1, dated June 25, 2026, refer to the original issue date or the Revision 1 date of Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, this AD requires using the effective date of this AD.
(i) Credit for Previous Actions
This paragraph provides credit for the actions specified in paragraph (g) of this AD, if those actions were performed before the effective date of this AD using Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, dated October 3, 2025, except as specified by paragraphs (i)(1) through (3) of this AD:
(1) Where Table 1 and Table 2 in the Compliance and Accomplishment Instructions paragraphs of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, dated October 3, 2025, specifies “Do a fluid leak test of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for any leak. If any leak is found, do all applicable on-condition corrective action(s) and repeat the leak test until no leak is found”, this AD requires replacing that text with “Do a fluid leak test of the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel for any leak. If any leak is found, replace the FiP gasket and repeat the leak test until no leak is found”.
(2) Where step 4.b. of Appendix A in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, dated October 3, 2025, specifies “If any water leaks from the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel in less than two minutes, the fluid leak test has failed”, this AD requires replacing that text with “If any water leaks from the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel in less than two minutes, the fluid leak test has failed. Replace the FiP gasket in accordance with Figure 3 and repeat the leak test until no leak is found”.
(3) Where step 4.b. of Appendix B in Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 737-57A1359 RB, dated October 3, 2025, specifies “If any water leaks from the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel in less than two minutes, the fluid leak test has failed”, this AD requires replacing that text with “If any water leaks from the engine fuel shutoff valve access panel in less than two minutes, the fluid leak test has failed. SUMMARY:
FMCSA requests public comment on Nick Castello's application for an exemption from the eligibility requirements related to immigration status to allow State Driver's Licensing Agencies (SDLAs) to issue non-domiciled commercial learner's permits (CLP) and commercial driver's licenses (CDL) for certain drivers who are in humanitarian or protection-based categories such as Uniting for Ukraine (U4U), Temporary Protected Status (TPS), asylum, and pending asylum. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Public Participation and Request for Comments
FMCSA encourages you to participate by submitting comments and related materials.
A. Submitting Comments
If you submit a comment, please include the docket number for this notice (FMCSA-2026-3268), indicate the specific section of this document to which the comment applies, and provide a reason for your suggestions or recommendations. You may submit your comments and material online or by fax, mail, or hand delivery, but please use only one of these means. FMCSA recommends that you include your name and a mailing address, an email address, or a phone number in the body of your document so the Agency can contact you if it has questions regarding your submission.

                    1/2

B. Confidential Business Information (CBI)
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to the notice contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to the notice, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Sarah Stella, Chief, Regulatory Development Division, Office of Policy, FMCSA, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001 or via email at
sarah.stella@dot.gov
.

,
insert FMCSA-2026-3268 in the keyword box, select the document tab and choose the document to review. To view comments, click this notice, then click “Browse Comments.” If you do not have access to the internet, you may view the docket by visiting Dockets Operations in the DOT West Building, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, Washington, DC 20590-0001, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
II. Legal Basis
FMCSA has authority under
49 U.S.C. 31136(e)
and
31315(b)
to grant exemptions from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs). FMCSA must publish a notice of each exemption request in the
Federal Register
(
49 CFR 381.315(a)
). The Agency must provide the public an opportunity to inspect the information relevant to the application, including the applicant's safety analysis. The Agency must provide an opportunity for public comment on the request.
The Agency reviews the application, safety analyses, and public comments submitted and determines whether granting the exemption would likely achieve a level of safety equivalent to, or greater than, the level that would be achieved absent such exemption, pursuant to the standard set forth in
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)(1)
. The Agency must publish its decision in the
Federal Register
(
49 CFR 381.315(b)
). If granted, the notice will identify the regulatory provision(s) from which the exempted party will be exempt, the effective period, and all terms and conditions of the exemption (
49 CFR 381.315(c)(1)
). If the exemption is denied, the notice will explain the reason for the denial (
49 CFR 381.315(c)(2)
). The exemption may be renewed (
49 CFR 381.300(b)
).
III. Applicant's Request
Current Regulatory Requirements
On February 13, 2026, FMCSA published a final rule amending the Federal regulations for State Driver's Licensing Agencies (SDLAs) issuing commercial driving credentials to foreign-domiciled individuals, effective March 16, 2026 (
91 FR 7044
). Under
49 CFR 383.73(f)(3)(ii)(A)
, as amended, SDLAs must not issue non-domiciled commercial learner's permits or CDLs unless the applicant provides evidence of lawful immigration status, as defined under
49 CFR 383.5
. Section 383.5 provides that
evidence of lawful immigration status,
for applicants domiciled in foreign jurisdictions (other than U.S. territories), consists of an unexpired foreign passport and a Form I-94/94A issued by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security with an unexpired foreign passport and a Form I-94/94A with an unexpired Admit Until date indicating a classification of H-2A-Temporary Agricultural Workers, H-2B-Temporary Non-Agricultural Workers, or E-2-Treaty Investors.
Applicant's Request
Nick Castello states that he is a U.S. Marine Corps veteran and disabled veteran business owner, submitting this application as a public safety and workforce continuity initiative. The applicant specifically requests relief from portions of
49 CFR parts 383
and
384
, including 383.5, 383.71(f), 383.73(f) and (m), and 383.153(c), to the extent necessary to permit SDLAs to issue non-domiciled CDLs and CLPs to Department of Homeland Security (DHS)-documented, work-authorized
(
printed page 75964)
drivers who are otherwise qualified but excluded solely because they are in humanitarian or protection-based categories such as U4U, TPS, asylum, and pending asylum (rather than H-2A, H-2B, or E-2, who are otherwise qualified). He requests relief for up to five years, or any shorter period FMCSA determines appropriate (such as an interim two-year exemption, emergency transition period, pilot, or other time-limited or conditional relief sufficient to prevent immediate job loss while FMCSA, SDLAs, DHS, courts, or Congress address the broader issue). The applicant states that the exemption is needed because the drivers' employment and income are at risk solely because their immigration status categories are not recognized under the current non-domiciled CLP and CDL eligibility requirements. The applicant asserts that he has collected 93 responses from drivers who have experienced recurring problems involving non-domiciled CLP/CDL issuance, renewal, transfer, restoration, correction, replacement, and upgrade transactions as a result of the non-domiciled CDL final rule.
Applicant's Equivalent Level of Safety
Mr. Castello believes the exemption would maintain an equivalent level of safety because it preserves all substantive safety controls and adds clear, exemption-specific conditions. Covered drivers would remain subject to all applicable CDL qualification and safety requirements, including testing, medical qualification, driver training, and disqualification requirements. The applicant also proposes that FMCSA could verify each driver's identity, immigration status, and work authorization through FMCSA- or DHS-approved systems. He requests that drivers covered under the exemption be eligible for non-domiciled CLPs and CDLs that would be limited to the individual's verified period of lawful presence or work authorization, one year, or another FMCSA-approved period. He notes that the exemption would allow the covered drivers to remain inside the regulated, verified, CDL framework, rather than forcing an abrupt loss of work based solely on status category.
A copy of Mr. Castello's application for exemption is available for review in the docket for this notice.
IV. Request for Comments
In accordance with
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)
, FMCSA requests public comment from all interested persons on Mr. Castello's application for an exemption from certain provisions of the requirement in
49 CFR parts 383
and
384
governing non-domiciled CLPs and CDLs to allow SDLAs to process non-domiciled CLP and CDL transactions for DHS documented, work-authorized drivers and drivers in humanitarian or protection based categories such as U4U, TPS, asylum, and pending asylum. All comments received before the close of business on the comment closing date will be considered and will be available for examination in the docket at the location listed under the Addresses section of this notice. Comments received after the comment closing date will be filed in the public docket and will be considered to the extent practicable. In addition to late comments, FMCSA will also continue to file, in the public docket, relevant information that becomes available after the comment closing date. Interested persons should continue to examine the public docket for new material.

Associate Administrator for Policy.

Mr. Kostarev requests that the exemption last until he receives his Form I-551 or for two years from the date FMCSA grants his request, whichever is earlier.
Applicant's Equivalent Level of Safety
Mr. Kostarev believes the exemption would not compromise safety because he has a multi-year CDL history in the United States and a current or recent medical examiner's certificate. In addition, he indicates that, if the exemption is granted, he would retain a valid medical certificate, operate only for Jacob Transport Inc., and submit to any further monitoring FMCSA or the licensing State requires. Mr. Kostarev indicates that there is no basis in his record to treat him as an unvetted, foreign-domiciled, new driver. He asserts that without the exemption, he would face severe financial loss because he owns his truck and commercial driving is his livelihood. The exemption application includes a letter of support from Jacob Transport Inc.

ACTION:
Notice of application for exemption; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
FMCSA requests public comment on Luca Donati's application for an exemption from the non-domiciled Commercial Driver's License (CDL) eligibility provisions. Mr. Donati requests that the Agency allow a State Driver's Licensing Agency (SDLA) to accept his E-1 visa and Form I-94 as evidence of lawful immigration status and issue or renew his non-domiciled Class A CDL. FMCSA is required by statute to publish a notice explaining each exemption request. This notice does not indicate what decision FMCSA will ultimately reach on the request. After reviewing the application, safety analyses, and public comments submitted, FMCSA will grant or deny the exemption.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Public Participation and Request for Comments
FMCSA encourages you to participate by submitting comments and related materials.
A. Submitting Comments
If you submit a comment, please include the docket number for this notice (FMCSA-2026-3169), indicate the specific section of this document to which the comment applies, and provide a reason for your suggestions or recommendations. You may submit your comments and material online or by fax, mail, or hand delivery, but please use only one of these means. FMCSA recommends that you include your name and mailing address, an email address, or a phone number in the body of your document so the Agency can contact you if it has questions regarding your submission.

,
click on this notice, click “Comment,” and type your comment into the text box on the following screen.
If you submit your comments by mail or hand delivery, submit them in an unbound format, no larger than 8
                    1/2

FMCSA will consider all comments and material received during the comment period. Comments received after the comment closing date will be filed in the public docket and will be considered to the extent practicable.
B. Confidential Business Information (CBI)
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to the notice contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to the notice, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission that constitutes CBI as “PROPIN” to indicate it contains proprietary information. FMCSA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the Freedom of Information Act, and they will not be placed in the public docket of the notice. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Sarah Stella, Chief, Regulatory Development Division, Office of Policy, FMCSA, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001 or via email at
sarah.stella@dot.gov
.
At this time, you need not send a duplicate hardcopy of your electronic CBI submissions to FMCSA headquarters. Any comments FMCSA receives not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this notice.

II. Legal Basis
FMCSA has authority under
49 U.S.C. 31136(e)
and
31315(b)
to grant exemptions from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs). FMCSA must publish a notice of each exemption request in the
Federal Register
(
49 CFR 381.315(a)
). The Agency must provide the public an opportunity to inspect the information relevant to the application, including the applicant's safety analysis. The Agency must provide an opportunity for public comment on the request.
The Agency reviews the application, safety analyses, and public comments submitted and determines whether granting the exemption would likely achieve a level of safety equivalent to, or greater than, the level that would be achieved absent such exemption, pursuant to the standard set forth in
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)(1)
. The Agency must publish its decision in the
Federal Register
(
49 CFR 381.315(b)
). If granted, the notice will identify the regulatory provision(s) from which the exempted party will be exempt, the effective period, and all terms and conditions of the exemption (
49 CFR 381.315(c)(1)
). If the exemption is denied, the notice will explain the reason for the denial (
49 CFR 381.315(c)(2)
). The exemption may be renewed (
49 CFR 381.300(b)
).
III. Applicant's Request
Current Regulatory Requirements
On February 13, 2026, FMCSA published a final rule amending the Federal regulations for SDLAs issuing commercial driving credentials to foreign-domiciled individuals, effective March 16, 2026 (
91 FR 7044
). Under
49 CFR 383.73(f)(3)(ii)(A)
, as amended, SDLAs must not issue non-domiciled commercial learner's permits (CLPs) or CDLs unless the applicant provides evidence of lawful immigration status, as defined under
49 CFR 383.5
. Section 383.5 provides that
evidence of lawful immigration status,
for applicants domiciled in foreign jurisdictions (other than U.S. territories), consists of an unexpired foreign passport and a Form I-94/94A issued by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security with an unexpired Admit Until Date indicating a classification of H-2A-Temporary Agricultural Workers, H-2B-Temporary Non-Agricultural Workers, or E-2-Treaty Investors.
Applicant's Request
Luca Donati seeks a 5-year exemption from the Federal requirements in
49 CFR 383.71(f)
and the definition of “evidence of lawful immigration status” in
49 CFR 383.5
insofar as they permit issuance or renewal of a non-domiciled CLP or CDL only to applicants in H-2A, H-2B, or E-2 nonimmigrant statuses. The applicant specifically requests that FMCSA allow an SDLA to issue or renew his non-domiciled Class A CDL based on his valid Form 1-94 and E-1 Visa.
Mr. Donati states that he is a citizen of Italy who is present lawfully in the United States in E-1 nonimmigrant status. He states that his Form I-94 is valid until April 4, 2027, and his E-1 visa is valid through May 16, 2027. He says that the State of New Jersey issued his non-domiciled Class A CDL on August 12, 2024, and provided a copy of his foreign passport that shows an expiration date of May 16, 2027. In February 2026, when Mr. Donati appeared in person to renew his CDL, he indicates that the State of New Jersey downgraded his Class A license to Class D, despite FMCSA's September 2025 interim final rule having been judicially stayed and the February 13, 2026 final rule not taking effect until March 16, 2026. He states that without the relief he is seeking, he is unable to work in the occupation for which he is trained and lawfully authorized, notwithstanding that he remains lawfully present and authorized to work in the United States.
Applicant's Equivalent Level of Safety
Mr. Donati believes the exemption would not compromise safety, as the documentary requirement from which he seeks relief “is not a measure of driver competence, medical fitness, or safety performance.” He claims that granting this exemption would not alter any substantive safety requirement that is applicable to him. The applicant would remain fully subject to all testing, medical certification, controlled substance and alcohol testing requirements, hours of service, and disqualification requirements of
49 CFR parts 380
through
399
. The applicant would also present an unexpired passport and Form I-94 at each licensing transaction, and consent to the same verification process of his status as is required of H-2A, H-2B, and E-2 applicants under
49 CFR 383.73(m)
. Mr. Donati further indicates that he would accept an immediate downgrade of the commercial privilege should he cease to hold lawful status consistent with
49 CFR 383.73(f)(5)
, and states that he would meet every safety-related and verification requirement that applies to the permitted classifications, thereby ensuring an equivalent level of safety.
A copy of Luca Donati's application for exemption is available for review in the docket for this notice.
IV. Request for Comments
In accordance with
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)
, FMCSA requests public comment from all interested persons on Luca Donati's application for an exemption from the non-domiciled CDL eligibility provisions to the extent those provisions limit eligibility to H-2A, H-2B, and E-2 non-immigrant classifications. All comments received before the close of business on the comment closing date will be considered and will be available for examination in the docket at the location listed under the Addresses section of this notice. Comments received after the comment closing date will be filed in the public docket and will be considered to the extent practicable. In addition to late comments, FMCSA will also continue to file, in the public docket, relevant information that becomes available after the comment closing date. Interested persons should continue to examine the public docket for new material.

Associate Administrator for Policy.

Current Regulatory Requirements
To obtain a standard CDL, a person must provide proof of citizenship or lawful permanent residence as specified in Table 1 to

; otherwise, a person seeking to obtain a CDL would need to apply for a non-domiciled CDL (
49 CFR 383.71(b)(9)

(f)

91 FR 7044
). Under
49 CFR 383.73(f)(3)(ii)(A)

. Section 383.5 provides that
evidence of lawful immigration status,

Applicant's Request
Mr. Kapach states that he was born in Israel and resides in North Carolina. He adds that he holds an unexpired Employment Authorization Document (EAD), which was issued under category C08 due to his pending asylum application. He previously held a Class A CDL with Passenger (P) and School bus (S) endorsements issued by the State of North Carolina in August 2023. The CDL, which bore the designation “LIMITED-TERM,” was due to expire in July 2028. In August 2026, the North Carolina DMV downgraded Mr. Kapach's Class A CDL to a Class C CDL. He states that the DMV did not offer any explanation of the legal basis for doing so in writing; rather, he was told orally that this was based on his lack of lawful permanent resident status.
Mr. Kapach requests a 5-year exemption from
49 CFR 383.71(b)(9)
and Table 1 to
49 CFR 383.71
(to the extent they exclude an unexpired Employment Authorization Document issued by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services) to allow the State of North Carolina to reinstate his Class A CDL with the P and S endorsements despite that he is not a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident. He also requests an exemption from the corresponding verification duties in
49 CFR 383.73(b)(6)
,
(c)(7)
,
(d)(7)
, and
(e)(5)
and the requirement in
49 CFR 384.201(a)
for a State to administer its licensing program in accordance with the minimum standards in
49 CFR part 383
, to the extent that standard includes
49 CFR 383.71(b)(9)
and Table 1. In the alternative, Mr. Kapach requests an exemption from
49 CFR 383.73(f)(3)(ii)(A)
and paragraph (1)(ii) of the definition of
evidence of lawful immigration status
in
49 CFR 383.5
, to the extent that paragraph confines qualifying classifications to H-2A, H-2B, and E-2, to allow the State to issue him a non-domiciled CDL.
Mr. Kapach reasons that the Agency granted relief from the CDL list of acceptable proofs of citizenship or lawful permanent residency in Table 1 in an exemption to the Oregon Department of Transportation (
89 FR 78428
) (now superseded) that allowed Oregon to issue standard, full-term CDLs to the covered class and in a similar exemption (filed by the Hawaii Department of Transportation) that allows all SDLAs to issue a non-domiciled CDL to citizens of Freely Associated States who reside in the United States (

). Mr. Kapach argues that although the latter exemption did not allow citizens of Freely Associated States to receive standard CDLs, he should be eligible for a standard, rather than non-domiciled, CDL because North Carolina is his State of domicile within the meaning of
49 CFR 383.4
—it is where he has his true, fixed, and permanent home and principal residence.

He also states he will not operate as an owner-operator, motor carrier, or lessor, will consent to the credential being marked in any manner FMCSA directs, will consent to its period of validity being limited to one year at a time, and acknowledges the exemption may be revoked without prior notice to him. He believes these conditions place him under closer supervision than a driver holding an unrestricted credential and that this shows the exemption would achieve a “greater” level of safety.
