18 CFR Part 385
[Docket No. RM26-13-000; Order No. 920]
RIN 1902-AG51
AGENCY:
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission) is revising its regulations addressing the circumstances under which a request for rehearing is denied absent Commission action within a particular time frame. Currently, the Commission's regulations provide that unless the Commission acts upon a request for rehearing within 30 days after the request is filed, the request is denied. As revised in this final rule, the regulation will apply only to matters subject to the rehearing and judicial review provisions in the Federal Power Act (FPA) and Natural Gas Act (NGA).
DATES:
This rule is effective December 24, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Benjamin Carlisle, Office of the General Counsel, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 888 First Street NE, Washington, DC 20426. (202) 502-6040.
benjamin.carlisle@ferc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
A. Commission Rule of Practice and Procedure 713(f)
1. In this final rule, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (Commission) is revising Part 385 of its Rules of Practice and Procedure to modify the circumstances under which a request for rehearing is denied absent Commission action within a particular time frame. Currently, Rule 713(f) of the Commission's regulations provides that unless the Commission acts upon a request for rehearing within 30 days after the request is filed, the request is denied.
[
1
]
As revised, Rule 713(f) will be applicable only to matters subject to the rehearing and judicial review provisions in the Federal Power Act (FPA)
[
2
]
and Natural Gas Act (NGA)
[
3
]
and will continue to provide that as to such matters, a request for rehearing is denied unless the Commission acts upon that request within 30 days after the request is filed.
2. Under both the NGA and the FPA, if a party seeks rehearing of an order issued by the Commission, and if the Commission does not “act[ ] upon” the rehearing request within 30 days after it is filed, then rehearing “may be deemed to have been denied.”
[
4
]
At that point, an aggrieved rehearing applicant may file a petition for judicial review of the Commission's orders within 60 days.
[
5
]
Until the administrative record is filed with the court, the Commission may “modify or set aside, in whole or in part,” its orders without leave of court.
[
6
]
3. Rule 713(f) was first promulgated to effectuate the statutory process under the FPA and NGA and remove ambiguity regarding whether a request for rehearing remains pending if the Commission does not act on that request during the 30-day period specified in those statutes. In particular, the Federal Power Commission (FPC) promulgated what is now Rule 713(f) in response to the 1953 decision of the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit (D.C. Circuit) in
Texas-Ohio Gas Co.
v.
FPC.
[
7
]
On the facts of that case, the court disagreed with the FPC's position that a rehearing applicant had failed to timely petition for review within the requisite 60 days under NGA section 19(b) where the Commission had issued neither an order nor a notice addressing the rehearing request.
[
8
]
In reaching its decision, the court explained that “[t]he literal terms of Section 19(a) . . . are that the application may be deemed to have been denied, not that it must be.”
[
9
]
The court inferred that Congress's primary intent was “to permit an appeal to the courts by a disappointed litigant as soon as thirty days have passed, without waiting longer for the Commission to act
(
printed page 75776)
on his application for rehearing.”
[
10
]
The court interpreted NGA section 19(b)—under which the 60-day deadline is tethered to “the order of the Commission upon the application for rehearing”
[
11
]
—as “contemplat[ing],” but not requiring, that the Commission issue a formal order granting or denying rehearing.
[
12
]
The court, however, interpreted the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) as requiring “prompt notice” of a denial, which “[p]erhaps . . . could be sufficiently supplied by a published regulation” or notice of “general applicability.”
[
13
]
The court suggested that such a notice could, “for example, stat[e] that on the thirtieth day after the filing of an application for rehearing the application shall be deemed denied, with the same force and effect as if a formal order had been entered.”
[
14
]
4. The FPC first proposed what is now Rule 713(f) in 1954, describing the Rule as, “in effect, an interpretation of” NGA section 19(a) and FPA section 313(a).
[
15
]
Relying on its authority in NGA section 16
[
16
]
and FPA section 309,
[
17
]
the FPC explained that the Rule 713(f)'s “adoption is made desirable by the decision of the” D.C. Circuit in
Texas-Ohio.
[
18
]
In Order No. 175, the FPC later adopted this language as proposed in the 1954 NOPR.
[
19
]
In Order No. 225, the Commission reorganized its Rules of Practice and Procedure, and announced its intention to extend its Rules of Practice and Procedure to proceedings governed by the Interstate Commerce Act (ICA).
[
20
]
Explaining Rule 713(f), the Commission stated that, “[t]o alleviate a potential administrative burden on the Commission, a request for rehearing is denied by operation of law after 30 days if no Commission action is taken within that time.”
[
21
]
B. Allegheny Defense Project v. FERC (Allegheny)
5. Prior to the D.C. Circuit's 2020
en banc
decision in
Allegheny,
the Commission routinely issued orders tolling the 30-day period for action on rehearing requests specified in the FPA and NGA, as well as Rule 713(f). These orders stated that the Commission was granting rehearing for the limited purpose of further consideration. In
Allegheny,
the D.C. Circuit, sitting
en banc,
held that tolling orders do not amount to “action” on rehearing applications within the meaning of NGA section 19(a), and thus do not prevent requests for rehearing from being “deemed” denied after 30 days.
[
22
]
6. After
Allegheny,
the Commission no longer issues tolling orders to extend the 30-day period for action on rehearing requests under the NGA or FPA.
[
23
]
Instead, the Commission keeps the public apprised of the status of proceedings by issuing one of two types of notices on or after the 31st day following receipt of a rehearing request. The first type, a Notice of Denial of Rehearing by Operation of Law, states only that rehearing may be deemed denied by operation of law, thus indicating that a further order addressing the merits of the rehearing request is not forthcoming.
[
24
]
The second type, a Notice of Denial of Rehearing by Operation of Law and Providing for Further Consideration, states that, although rehearing may be deemed denied by operation of law, the Commission intends to issue a further order addressing the merits of the rehearing request under the Commission's retained authority under the FPA and NGA to modify or set aside the underlying order in whole or in part until the record in a proceeding has been filed in a court of appeals.
[
25
]
In proceedings where the Commission issues this second type of notice, litigants often file “protective” petitions for review within 60 days of the date rehearing may be deemed denied—
i.e.,
within the statutory timeframe to seek judicial review following Commission action on an application for rehearing.
[
26
]
C. ICA
7. The ICA is materially different from the FPA and NGA with respect to rehearing of Commission orders. Although both the FPA and NGA contain mandatory and jurisdictional rehearing requirements, the ICA does not require that an aggrieved party seek rehearing from the Commission prior to petitioning for judicial review.
[
27
]
Rather, rehearing requests are permissive in nature.
[
28
]
The Supreme Court has held that, if a party requests rehearing, the time for that party to file a petition for review in an ICA case runs from the date the order acting on the rehearing request is issued.
[
29
]
Under the ICA, a party that has requested rehearing of an agency decision is precluded from seeking judicial review before the agency has acted on that rehearing request.
[
30
]
8. Unlike the FPA and NGA, the ICA contains no provision specifying that an application for rehearing may be deemed denied if the Commission does not “act[ ] upon”
[
31
]
the rehearing request before a particular period of time has elapsed. Rather, it more generally provides that such applications under the ICA are “governed by such general rules as the
(
printed page 75777)
Commission may establish,”
[
32
]
which currently includes denial pursuant to Rule 713(f) absent Commission action within 30 days of the filing of the rehearing request. Following
Allegheny,
the Commission has continued its practice of issuing orders tolling the deadline in Rule 713(f) to allow additional time for further consideration of the matters raised on rehearing.
II. Discussion
9. The Commission is revising Rule 713(f) to apply only to cases subject to the rehearing and judicial review provisions in the FPA,
16 U.S.C. 825
l,
and NGA,
15 U.S.C. 717r
. We find that revising Rule 713(f) as provided herein will conform with the statutory authorities governing rehearing of Commission orders, continue to provide parties seeking rehearing with appropriate notice of the disposition of their rehearing requests, and increase administrative efficiency by streamlining the Commission's processes in certain cases.
10. Specifically, the Commission is revising Rule 713(f) to provide that, as to matters subject to the rehearing and judicial review provisions in
16 U.S.C. 825
l
and
15 U.S.C. 717r
, a request for rehearing is denied unless the Commission acts upon that request within 30 days after the request is filed. This revised version of Rule 713(f) will thus apply to matters arising under the FPA and NGA, consistent with the reasons for the initial adoption of the Rule.
[
33
]
11. Rule 713(f), as revised, will not result in any change in the Commission's practices or procedures with respect to matters subject to the rehearing and judicial review provisions of the FPA and NGA. Each of those statutes' rehearing provisions states that if the Commission does not “act[ ] upon” a rehearing request within 30 days, rehearing “may be deemed to have been denied.”
[
34
]
Rule 713(f), as revised, continues to provide that a request for rehearing
is
denied when this 30-day period has elapsed without Commission action, thereby providing notice to parties that have sought rehearing as to the status of their request for administrative rehearing.
[
35
]
In matters falling within the scope of revised Rule 713(f), the Commission will continue its practice of issuing the two types of notices described above,
[
36
]
so that a party whose rehearing request has been denied by operation of law has additional notice as to whether the Commission expects to issue a further order.
12. As noted above, in matters subject to the FPA and NGA parties have often filed “protective” petitions for review in cases where the Commission issues a Notice of Denial of Rehearing by Operation of Law and Providing for Further Consideration. Such notices indicate that although the 30-day time period has elapsed, the Commission intends to issue a future order addressing the merits of the rehearing request. Because the Commission intends to continue its existing notice practice in cases that remain subject to the revised Rule 713(f), the Commission finds it appropriate to address the concerns that have motivated parties to file “protective” petitions for review in the wake of such notices. The Commission observes that the D.C. Circuit has held that the 60-day window for petitioners to seek judicial review under the FPA or NGA does not preclude the court from considering “a petition for review from a final denial of relief, even if there had been a deemed denial in the interim and the petition for review was filed more than 60 days following that deemed denial.”
[
37
]
Consistent with that holding, the Commission has not sought—and does not intend to seek—dismissal of a petition for review on grounds of untimeliness where that petition was filed within 60 days from such a final denial of relief, even if it was filed more than 60 days following the date that the rehearing request may have been “deemed to have been denied” under FPA section 313(a) or NGA section 19(a).
13. As revised, Rule 713(f) will not apply to matters that are not subject to the rehearing and judicial review provisions in the FPA and NGA, notably including matters arising under the ICA.
[
38
]
As explained above, the ICA does not provide that an application for rehearing may be deemed denied if the Commission does not act upon the rehearing request within 30 days or, indeed, before any particular period of time has elapsed.
[
39
]
Revising Rule 713(f) as stated is thus consistent with the ICA's statutory text regarding rehearing, including in removing Rule 713(f)'s 30-day deadline for the Commission to either act on a rehearing request in an ICA matter or issue a tolling order extending this deadline. In addition, these revisions to Rule 713(f) obviate any need for the Commission to continue its practice of issuing tolling orders as to rehearing requests in ICA cases. Because the Commission has issued such tolling orders in most matters arising under the ICA, revising Rule 713(f) in this manner simplifies and streamlines the Commission's processes in ICA cases, resulting in administrative efficiencies and continuing the Commission's practice of timely resolving such cases.
14. A party seeking rehearing in an ICA matter will receive notice of the disposition of its rehearing request through the issuance of an appropriate Commission order. In light of the statutory text governing rehearing applications filed in ICA matters, this approach provides sufficient notice to rehearing applicants regarding the pendency and status of their rehearing requests.
[
40
]
III. Information Collection Statement
15. Office of Management and Budget (OMB) regulations require OMB to approve certain information collection requirements imposed by agency rule.
[
41
]
This final rule, however, results in no new, additional, or different public reporting burden. This final rule does not require public utilities or natural gas
(
printed page 75778)
companies to file new, additional, or different information, and it does not change the frequency with which they must file information.
IV. Environmental Analysis
16. The Commission is required to prepare an Environmental Assessment or an Environmental Impact Statement for any action that may have a significant adverse effect on the human environment.
[
42
]
Excluded from this requirement are rules that are procedural, ministerial, or internal administrative and management actions, programs or decisions.
[
43
]
This rule falls within this exception; consequently, no environmental consideration is necessary.
V. Regulatory Flexibility Act
17. The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (RFA)
[
44
]
generally requires a description and analysis of final rules that will have significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. This final rule revises certain of the Commission's procedural regulations related to addressing requests for rehearing and does not create any additional requirements for filers. The Commission thus certifies that it will not have a significant economic impact upon participants in Commission proceedings. An analysis under the RFA is therefore not required.
VI. Regulatory Planning and Review
18.
Executive Order 12866
(Regulatory Planning and Review),
[
45
]
as amended by
Executive Order 14215
(Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies)
[
46
]
and supplemented by
Executive Order 13563
(Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review),
[
47
]
directs agencies to assess the costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety effects, distributive impacts, and equity).
Executive Order 13563
emphasizes the importance of quantifying costs and benefits, reducing costs, harmonizing rules, and promoting flexibility. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) has determined that this regulatory action is a “significant regulatory action,” under section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
, as amended, though not economically significant under section 3(f)(1). Accordingly, OIRA has reviewed this regulatory action for compliance with the analytical requirements of
Executive Order 12866
. In general, this regulatory action is intended to simplify the Commission's processes and improve stakeholders' interactions with the Commission by eliminating unnecessary administrative steps resulting from the Commission's existing regulations. This regulatory action will increase administrative efficiency by eliminating a purely procedural step in the disposition of certain rehearing requests, thereby supporting the Commission's timely resolution of pending matters. In addition, this final rule is considered a deregulatory action under
Executive Order 14192
(Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation).
VII.
Executive Order 13132
(Federalism)
19.
Executive Order 13132
(Federalism)
[
48
]
imposes certain requirements on Federal agencies formulating and implementing policies or regulations that preempt State law or that have federalism implications. The Executive Order requires agencies to examine  the constitutional and statutory authority supporting any action that would limit the policymaking discretion of the States and to carefully assess the necessity for such actions. The Commission has determined that this final rule would not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. Therefore, the Commission has not prepared a federalism assessment.
VIII. Document Availability
20. In addition to publishing the full text of this document in the
Federal Register
, the Commission provides all interested persons an opportunity to view and/or print the contents of this document via the internet through the Commission's Home Page (
http://www.ferc.gov
).
21. From the Commission's Home Page on the internet, this information is available on eLibrary. The full text of this document is available on eLibrary in PDF and Microsoft Word format for viewing, printing, and/or downloading. To access this document in eLibrary, type the docket number excluding the last three digits of this document in the docket number field.
22. User assistance is available for eLibrary, the Public Reference Service, and the Commission's website during normal business hours from FERC Online Support at (202) 502-6652 (toll free at (866) 208-3676) or email at
ferconlinesupport@ferc.gov
.
IX. Notice and Effective Date
23. This rule is effective December 24, 2026. The Commission is issuing this rule as a final rule without a period for public comment. Public notice and comment, otherwise required by
5 U.S.C. 553
, do not apply to “rules of agency organization, procedure, or practice.”
[
49
]
This rule concerns only matters of agency procedure, and will not significantly affect regulated entities or the general public.

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Notice and request for information.
SUMMARY:
This document announces and initiates an EPA effort to streamline the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) permit program and to remove associated barriers to redevelopment. This effort will satisfy an Agency Priority Goal established by the EPA Administrator to streamline the permitting process and improve efficiencies to unleash economic growth. In this document, EPA seeks information to help identify inefficiencies in the permit process and ideas for streamlining, including ideas that would reduce the time, uncertainty, and costs involved in issuing a permit. EPA also seeks information to help identify situations where the RCRA permit presents barriers to redevelopment of and/or parceling of RCRA treatment, storage, and disposal facilities, and ideas to overcome those barriers. EPA will consider information submitted as it develops a plan to address the inefficiencies in, and barriers presented by, the current RCRA permit program. This document also announces four virtual public engagement sessions that will supplement the request for information by providing individual participants an opportunity to provide oral comments on these issues as well.
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before January 25, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
Any member of the public may send comments, identified by Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OLEM-2026-9571, by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
(our
(
printed page 75853)
preferred method). Follow the online instructions for submitting comments.
Mail:
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, EPA Docket Center, Office of Land and Emergency Management Docket, 1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20460.
Email:
docket_OLEM@epa.gov
.
Include Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OLEM-2026-9571 in the subject line of the message.
Hand Delivery or Courier:
EPA Docket Center, WJC West Building, Room 3334, 1301 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC. The Docket Center's hours of operation are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. EST, Monday-Friday (except Federal Holidays).
Instructions: All submissions received must include the Docket ID No. for this action.
Comments received may be posted without change to
https://www.regulations.gov/​
,
including any personal information provided. For detailed instructions on sending comments and participating in the virtual public engagement sessions, see the “Public Participation” heading of the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section of this document.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For further information on the sections of this document addressing improvements to the permit process, contact Nadja Solis Marcano, Waste and Chemical Implementation Division, Office of Resource Conservation and Recovery, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, telephone number (202) 566-0356, email address:
nadja.solismarcano@epa.gov
;
or Lilybeth Colon, Waste and Chemical Implementation Division, Office of Resource Conservation and Recovery, telephone number (202) 566-0320, email address:
colon.lilybeth@epa.gov
.
For information on the sections of this document addressing barriers to redevelopment and parceling of RCRA facilities, contact Barbara Foster, Waste and Chemical Implementation Division, Office of Resource Conservation and Recovery, telephone number (202) 566-0382, email address:
foster.barbara@epa.gov
.
To register for the virtual engagement sessions, please either submit the online registration form available at EPA's Hazardous Waste Permitting website at
https://www.epa.gov/​hwpermitting
or contact Nadja Solis Marcano at the contact information above. For information on access or services for individuals with disabilities, or to request accommodation of a disability, please contact Nadja Solis Marcano, at the contact information above, at least ten (10) days prior to the meeting to give the EPA as much time as possible to process your request.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Public Participation
The Agency requests public comment on issues described later in this document. Public comment can be submitted to the docket for this rulemaking as described in the Addresses section above. The Agency also announces four public engagement sessions during which EPA will also accept oral comments on the issues discussed in this document. The public engagement sessions are intended to supplement the requests for information in this document; participation in the public engagement sessions is not required to submit public comment on the issues discussed in this document. EPA will take notes to document comments made at the public engagement sessions, which will be made available in the docket, but the Agency strongly encourages speakers to submit their presentations to the docket as well.
The dates and times of these public engagement session and instructions for participating are available on the Hazardous Waste Permitting Program's website at
https://www.epa.gov/​hwpermitting
.
For purposes of organization, each of the virtual public engagement sessions is targeted to an audience representing a sector of the general public. Though participants are encouraged to attend their targeted session, all sessions are open to the general public.
Advance registration is encouraged to secure a place on the agenda. A general agenda listing pre-registered speakers in approximate order will be available in the docket and on EPA's Hazardous Waste Permitting website at
https://www.epa.gov/​hwpermitting
the day before each meeting.
II. Request for Comment
A. The Permit Process
The EPA Strategic Plan for FY 2026-2030 (Strategic Plan) establishes as a priority goal to, by September 30, 2027, streamline the permitting process and improve efficiencies so the Nation can unleash economic growth while providing cost savings to hardworking Americans. The Strategic Plan explains that by implementing cost-effective regulations and streamlining permitting processes, the EPA will demonstrate that protecting human health and the environment goes hand-in-hand with economic prosperity, and that streamlining permitting processes is a crucial step for facilitating investment and promoting economic growth. The Strategic Plan further explains that the effort to simplify regulations will remove redundancies and reduce delays, while providing clear guidelines to aid businesses in navigating requirements.
The Agency is issuing this document to obtain information from the public that will support RCRA's implementation of the permitting effort announced in the Strategic Plan. EPA is requesting comment in two general areas—comment that will help identify inefficiencies and redundancies in the current RCRA permit process, and comment that will provide innovative solutions to overcome those inefficiencies and redundancies.
EPA seeks comment on situations where the regulated community has experienced inefficiencies, including unreasonable delays and/or redundancies, in all areas of the permit process including but not limited to:
Permit issuance and renewal—information required by the application process, turnaround timeframes, process redundancies or unnecessary processes.
Permit modification—determining the applicable class of permit modification, information required, process redundancies or unnecessary processes.
EPA seeks comment on ways to improve the efficiency of the permit process including but not limited to:
Ways to modernize application and renewal procedures through electronic tools.
Revisions to the permitting process, including the permit modification processes, that might avoid redundancy and repetition.
Streamlined processes or information requirements that could be implemented at particular phases of a facility's life (
e.g.,
post-closure).
Ways to promote risk-based clean closure to eliminate the need for post-closure permits.
B. Financial Assurance
A key goal of RCRA is to avoid the creation of Superfund sites, and adequate financial assurance for closure, post-closure, third-party liability, and corrective action is a vital component of the regulatory scheme established to meet that goal. EPA is considering whether revisions to the RCRA financial assurance program are necessary to ensure that adequate and effective financial assurance mechanisms are available at RCRA facilities.
EPA is requesting comment to identify situations where the current RCRA Subtitle C financial assurance
(
printed page 75854)
program is outdated, inefficient, or ineffective including, but not limited to:
Outdated aspects of the financial assurance mechanisms in
40 CFR part 264 subpart H
and
part
265, subpart H to reflect changes in commercial practice, experience, and standards since the mechanisms were promulgated.
Experiences related to unavailability of instruments or instrument failure due to constraints imposed by the current regulations.
How to best address situations and promote redevelopment where there is no longer a viable owner or operator, and no financial assurance is available.
EPA is also requesting comment on ways to improve the current financial assurance program including but not limited to:
Ways that use of electronic financial assurance documents and other electronic practices could improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the financial assurance program.
Improvements that could be made to the financial assurance regulations to overcome barriers to the availability and effectiveness of the financial assurance instruments.
Improved methods to provide financial assurance for long-term obligations such as post-closure care obligations (including those that extend beyond the 30-year period) and corrective action obligations.
Potential streamlining of the process for obtaining instruments by expanding the scope of closure and post-closure mechanisms to include corrective action costs.
C. Transferring Permit Obligations to Alternate Authorities
1. Background
RCRA section 3005(c)(3) requires that permits contain terms and conditions as necessary to protect human health and the environment. Section 3004(u) provides that, where corrective action is not completed before permit issuance, permits issued to RCRA treatment, storage, and disposal facilities must contain schedules of compliance for corrective action for all releases of hazardous waste or hazardous constituents from any solid waste management unit and assurances of financial responsibility for completing such corrective action. RCRA section 3004(v) further requires that corrective action be taken beyond the facility boundary as necessary to protect human health and the environment.
Currently, EPA has implemented these statutory requirements by requiring renewal of RCRA permits until the post-closure period is complete,
[
1
]
and until the obligation to address facility-wide corrective action for releases of hazardous waste and hazardous constituents from all solid waste management units at the facility is satisfied.
Increasingly, facilities are completing closure of their treatment, storage, and disposal units, and these post-closure and/or corrective action requirements are the only remaining permit obligations. EPA is considering whether continuation of the permit throughout the post-closure care period and until corrective action is complete is necessary to meet the requirements of the statute or whether, and under what conditions, the statutory requirements of section 3005(c)(3) and sections 3004(u) and (v) could be met if post-closure and/or corrective action requirements were transferred to an alternate state authority.
EPA has long recognized that state authorities such as enforcement orders, if used as an alternative to RCRA corrective action requirements for releases from solid waste management units, may impose substantive cleanup requirements that are equivalent to those imposed under a RCRA permit through RCRA corrective action authority. However, EPA also recognizes that the existing RCRA permit systems in place that provide for implementation and oversight of corrective action and post-closure care provide procedural protections to help ensure protectiveness.
2. Request for Comment on the Benefits of an Alternate Authority Approach to Post-Closure Care and Corrective Action
EPA requests comment on the benefits of replacing RCRA permits with alternate authorities to implement post-closure care and/or corrective action obligations where the RCRA permit obligations present barriers including but not limited to:
Examples of situations where the RCRA permit has been a barrier to redevelopment of contaminated property.
Aspects of the permit or the permitting process that are of particular concern in redevelopment scenarios.
Aspects of alternate authorities that make them preferable to the RCRA permit to implement post-closure care and corrective action for releases from solid waste management units.
3. Request for Comment on Alternate Approaches to Meeting the Statutory Requirements
EPA is soliciting comment on how alternative authorities can provide equivalent statutory corrective action and post-closure requirements. EPA is also soliciting comment on how alternative authorities can provide the protections currently afforded by the permit process—that is, if post-closure and/or corrective action permit conditions were transferred to an alternate authority, how the standard to protect human health and the environment would continue to be met until post-closure and/or corrective action is complete. EPA is soliciting comment on how alternative authorities could replace the protections currently provided by a permit including but not limited to:
Reporting and notice—Procedural requirements that ensure releases, corrective action needs, and possible post-closure extensions are brought to the permitting authority's attention.
Continuity of responsibility—Transfer of permit responsibilities to a new owner/operator, long-term responsibility for post-closure care and corrective action obligations, and protections to ensure these responsibilities remain enforceable during bankruptcy.
Accountability and inspection—Authority to make enforceable comments on draft permits to ensure protective conditions are included, as well as authority to inspect and enforce permit conditions, including state-issued conditions.
Financial assurance—Requirements for financial assurance for post-closure care and corrective action.
Public participation and transparency—Requirements for public participation during permit issuance, modification, and renewal.
D. Parceling
The issue of transferring permit obligations to an alternate authority also arises when an owner sells a portion of a RCRA permitted facility. Owners and operators of RCRA facilities may seek to amend the boundaries of the facility described in the RCRA permit to remove a parcel being sold from the facility. Purchasers of property may be hesitant to sign on to a RCRA permit and become jointly and severally liable for facility-wide corrective action obligations and
(
printed page 75855)
seek to address remaining corrective action obligations through an alternate authority. Regulators may be hesitant in parceling scenarios to release owners and operators and property purchasers from RCRA permit obligations because of concerns that doing so may allow them to avoid corrective action obligations. Regulators further may be concerned that selling parcels of a facility may deplete resources available to address corrective action obligations on the remaining facility.
These concerns may slow parceling decisions and hinder or even prevent real estate transactions, including transactions that might have provided for cleanup of facilities that might otherwise not be addressed. EPA is seeking to develop parceling practices for RCRA facilities that will provide guidelines for regulators enabling them to make timely and informed parceling decisions that promote redevelopment while ensuring that the goals of the statute are satisfied.
1. Benefits of Parceling
EPA requests comment on, and specific examples demonstrating, the benefits of removing portions of facilities from RCRA permits upon property transfer including but not limited to:
Situations where removing the RCRA permit requirement from a facility parcel provided funds that otherwise would not have been available to implement corrective action as necessary to protect human health and the environment, including situations where the permittee was no longer viable.
2. Barriers to Parceling
EPA requests comment to help identify and better understand any barriers to parceling that may be created by the RCRA permit including but not limited to:
Information explaining why the permit may be a barrier to a property transaction.
Examples where the RCRA permit may have prevented or slowed property transfer, particularly where the transfer of property would have promoted cleanup.
3. Concerns Raised by Parceling Actions
EPA requests comment to help identify and better understand how parceling of a RCRA permitted facility and releasing the owner/operator and/or purchaser from permit obligations may impact whether the statutory obligation to protect human health and the environment is satisfied. EPA requests comment on regulators' experiences including but not limited to examples where parceling transactions have created incentives or hinderances for cleanup and redevelopment.
4. Overcoming Barriers to Parceling
EPA also requests comment on ways to overcome the barriers to parceling RCRA facilities while ensuring that the statutory requirement of RCRA for permit conditions necessary to protect human health and the environment, and for corrective action permit conditions and financial responsibility until corrective action is complete, discussed above, are met. In particular, EPA solicits comment on:
Examples where a facility was parceled successfully and the permit was retained, and how barriers were overcome in that process.
Ways to support program implementers processing requests for permit modifications associated with parceling transactions to enable them to process those requests in a timely manner.
Practices or components of regulatory alternatives relied on in parceling actions that regulators have found to effectively assure that corrective action obligations at both the remaining RCRA permitted facility and at the parcel will be addressed after the parcel is sold and separated from the facility.
Financial mechanisms that program implementers can rely on to finance future cleanup actions when RCRA financial assurance requirements no longer apply.
E. Other Areas for Permitting Reform
Finally, EPA is soliciting comment on any other opportunities for the Agency to improve the RCRA permitting program, streamline the RCRA permitting process, and improve efficiencies so the Nation can unleash economic growth while providing cost savings to hardworking Americans. Because protecting human health and the environment goes hand-in-hand with economic prosperity, the Agency requests input on ways to simplify regulations, remove redundancies, and reduce delays, while providing clear guidelines to aid businesses in navigating requirements and maintaining protectiveness. EPA is generally soliciting comment on RCRA permitting and specifically seeks ideas that would reduce the time, uncertainty, and costs involved in issuing a permit and enable the Agency to advance its strategic objective of achieving operational efficiencies while upholding its mission to protect human health and the environment.
III. Authority
EPA is authorized to implement the Hazardous Waste Permit Program under the authority of sections 1006, 2002(a), 3002, 3003, 3004, 3005, 3010, 3013, and 7004 of the Solid Waste Disposal Act of 1970, as amended by the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976, as amended, by the Hazardous and Solid Waste Amendments of 1984 (HSWA),
42 U.S.C. 6905
,
6912(a)
,
6922
,
6923
,
6924
,
6925
,
6930
,
6934
, and
6974
. These public laws combined are commonly referred to as the “Resource Conservation and Recovery Act” (RCRA). EPA is soliciting comments and announcing the virtual public engagement sessions to help inform future policy actions under this RCRA authority.
Steven Cook,
Principal Deputy Assistant Administrator, Office of Land and Emergency Management.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-10-10, which applies to all Airbus Helicopters Model SA 365 N, SA 365 N1, AS 365 N2, and AS 365 N3 helicopters. AD 2024-10-10 requires a one-time inspection for proper positioning of the tail rotor (TR) actuator harness and cable tie installation and, depending on the results, corrective action. Since the FAA issued AD 2024-10-10, the manufacturer developed a modification to reroute the yaw harness that would apply to certain model helicopters. This proposed AD would retain some of the actions of AD 2024-10-10 and would also require, for certain model helicopters, modifying the helicopter. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

Background
The FAA issued AD 2024-10-10, Amendment 39-22756 (
89 FR 51401
, June 18, 2024), (AD 2024-10-10), for all Airbus Helicopters Model SA-365N, SA-365N1, AS-365N2, and AS 365 N3 helicopters. AD 2024-10-10 was prompted by an MCAI originated by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued EASA AD 2023-0090, dated May 4, 2023 (EASA AD 2023-0090) to correct an unsafe condition identified as a TR pedal control that was blocked during flight.
AD 2024-10-10 requires a one-time inspection for proper positioning of the TR actuator harness and cable tie installation and, depending on the results, corrective action. The FAA issued AD 2024-10-10 to detect and address interference of the TR pedal control.

The MCAI states that the manufacturer has developed a modification to reroute the yaw harness of the TR actuator part number (P/N) 704A47135059 to prevent interference between the cable tie head of the TR actuator harness and the pin fastener of the tail gearbox cowling.

FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority (CAA) of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this AD after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified in EASA AD 2026-0118, described previously, as incorporated by reference, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD. See “Differences Between this Proposed AD and the MCAI” for a discussion of the general differences included in this proposed AD.
Differences Between This Proposed AD and the MCAI
Where the MCAI requires accomplishing the initial inspection within 165 flight hours after May 18, 2023 [the effective date of EASA AD 2023-0090], this proposed AD would require accomplishing the inspection within 100 hours time-in-service after the effective date of this AD.

SUMMARY:
The FAA is superseding Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2025-08-06 which applied to certain Airbus Helicopters Model SA330J helicopters. AD 2025-08-06 required repetitively inspecting for a gap between the main gearbox (MGB) oil cooling fan assembly rotor blade and the upper section of the guide vane bearing housing, replacing the MGB fan rotor bearings with serviceable bearings if necessary, and at a later compliance time replacing the MGB fan rotor bearing assembly with an improved MGB fan rotor bearing assembly, which constitutes terminating action for the repetitive inspections. Since AD 2025-08-06 was issued, the FAA determined that the compliance time for installing the improved MGB fan rotor bearing assembly should be extended. This AD continues to require the actions in AD 2025-08-06 and increases the compliance time for installing the improved MGB fan rotor bearing assembly. This AD also prohibits installing any MGB fan rotor bearings and any MGB fan rotor bearing assembly, unless certain requirements are met. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

This AD is effective December 29, 2026.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
The FAA issued a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) to amend
14 CFR part 39
to supersede AD 2025-08-06, Amendment 39-23019 (
90 FR 19255
, May 7, 2025), (AD 2025-08-06). AD 2025-08-06 applied to certain Airbus Helicopters Model SA330J helicopters. AD 2025-08-06 required repetitively inspecting for a gap between the MGB fan rotor blade and the upper section of the guide vane bearing housing, replacing the MGB fan rotor bearings with serviceable bearings if necessary, and at a later compliance time replacing the MGB fan rotor bearing assembly with an improved assembly, which constitutes terminating action for the repetitive inspections. The FAA issued AD 2025-08-06 to prevent rotor burst of the MGB fan, damage to the hydraulic lines and flight controls, and subsequent loss of control of the helicopter.
The NPRM was published in the
Federal Register
on September 1, 2026 (
91 FR 56081
). The NPRM was prompted by an MCAI originated by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued EASA AD 2022-0191R1, dated December 9, 2025 (EASA AD 2022-0191R1) (also referred to as the MCAI). The MCAI states that the manufacturer determined that the compliance time for the required modification can be extended due to industrial constraints linked to the availability of replacement parts.
In the NPRM, the FAA proposed to require the actions in AD 2025-08-06 and increase the compliance time for installing the improved MGB fan rotor bearing assembly. In the NPRM, the FAA also proposed to prohibit installing any MGB fan rotor bearings and any MGB fan rotor bearing assembly, unless certain requirements are met.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-8790.
Explanation of Retained Requirements
Although this AD does not explicitly restate the requirements of AD 2025-08-06, this AD retains the requirements of AD 2025-08-06. Those requirements are referenced in EASA AD 2022-0191R1, which, in turn, is referenced in paragraph (g) of this AD.
Discussion of Final Airworthiness Directive
Comments
The FAA received comments from one individual commenter. The commenter supported the NPRM without change.
Conclusion
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA reviewed the relevant data, considered any comments received, and determined that air safety requires adopting this AD as proposed. Accordingly, the FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products. Except for minor editorial changes, this AD is adopted as proposed in the NPRM. None of the changes will increase the economic burden on any operator.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2022-0191R1, which specifies procedures for repetitively inspecting for play (a gap) between the MGB fan rotor blade and the upper section of the guide vane bearing housing. If there is play that does not meet the minimum requirement, EASA AD 2022-0191R1 requires replacing the affected MGB fan rotor bearings with serviceable bearings (both rear and front). EASA AD 2022-0191R1 also specifies procedures for replacing the MGB fan bearing assembly with an improved assembly, which constitutes terminating action for the repetitive inspections. Additionally, EASA AD 2022-0191R1 prohibits installing any MGB fan rotor bearings unless they are serviceable bearings and prohibits installing any MGB fan bearing assembly unless it is an improved MGB fan bearing assembly.

This AD was prompted by the development of a modification for an improved main gearbox (MGB) fan rotor bearing assembly and the determination that the compliance time for installation should be extended. The FAA is issuing this AD to prevent rotor bursting of the MGB fan. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in damage to the hydraulic lines and flight controls and loss of control of the helicopter.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Final rule; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Bell Textron Canada Limited (Bell) Model 429 helicopters. This AD was prompted by reports of premature wear-out of certain spherical bearings due to a quality escape of the spherical bearing monoballs not receiving the required hard coating. This AD requires repetitively inspecting the tail rotor (TR) pitch link assemblies and their bearings for cracks, wear, and mechanical or corrosion damage and, depending on the results, replacing any affected TR pitch link assembly. This AD also allows an affected part to be installed in a helicopter if certain requirements are met. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
This AD is effective December 9, 2026.
The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by reference of a certain publication listed in this AD as of December 9, 2026.
The FAA must receive comments on this AD by January 8, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
You may send comments, using the procedures found in
14 CFR 11.43
and
11.45
, by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
regulations.gov
. Follow the instructions for submitting comments.
Fax:
(202) 493-2251.
Mail:
U.S. Department of Transportation, Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
Hand Delivery:
Deliver to Mail address above between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
AD Docket:
You may examine the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13825; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this final rule, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The street address for Docket Operations is listed above.
Material Incorporated by Reference:
For Transport Canada material identified in this AD, contact Transport Canada, Transport Canada National Aircraft Certification, 159 Cleopatra Drive, Nepean, Ontario, K1A 0N5, Canada; phone: (888) 663-3639; email:
tc.airworthinessdirectives-consignesdenavigabilite.tc@tc.gc.ca
;
website:
tc.canada.ca/en/aviation.
You may view this material at the FAA, Airworthiness Products Section, Operational Safety Branch, 10101 Hillwood Parkway, Fort Worth, TX 76177. For information on the availability of this material at the FAA, call (817) 222-5110. It is also available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13825.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Steven Warwick, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590; phone: (817) 222-5225; email:
steven.r.warwick@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written data, views, or arguments about this final rule. Send your comments using a method listed under
ADDRESSES
. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-13825; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-01123-R” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the final rule, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend this final rule because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to
regulations.gov,
including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this final rule.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this AD contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this AD, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this AD. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Steven Warwick, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590. Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically
(
printed page 75762)
designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
Transport Canada, which is the aviation authority for Canada, has issued Transport Canada AD CF-2026-50, dated October 9, 2026 (Transport Canada AD CF-2026-50) (also referred to as the MCAI), to correct an unsafe condition for certain Bell Textron Canada Limited Model 429 helicopters. The MCAI states Bell has received reports of premature wear-out of the spherical bearings, (P/N) 429-312-117-103, due to a quality escape at the sub-supplier wherein the spherical bearing monoballs did not receive the required hard coating. The MCAI further states this lack of hard coating reduces the wear resistance of the ball and causes it to fret upon contact with the inner bearing race.
The FAA is issuing this AD to detect a worn-out bearing, which could result in the failure of the TR pitch link assembly and loss of control of the helicopter.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13825.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed Transport Canada AD CF-2026-50, which specifies procedures for repetitively inspecting TR pitch link assembly P/N 429-012-212-105 or P/N 429-012-212-107 having a serial number identified in the manufacturer's material and its associated bearings for cracks, wear, and mechanical or corrosion damage, and depending on the results, replacing an affected TR pitch link assembly and the associated hardware. In addition, Transport Canada AD CF-2026-50 specifies an affected part is allowed to be installed on a helicopter if the required inspections have been accomplished.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority (CAA) of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this AD after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
AD Requirements
This AD requires accomplishing the actions specified in Transport Canada AD CF-2026-50, described previously, as incorporated by reference, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this AD.
Explanation of Required Compliance Information
In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD process, the FAA developed a process to use some CAA ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with requirements for corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, Transport Canada AD CF-2026-50 is incorporated by reference in this AD. This AD requires compliance with Transport Canada AD CF-2026-50 in its entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this AD. Material required by Transport Canada AD CF-2026-50 for compliance will be available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13825 after this AD is published.
Justification for Immediate Adoption and Determination of the Effective Date
Section 553(b) of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (
5 U.S.C. 551
et seq.
) authorizes agencies to dispense with notice and comment procedures for rules when the agency, for “good cause,” finds that those procedures are “impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” Under this section, an agency, upon finding good cause, may issue a final rule without providing notice and seeking comment prior to issuance. Further, section 553(d) of the APA authorizes agencies to make rules effective in less than thirty days, upon a finding of good cause.
An unsafe condition exists that requires the immediate adoption of this AD without providing an opportunity for public comments prior to adoption. The FAA has found that the risk to the flying public justifies forgoing notice and comment prior to adoption of this rule because the affected components are part of an assembly that is critical to the control of a helicopter. Further, the compliance time for the initial inspection required by this AD for TR pitch link assemblies with 120 hours time-in-service (TIS) or more is within 30 hours TIS, a time period of less than two months based on the average monthly utilization rates of these helicopters. Therefore, the initial compliance time of this AD for TR pitch link assemblies with 120 hours TIS or more is shorter than the time necessary for the public comment and for publication of the final rule. Accordingly, notice and opportunity for prior public comment are impracticable and contrary to the public interest pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)
.
In addition, the FAA finds that good cause exists pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)
for making this amendment effective in less than 30 days, for the same reasons the FAA found good cause to forgo notice and comment.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The requirements of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) do not apply when an agency finds good cause pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553
to adopt a rule without prior notice and comment. Because the FAA has determined that it has good cause to adopt this rule without prior notice and comment, RFA analysis is not required.
Costs of Compliance
The FAA estimates that this AD affects 152 helicopters of U.S. registry.
The FAA estimates the following costs to comply with this AD:

The FAA estimates the following costs to do any replacement that would be required based on the results of the inspection. The agency has no way of determining the number of helicopters that might need this replacement:

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
This AD will not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This AD will not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
For the reasons discussed above, I certify that this AD:
(1) Is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
, and
(2) Will not affect intrastate aviation in Alaska.

A. Overview of Information Collection
Title of Information Collection:
Evaluation of the Community Choice Demonstration.
OMB Approval Number:
2528-0337.
Type of Request:
Revision of a currently approved collection.
Form Number:
N/A.
Description of the need for the information and proposed use:
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) has contracted with Abt Global to conduct an evaluation of the Community Choice Demonstration (formerly the Housing Choice Voucher Mobility Demonstration). The primary purpose of the Demonstration is to provide voucher assistance and mobility-related services to families with children to encourage families to move to lower-poverty areas and expand their access to opportunity areas. The evaluation is studying whether the program helps families with children access and remain in opportunity areas and exploring which services appear to be most effective and cost-effective in achieving the goals of the program. This proposed information collection includes 3 instruments administered in all demonstration sites; and 20 instruments administered in a subset of demonstration sites participating in the Child Assessment and the Obesity and Diabetes Risk Assessment studies. Assessments study are funded by HUD and conducted by Abt Global. HUD's contract with Abt Global provides the flexibility to explore collaborations with other researchers and funders to support additional knowledge-building efforts that build on the foundation laid by the demonstration. Research collaborations need to advance important research objectives, not interfere with the core Demonstration and evaluation, and be structured to minimize overall respondent burden. The Obesity and Diabetes Risk Assessment represents such collaboration; it is funded by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) and led by Johns Hopkins University (JHU) as part of a study called the Mobility Opportunity Vouchers for Eliminating Diabetes and Obesity (MOVED) study. The data collection for the Child Assessment and the MOVED studies will be conducted by JHU. While NIH-funded studies do not normally require the submission of an information collection request for compliance with the Paperwork Reduction Act, we included the Obesity and Diabetes Risk Assessment as part of this information collection request because it will be administered to a subset of households participating in the HUD-funded Demonstration. In addition, the Child Assessment will be administered during the same visit, to the same households, and by the same interviewers as the Obesity and Diabetes Risk Assessment. On May 31, 2022, and June 9, 2022, OMB approved the administration of a series of data collection instruments as part of the core Demonstration. On October 6, 2022, OMB approved non-substantive changes to this information collection; on December 18, 2023, OMB approved a revision to the collection to add three studies: the Home Assessment, the Child Assessment, and the Obesity and Diabetes Risk Assessment; on March 27, 2024, October 22, 2024, and May 28, 2025, OMB approved additional non-substantive changes to select instruments. Through this revised information collection request, HUD is seeking approval to continue the information collection using a subset of the previously approved instruments, outlined in the table below. No new instruments are being added to this collection.

AGENCY:
Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2026-08-51, which applies to all Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Model MBB-BK 117 D-3 helicopters. AD 2026-08-51 requires inspecting the rotor hub-shaft for cracks, replacing any rotor hub-shaft that has any crack, and reporting information after accomplishment of the replacement. AD 2026-08-51 also prohibits installing any
(
printed page 75786)
affected rotor hub-shaft on any helicopter, unless certain requirements are met. Since the FAA issued AD 2026-08-51, it was determined that additional repetitive inspections (including eddy current inspections) are necessary, and that revising the compliance time to account for hoist operations is necessary. This proposed AD would retain the actions of AD 2026-08-51 and would require additional repetitive inspections. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.
DATES:
The FAA must receive comments on this NPRM by January 8, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
You may send comments, using the procedures found in

and

, by any of the following methods:

You may examine the AD docket at

under Docket No. FAA-2026-13831; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD docket contains this NPRM, the mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The street address for Docket Operations is listed above.

For European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) material identified in this proposed AD, contact EASA, Konrad-Adenauer-Ufer 3, 50668 Cologne, Germany; phone: +49 221 8999 000; email:

david.enns@faa.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed under
ADDRESSES
. Include “Docket No. FAA-2026-13831; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00809-R” at the beginning of your comments. The most helpful comments reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data. The FAA will consider all comments received by the closing date and may amend the proposal because of those comments.
Except for Confidential Business Information (CBI) as described in the following paragraph, and other information as described in
14 CFR 11.35
, the FAA will post all comments received, without change, to
regulations.gov
, including any personal information you provide. The agency will also post a report summarizing each substantive verbal contact received about this NPRM.
Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to David Enns, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 1600 Stewart Avenue, Suite 410, Westbury, NY 11590. Any commentary that the FAA receives which is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
The FAA issued AD 2026-08-51, Amendment 39-23249 (
91 FR 22995
, April 29, 2026) (AD 2026-08-51), for all AHD Model MBB-BK 117 D-3 helicopters. AD 2026-08-51 was prompted by an MCAI originated by EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union. EASA issued EASA Emergency AD 2026-0078-E, dated April 13, 2026 (EASA Emergency AD 2026-0078-E), to correct an unsafe condition identified as cracking of the rotor hub-shaft, manufacturer part numbers D623M1501203 and D623M1501204. EASA then superseded EASA Emergency AD 2026-0078-E and issued EASA AD 2026-0091, dated May 8, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0091), to revise the compliance time inspection thresholds and add repetitive visual inspections. The FAA did not issue an AD corresponding to EASA AD 2026-0091.
AD 2026-08-51 requires inspecting the rotor hub-shaft for cracks, replacing any rotor hub-shaft that has any crack, and reporting information after accomplishment of the replacement. AD 2026-08-51 also prohibits installing any affected rotor hub-shaft on any helicopter, unless certain requirements are met. The FAA issued AD 2026-08-51 to address cracking of the rotor hub-shaft, which, if not addressed, could lead to failure of the main rotor transmission and loss of control of the helicopter.
Actions Since AD 2026-08-51 Was Issued
Since the FAA issued AD 2026-08-51, EASA superseded EASA AD 2026-0091 and issued EASA AD 2026-0151, dated July 30, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0151) (also referred to as the MCAI). The MCAI states that repetitive eddy current inspections and revised compliance times for helicopters used for hoist operations are necessary.
In addition, since the FAA issued AD 2026-08-51, the FAA received a comment from Air Methods LLC (Air Methods) requesting changes to the requirements of AD 2026-08-51. The comment disposition below specifically addresses this comment.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13831.
Comment on AD 2026-08-51
The FAA gave the public the opportunity to comment on AD 2026-08-51. The following presents the comment received on AD 2026-08-51 and the FAA's response to the comment.
Request To Define the Terms Used in the Final Rule
Air Methods requested that the FAA define “events,” as incorporated from paragraph (2) of EASA Emergency AD 2026-0078-E, which states “after each reporting of noticeable changes in vibrations, or balancing abnormalities of a helicopter, accomplish an inspection.” Air Methods also requested the FAA provide a more objective definition of the events that mandate the inspection. Specifically, they requested clarity on what defines reporting and balancing abnormalities of a helicopter, and
(
printed page 75787)
whether the vibrations have a measurable magnitude.
The FAA acknowledges the importance of having clear and objective criteria for determining when inspections are necessary. However, the FAA disagrees with revising the descriptions for the requested definitions. The FAA incorporated EASA Emergency AD 2026-0078-E by reference and believes its definitions are justified given the complex and varied nature of helicopter operations. At this time, the FAA has no alternative method or additional information to define or create alternative inspection criteria, without potentially overlooking critical safety considerations. The referenced material in the EASA Emergency AD 2026-0078-E states that if there are noticeable vibrations during the last flight, operators of helicopters equipped with a Health Monitoring System (HMS) should analyze the HMS data download for step changes, data that exceeds the amber or red threshold, or trends. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Request To Revise the Inspection Criteria
Air Methods requested the FAA revise AD 2026-08-51 by requiring a repetitive inspection based on hours time-in-service or flight cycles instead of a one-time inspection.
The FAA is superseding AD 2026-08-51 to require repetitive inspections. EASA Emergency AD 2026-0078-E was superseded by EASA AD 2026-0091, and then EASA AD 2026-0091 was superseded by EASA AD 2026-0151. This NPRM proposes to incorporate by reference EASA AD 2026-0151, which requires repetitive inspections of the rotor hub-shaft. The FAA did not change this AD as a result of this comment.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2026-0151, which specifies procedures for repetitive visual and eddy current inspection of the rotor hub-shaft, replacing any rotor hub-shaft that has cracks or suspicion of cracks, and reporting the results of the inspection to Airbus Helicopters. EASA AD 2026-0151 also prohibits installing any affected rotor hub-shaft that has not passed an inspection on any helicopter.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority (CAA) of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified in EASA AD 2026-0151, described previously, as incorporated by reference, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this AD. See “Differences Between this Proposed AD and the MCAI,” for a detailed description of the differences.
Differences Between This Proposed AD and the MCAI
The MCAI applies to MBB-BK117 D-3m helicopters, whereas this proposed AD does not because that model does not have an FAA type certificate.
Explanation of Required Compliance Information
In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD process, the FAA developed a process to use some CAA ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with requirements for corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, the FAA proposes to incorporate EASA AD 2026-0151 by reference in the FAA final rule. This proposed AD would, therefore, require compliance with EASA AD 2026-0151 in its entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD. Using common terms that are the same as the heading of a particular section in EASA AD 2026-0151 does not mean that operators need comply only with that section. For example, where the AD requirement refers to “all required actions and compliance times,” compliance with this AD requirement is not limited to the section titled “Required Action(s) and Compliance Time(s)” in EASA AD 2026-0151. Material required by EASA AD 2026-0151 for compliance will be available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13831 after the FAA final rule is published.
Interim Action
The FAA considers that this proposed AD would be an interim action. If final action is later identified, the FAA might consider additional rulemaking.

Paperwork Reduction Act
A federal agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, nor shall a person be subject to a penalty for failure to comply with a collection of information subject to the requirements of the Paperwork Reduction Act unless that collection of information displays a currently valid OMB Control Number. The OMB Control Number for this information collection is 2120-0056. Public reporting for this collection of information is estimated to be approximately 1 hour per response, including the time for reviewing instructions, searching existing data sources, gathering and maintaining the data needed, and completing and reviewing the collection of information. All responses to this collection of information are mandatory. Send comments regarding this burden estimate or any other aspect of this collection of information, including suggestions for reducing this burden, to: Information Collection Clearance Officer, Federal Aviation Administration, 10101 Hillwood Parkway, Fort Worth, TX 76177-1524.
Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
The FAA determined that this proposed AD would not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This proposed AD would not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national Government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
For the reasons discussed above, I certify that the proposed regulation:
(1) Is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
,
(2) Would not affect intrastate aviation in Alaska, and
(3) Would not have a significant economic impact, positive or negative, on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

The Proposed Amendment
Accordingly, under the authority delegated to me by the Administrator, the FAA proposes to amend
14 CFR part 39
as follows:
PART 39—AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVES
1.
The authority citation for part 39 continues to read as follows:
Authority:
49 U.S.C. 106(g)
,

,
