printed page 75949)
November 19, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on November 6, 2026, Nasdaq MRX, LLC (“MRX” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule General 8, Section 1(b) to provide that the installation fee and ongoing monthly fee for interfirm cabinet connectivity will apply separately to each of the two customers connected through an interfirm cabinet connectivity order, as described further below.
The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/​rulebook/​mrx/​rulefilings
,
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Rule General 8, Section 1(b) to provide that the installation fee and ongoing monthly fee for interfirm cabinet connectivity will apply separately to each of the two customers connected through an interfirm cabinet connectivity connection, as described below. Currently, the Exchange assesses the applicable installation fee and ongoing monthly fee only to the customer that submits the order. The other customer that accepts and participates in the connection is not separately assessed those fees. Under the proposal, each customer participating in a new interfirm cabinet connectivity connection will be assessed the existing $550 installation fee and $385 ongoing monthly fee for its respective leg of the connectivity path. For interfirm cabinet connectivity connections already in place as of the implementation date, the accepting customer will be assessed the ongoing monthly fee, but not the installation fee, for its respective leg, and the fees assessed to the ordering customer will not change.
Background
The Exchange's data center campus consists of the original data center (“NY11”), an initial expansion area (“NY11-4”), and a second expansion area (“NY11-5”) (collectively, the “Data Center” or “Data Center Campus”). Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is a fiber-based connectivity service that links cabinets used by two different colocation customers (“Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity”) throughout the Data Center Campus. The interfirm cabinet connection consists of two customer-side legs that meet at the Nasdaq-provided distribution point:
[
3
]
one leg extends from the first customer's cabinet to the Nasdaq-provided distribution point, and the other extends from the Nasdaq-provided distribution point to the second customer's cabinet.
Before the Exchange implemented equalized connectivity
[
4
]
throughout its Data Center, a customer would order Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity through the Nasdaq customer portal and identify the customer to which the ordering customer wanted to connect, with the ordering customer being solely responsible for both the installation and the ongoing monthly fiber connectivity fees. No separate installation or ongoing monthly fees were assessed, or are currently assessed, to the non-ordering customer for its side of the Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity.
With respect to provision and installation of the service, the fiber for the Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity was provided and installed by a third-party provider or by the customer. The Exchange did not provide or install such fiber or manage such services.
Equalization places greater emphasis on the way Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is supervised and managed, with Nasdaq taking a more central role in those functions. While customers still request the interfirm cabinet connection through the Nasdaq Customer Portal, the pre-existing fiber in the Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity has been replaced with Exchange-provided, equalized fiber. Under this structure, the Exchange supervises and audits the interfirm cabinet connection on an ongoing basis.
[
5
]
As discussed above, the Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity consists of two customer-side legs that meet at the Nasdaq-provided distribution point: one leg extends from the first customer's cabinet to the Nasdaq-provided distribution point, and the other extends from the Nasdaq-provided distribution point to the second customer's cabinet. The Exchange provides and manages the cabling and standardized demarcation points and performs inventory management, implementation support, ongoing maintenance, monitoring, audit, and operational oversight for the connection.
Both customers must act before the connection is implemented: one customer initiates the Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity order through the Nasdaq Customer Portal, and the other customer
(
printed page 75950)
accepts it. If the second customer does not accept the order, the connection is not implemented. Each participating customer consequently receives a distinct customer-side leg of a Nasdaq-provided, Nasdaq-managed, equalized connectivity path. Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is optional and is not required for a customer to obtain colocation services or to connect to the Exchange's trading systems.
Proposal
The Exchange proposes to retain the existing installation and ongoing monthly fees for Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity and extend their application to the non-ordering, accepting customer side of the connection. Under the proposal, each customer participating in a new Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity connection will be assessed the existing $550 installation fee and $385 ongoing monthly fee for its respective leg of the connectivity path. For Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity connections already in place as of the implementation date, the accepting customer will be assessed the ongoing monthly fee, but not the installation fee, for its respective leg, and the fees assessed to the ordering customer will not change.
The Exchange anticipates implementing the proposed rule change during the first quarter of 2027 and will announce that implementation date through an Equity Trader Alert or other customer communication.
The Exchange believes that assessing the existing fees separately to each customer appropriately reflects the Exchange's increased role in managing Data Center connectivity following Equalization. The Exchange now provides the fiber and manages, supervises, monitors, and audits the connection after installation. The proposal also aligns the allocation of fees with the structure of the service: two separately provided and managed customer-side legs join at the Nasdaq-provided distribution point, and each customer must authorize and receive the benefit of its own leg. The proposal therefore assesses each customer for the Nasdaq-provided and Nasdaq-managed connectivity furnished to that customer.
[
6
]
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
7
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
8
]
in particular, in that it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among members and issuers and other persons using any facility, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange believes that the proposed fees are reasonable because each customer receives a distinct leg of an equalized connectivity path that the Exchange actively provides and manages. Each customer-side leg is a defined, Exchange-managed component of that path. Following equalization, the Exchange provides the fiber connectivity and administers the cabling, standardized demarcation points, inventory, and ongoing operational support associated with each leg, and it supervises and audits the connection on an ongoing basis. Each customer's leg is a component the Exchange implements, administers, monitors, and supports. Applying the existing $550 installation fee and $385 monthly fee to each customer is reasonable because each customer receives, and the Exchange manages, a distinct leg of the equalized path.
[
9
]
The Exchange believes this approach equitably allocates the fees among the customers that receive and use each Exchange-managed leg of the connection. Each customer receives connectivity through its respective leg of the connectivity path, and each customer is accordingly responsible for the fees associated with the connectivity provided to it. The fact that the two connectivity paths collectively facilitate communication between the customers does not alter the fact that each customer receives a separately identifiable connectivity service. The Exchange further believes that assessing each customer for its respective connectivity leg avoids requiring one customer to pay for the leg that another customer receives. The Exchange therefore believes that its methodology represents an equitable allocation of fees among the customers using Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity.
The amount of each fee is also reasonable because it is unchanged from the Fiber connectivity fee amounts currently assessed to the ordering customer for Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity and is the same amount charged for certain other Fiber connectivity offerings.
[
10
]
The Exchange also believes that the proposal is reasonable because it supports a uniformly administered and auditable Interfirm Cabinet connectivity pathway within the Data Center. As the Exchange has explained, equalization is intended to enhance the integrity of the Data Center network by establishing standardized connectivity requirements for each component of the connectivity path and exercising greater management oversight over those components.
[
11
]
A
(
printed page 75951)
standardized, Nasdaq-managed path in which the Exchange oversees the cabling, demarcation points, and supporting architecture enhances the Exchange's ability to monitor, maintain, and audit that connectivity.
[
12
]
Each customer-side leg of Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is a component of that path. Assessing the existing fees to each customer for its own leg allocates those fees among the customers that receive and use each Exchange-managed leg of the path and does not alter the path's availability or operation.
The Exchange further believes the proposal is reasonable because Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is an optional service. Customers are not required to purchase Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity to obtain colocation services or to connect to the Exchange's trading systems. Rather, a customer purchases the service only if it elects to establish a fiber connection between its cabinet and the cabinet of another colocation customer, and each customer may determine for itself whether the service, at the proposed fees, is appropriate for its business.
The Exchange believes that applying the fees separately to both customers is equitable and not unfairly discriminatory because both customers receive a substantially similar customer-side service and both benefit from the Exchange's provision and ongoing management of the equalized path. Under the current billing model, only the ordering customer pays even though the accepting customer also receives a Nasdaq-provided and Nasdaq-managed leg of the connection. The proposal allocates the fees to both beneficiaries and treats the ordering and accepting customers alike. Each customer would pay the same, existing fee for the Exchange-provided and Exchange-managed leg that it receives, and no customer would be asked to bear the fees attributable to another customer's leg of the connection.
The Exchange also believes that it is reasonable, equitable, and not unfairly discriminatory not to assess the installation fee to the accepting customer for Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity connections already in place as of the implementation date. The installation fee is a one-time charge assessed when a connection is ordered and established. For a connection already in place, the connection has been established and the installation fee has already been assessed to the ordering customer. The Exchange therefore believes that it would be inappropriate to assess a one-time installation charge for a connection that is not being newly established. Those accepting customers will, however, be assessed the ongoing monthly fee beginning on the implementation date, which is consistent with the Exchange's rationale for assessing each customer for the Exchange-managed leg of the connection that it receives and uses. The distinction is drawn by whether a connection is in place as of the implementation date, and not by the identity, size, or trading activity of any customer, and it applies uniformly to every accepting customer with an existing connection.
The Exchange will apply the same fee amounts and billing methodology to all similarly situated customers. The proposal does not distinguish among customers based on their identity, trading activity, or anticipated use of the connection. Rather, each new customer will pay the same installation fee and monthly fee for its own leg of the standardized, equalized connectivity path.
[
13
]
Because both parties must affirmatively participate in the Nasdaq Customer Portal order process before implementation, as described above, each customer will have notice of the fee treatment before the Exchange provisions the connection.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
The Exchange does not believe that the proposal will impose an undue burden on intramarket competition because it will apply the same fees to each customer participating in an Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity order. The proposal will eliminate the current difference in the ongoing monthly fee treatment of the ordering and accepting customers, each of which receives a customer-side leg of the Exchange-provided and Exchange-managed connection, and, for new orders, the difference in their installation fee treatment.
The proposal therefore will treat similarly situated customers consistently. Each customer participating in an Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity arrangement through a new order will be assessed the same installation and recurring monthly fees for its respective connectivity leg. For connections already in place as of the implementation date, the Exchange will not assess a one-time installation fee to the accepting customer because the connection has already been established, but the accepting customer will be assessed the same ongoing monthly fee as the ordering customer. This distinction turns on whether a connection is in place as of the implementation date and applies uniformly to all such connections. It does not favor or disadvantage any customer relative to another. The fees do not distinguish among customers based on their identity, business model, trading activity, or the identity of the customer with which they establish connectivity.
The Exchange also does not believe that the proposal will impose an undue burden on intermarket competition. Interfirm Cabinet Connectivity is an optional service that customers are not required to purchase to obtain colocation services or connect to the Exchange's trading systems. The proposal does not alter the availability or technical operation of the service. Instead, it applies the existing fees separately to each customer that elects to participate in and receive a customer-side leg of the connection: for new orders, the existing installation fee and ongoing monthly fee, and for existing connections, the existing ongoing monthly fee.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were either solicited or received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act.
[
14
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is: (i) necessary or appropriate in the public interest; (ii) for the protection of investors; or (iii) otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
(
printed page 75952)
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number
SR-MRX-2026-45 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-MRX-2026-45. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-MRX-2026-45 and should be submitted on or before December 15, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
15
]
Vanessa A. Countryman,
Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106942; File No. SR-MRX-2026-46]
November 19, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on November 12, 2026, Nasdaq MRX, LLC (“MRX” or “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC” or “Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I, II, and III, below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend Options 7, concerning the fees and rebates for executions in NDXB.
[
3
]
The text of the proposed rule change is available on the Exchange's website at
https://listingcenter.nasdaq.com/​rulebook/​mrx/​rulefilings
,
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The Exchange has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
On April 30, 2026, the Commission approved the listing and trading on the Exchange of binary broad-based index options—particularly binary options on the Nasdaq-100 index and the Nasdaq-100 Micro index.
[
4
]
In November 2026, the Exchange plans to begin listing and trading binary options on the Nasdaq-100 index, under the symbol “NDXB.”
To help foster interest in this new product, the Exchange at this time proposes to set at $0.00 all transaction fees under Options 7, Sections 3 and 4 that would otherwise apply to executions in NDXB and to provide that no rebates under those sections will apply to NDXB executions. To that end, it proposes to add new provisions at the top of Options 7, Section 3 (Fees and Rebates for Regular Orders and All Crossing Orders) and Section 4 (Complex Order Fees). The provision at the top of Section 3 would read as follows:
For all Regular Order and Crossing Order executions in NDXB the fee will be $0.00 per contract. No other fees or rebates in Section 3 will apply to executions in NDXB.
Meanwhile, the provision at the top of Section 4 would read as follows:
For all Complex Order executions in NDXB, including interest in NDXB on the Regular Order Book that interacts with a Complex Order, the fee will be $0.00 per contract. No other fees or rebates in Section 4 will apply to executions in NDXB.
(
printed page 75934)
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that its proposal is consistent with Section 6(b) of the Act,
[
5
]
in general, and furthers the objectives of Sections 6(b)(4) and 6(b)(5) of the Act,
[
6
]
in particular, in that it provides for the equitable allocation of reasonable dues, fees and other charges among members and issuers and other persons using any facility, and is not designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Commission and the courts have repeatedly expressed their preference for competition over regulatory intervention in determining prices, products, and services in the securities markets. In Regulation NMS, while adopting a series of steps to improve the current market model, the Commission highlighted the importance of market forces in determining prices and SRO revenues and, also, recognized that current regulation of the market system “has been remarkably successful in promoting market competition in its broader forms that are most important to investors and listed companies.”
[
7
]
Likewise, in
NetCoalition
v.
Securities and Exchange Commission
[
8
]
(“NetCoalition”) the D.C. Circuit upheld the Commission's use of a market-based approach in evaluating the fairness of market data fees against a challenge claiming that Congress mandated a cost-based approach.
[
9
]
As the court emphasized, the Commission “intended in Regulation NMS that `market forces, rather than regulatory requirements' play a role in determining the market data . . . to be made available to investors and at what cost.”
[
10
]
Further, “[n]o one disputes that competition for order flow is `fierce.' . . . As the SEC explained, `[i]n the U.S. national market system, buyers and sellers of securities, and the broker-dealers that act as their order-routing agents, have a wide range of choices of where to route orders for execution'; [and] `no exchange can afford to take its market share percentages for granted' because `no exchange possesses a monopoly, regulatory or otherwise, in the execution of order flow from broker dealers'. . . .”
[
11
]
Although the court and the SEC were discussing the cash equities markets, the Exchange believes that these views apply with equal force to the options markets.
The Exchange believes that charging no fees and paying no rebates for executions in NDXB is reasonable because NDXB is a new binary broad-based index options product that has not yet developed trading history on MRX, and the proposed pricing is designed to encourage initial trading interest and market participant familiarity with the product. Nasdaq ISE likewise waived fees and rebates when NQX began trading and subsequently adopted pricing designed to promote trading activity in that new proprietary Nasdaq-100 index option product.
[
12
]
Here, eliminating transaction fees and rebates for NDXB at launch is a reasonable means of reducing transaction-cost frictions while Members and investors evaluate the product.
The Exchange further believes that the proposal is equitably allocated and not unfairly discriminatory because the same $0.00 per contract fee, and the same absence of rebates, will apply to all Regular Order, Crossing Order, and Complex Order executions in NDXB. The proposal does not differentiate by Member, capacity, volume tier, order-entry protocol, side of the market, or whether the execution occurs on the regular order book or in a complex order. No Member or category of Member will receive preferential transaction pricing in NDXB, and no Member or category of Member will be assessed a higher transaction fee or denied a transaction rebate that another similarly situated Member receives.
The Exchange also believes the proposal is consistent with the Act because NDXB will be traded under the Exchange's approved binary broad-based index options framework and will be subject to the Exchange rules that apply to options trading unless Options 3B provides otherwise. The Commission approved MRX's rules to list and trade binary broad-based index options on the Nasdaq-100 index and Nasdaq-100 Micro index, and the proposed pricing is limited to the transaction fees and rebates applicable to executions in NDXB, a product within that approved framework.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
Inter-Market Competition
The proposal does not impose an undue burden on inter-market competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The Exchange believes its proposal remains competitive with other options markets and will offer market participants another choice of where to transact options. The Exchange notes that it operates in a highly competitive market in which market participants can readily favor competing venues if they deem fee levels at a particular venue to be excessive, or rebate opportunities available at other venues to be more favorable. In such an environment, the Exchange must continually adjust its fees to remain competitive with other exchanges. Because competitors are free to modify their own fees in response, and because market participants may readily adjust their order routing practices, the Exchange believes that the degree to which fee changes in this market may impose any burden on competition is extremely limited.
Intra-Market Competition
With respect to intra-market competition, the Exchange does not believe that the proposal will place any category of market participant at a competitive disadvantage. The proposed NDXB pricing applies uniformly to all Members and all market participant types that execute NDXB transactions. Because no Member will be charged a transaction fee and no Member will receive a transaction rebate for NDXB executions, the proposal does not create pricing advantages based on volume, capacity, order type, order side, or the ability to satisfy a tier. The absence of differentiated fees and rebates also avoids competitive distinctions that may arise from maker/taker pricing, capacity-based fees, rebates, fee caps, or volume thresholds. To the extent that the proposal encourages additional participation in NDXB, that increased activity should benefit all market participants by supporting the development of liquidity and trading opportunities in the new product.
(
printed page 75935)
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
No written comments were either solicited or received.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The foregoing rule change has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act.
[
13
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is: (i) necessary or appropriate in the public interest; (ii) for the protection of investors; or (iii) otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.

Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov

Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-MRX-2026-46. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml

Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-MRX-2026-46 and should be submitted on or before December 15, 2026.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106934; File No. SR-LTSE-2026-29]
November 19, 2026.
Pursuant to the provisions of Section 19(b)(1) under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on November 10, 2026, Long-Term Stock Exchange, Inc. (“LTSE” or the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the self-regulatory organization. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange is filing with the Commission a proposed rule change to adopt new Rule 11.159 to enable Members to designate certain orders they submit to the Exchange on behalf of retail customers to be identified as retail orders. Under the proposed rule change, the Exchange would create a new class of market participant for any Member that satisfies the requirements under proposed Rule 11.159 called a Retail Member Organization (“RMO”), which would be eligible to submit certain retail order flow (“Retail Orders”) to the Exchange. Specifically, proposed Rule 11.159 would: (1) define a Retail Order and RMO; (2) set forth a RMO's qualification and application requirements and the Exchange's approval process; (3) outline procedures for when a RMO fails to abide by the Retail Order requirements; and (4) outline the procedures under which a Member may appeal the Exchange's decision to disapprove it or disqualify it as a RMO. Proposed Rule 11.159 is based on and is almost identical to MEMX LLC (“MEMX”) Rule 11.21.
[
3
]
The text of the proposed rule change is available at the Exchange's website at
https://longtermstockexchange.com/​
and at the principal office of the Exchange.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the Exchange included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The self-regulatory organization has prepared summaries, set forth in Sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to adopt new Rule 11.159 to enable Members to designate certain orders they submit to the Exchange on behalf of retail customers to be identified as retail orders. Under the proposed rule change, the Exchange would create a new class of market participant for any Member that satisfies the requirements under proposed Rule 11.159 called a Retail Member Organization (“RMO”), which would be eligible to submit certain retail order flow (“Retail Orders”) to the Exchange. Specifically, proposed Rule 11.159 would: (1) define a Retail Order and RMO; (2) set forth a RMO's qualification and application requirements and the Exchange's approval process; (3) outline procedures for when a RMO fails to abide by the Retail Order requirements; and (4) outline the procedures under which a Member may appeal the Exchange's decision to disapprove it or disqualify it as a RMO. Proposed Rule 11.159 is based on and is almost identical to MEMX LLC (“MEMX”) Rule 11.21.
[
4
]
Definitions.
The Exchange proposes to adopt the following definitions under proposed Rule 11.159(a). The term “Retail Member Organization” or “RMO” would be defined as a Member (or a division thereof) that has been approved by the Exchange to submit Retail Orders. The term “Retail Order” would be defined as an agency or riskless principal order that meets the criteria of FINRA Rule 5320.03 that originates from a natural person and is submitted to the Exchange by a RMO, provided that no change is made to the terms of the order with respect to price or side of market and the order does not originate from a trading algorithm or any other computerized methodology.
RMO Qualifications and Approval Process.
Under proposed Rule 11.159(b), any Member could qualify as a RMO if it conducts a retail business or routes retail orders on behalf of another broker-dealer. Proposed Rule 11.159(b)(1) makes clear that a RMO that carries retail customer accounts on a fully disclosed basis would be considered to conduct a retail business for purposes of the rule. The qualification standards and approval process under proposed Rule 11.159(b) are designed to ensure that Members are properly qualified as a RMO and only designate as Retail Orders those orders that meet the definition of Retail Orders under proposed Rule 11.159(a)(2) described above. Any Member that wishes to obtain RMO status would be required to submit: (1) an application form; (2) supporting documentation sufficient to demonstrate the retail nature and characteristics of the applicant's order flow;
[
5
]
and (3) an attestation, in a form prescribed by the Exchange, that substantially all orders submitted by the Member as a Retail Order will qualify as such under proposed Rule 11.159(b).
Under proposed Rule 11.159(b)(6), a RMO would be required to have written
(
printed page 75891)
policies and procedures reasonably designed to assure that it will only designate orders as Retail Orders if all requirements of a Retail Order are met. Such written policies and procedures must require the Member to: (1) exercise due diligence before entering a Retail Order to assure that entry as a Retail Order is in compliance with the requirements of proposed Rule 11.159; and (2) monitor whether orders entered as Retail Orders meet the applicable requirements. If the RMO does not itself conduct a retail business but routes Retail Orders on behalf another broker-dealer, the RMO's supervisory procedures must be reasonably designed to assure that the orders it receives from such other broker-dealer that it designates as Retail Orders meet the definition of a Retail Order. Such a RMO must: (1) obtain an annual written representation, in a form acceptable to the Exchange, from each other broker-dealer that sends it orders to be designated as Retail Orders that entry of such orders as Retail Orders will be in compliance with the requirements of proposed Rule 11.159; and (2) monitor whether Retail Order flow routed on behalf of such other broker-dealers continues to meet the applicable requirements.
[
6
]
Pursuant to proposed Rule 11.159(b)(2), to apply for RMO status, a Member must submit: (A) an application form; (B) supporting documentation, which may include sample marketing literature, website screenshots, other publicly disclosed materials describing the Member's retail order flow, and any other documentation and information requested by the Exchange in order to confirm that the applicant's order flow would meet the requirements of the Retail Order definition; and (C) an attestation, in a form prescribed by the Exchange, that substantially all orders submitted as Retail Orders will qualify as such under the proposed rule.
After an applicant submits those materials, the Exchange shall notify the applicant of its decision in writing. If the Exchange disapproves a Member's application to be a RMO, the Exchange would provide a written notice to the Member.
[
7
]
The disapproved applicant could appeal the disapproval by the Exchange as provided in proposed Rule 11.159(d) and/or reapply for RMO status 90 days after the disapproval notice is issued by the Exchange.
[
8
]
An RMO also could voluntarily withdraw from such status at any time by giving written notice to the Exchange.
[
9
]
As described above, under proposed Rule 11.159(b), any Member could qualify as a RMO if it conducts a retail business or routes retail orders on behalf of another broker-dealer, and Proposed Rule 11.159(b)(1) makes clear that a RMO that carries retail customer accounts on a fully disclosed basis would be considered to conduct a retail business for purposes of the rule. The Exchange proposes to distinguish a RMO's routing services on behalf of another broker-dealer from services provided by a RMO that carries retail customer accounts on a fully disclosed basis, as described below. As background with respect to this aspect of the proposed change, the Exchange first would like to describe the terms “introducing broker”, “carrying firm” or “carrying broker-dealer”, and “fully disclosed,” as such terms are commonly used in the securities industry.
An introducing broker-dealer is “one that has a contractual arrangement with another firm, known as the carrying or clearing firm, under which the carrying firm agrees to perform certain services for the introducing firm. Usually, the introducing firm submits its customer accounts and customer orders to the carrying firm, which executes the orders and carries the account. The carrying firm's duties include the proper disposition of the customer funds and securities after the trade date, the custody of customer securities and funds, and the recordkeeping associated with carrying customer accounts.
[
10
]
Further, a “fully disclosed” introducing arrangement is
distinguished from an omnibus clearing arrangement where the clearing firm maintains one account for all the customer transactions of the introducing firm. In an omnibus relationship, the clearing firm does not know the identity of the customers of the introducing firm. In a fully disclosed clearing arrangement, the clearing firm knows the names, addresses, securities positions and other relevant data as to each customer.
[
11
]
With respect to a broker-dealer that is routing on behalf of another broker-dealer, the Exchange does not believe that the routing broker-dealer has sufficient information to assess whether orders are truly retail in nature, and thus, requires a RMO routing on behalf of other broker-dealers to maintain additional supervisory procedures and obtain annual attestations, as described above, in order to submit Retail Orders to the Exchange. In contrast, however, if a broker-dealer is carrying a customer account on a fully disclosed basis, then such carrying broker-dealer is required to perform certain diligence regarding such account that the Exchange believes is sufficient to assess whether a customer is a retail customer in order to submit orders on behalf of such a customer to the Exchange as a Retail Order. The carrying broker of an account typically handles orders from its retail customers that are “introduced” by an introducing broker. However, as noted above, in contrast to a typical routing relationship on behalf of another broker-dealer, a carrying broker does obtain a significant level of information regarding each customer introduced by the introducing broker. Accordingly, the Exchange states in proposed Rule 11.159(b)(1) that for purposes of Rule 11.159, “conducting a retail business shall include carrying retail customer accounts on a fully disclosed basis.”
Failure of RMO to Abide by Retail Order Requirements.
Proposed Rule 11.159(c) addresses a RMO's failure to abide by Retail Order requirements. If a RMO designates orders submitted to the Exchange as Retail Orders and the Exchange determines, in its sole discretion, that those orders fail to meet any of the requirements of Retail Orders, the Exchange may disqualify a Member from its status as a RMO. When disqualification determinations are made, the Exchange would provide a written disqualification notice to the Member. A disqualified RMO could appeal the disqualification provided in proposed Rule 11.159(d) and/or reapply for RMO status 90 days after the disqualification notice issued by the Exchange.
Appeal of Disapproval or Disqualification.
Proposed Rule 11.159(d) provides appeal rights to Members. If a Member disputes the Exchange's decision to disapprove it as a RMO under proposed Rule 11.159(b) or disqualify it under proposed Rule 11.159(c), such Member may request, in writing, within five business days after notice of the decision is issued by the Exchange, that the Retail Member Organization Panel (“RMO Panel”) review the decision to determine if it was correct. The RMO Panel would consist of the Exchange's Chief Regulatory Officer (“CRO”), or a designee of the CRO, and two officers of the Exchange designated by the Exchange's Chief Executive Officer. The RMO Panel would review the facts and render a decision within the time frame prescribed by the Exchange. The RMO
(
printed page 75892)
Panel could overturn or modify an action taken by the Exchange and all determinations by the RMO Panel would constitute final action by the Exchange on the matter at issue.
Implementation.
The Exchange notes that, under the proposed rule change, an order involving any Regulation NMS security traded on the Exchange that meets the definition of Retail Order would be eligible to be designated as such by a RMO. The Exchange also notes that orders designated as Retail Orders would only be designated as such to the Exchange and would not be designated as such on the Exchange's market data feeds or otherwise identifiable as Retail Orders by any market participants or the public. Further, the Exchange notes that orders designated as Retail Orders would be handled in the exact same way under the Exchange's rules as if such orders were not designated as Retail Orders. In other words, the designation of an order as a Retail Order would not in any way affect the priority or other handling procedures applicable to such order under the Exchange's rules.
The purpose of enabling RMOs to designate orders as Retail Orders to the Exchange under the proposed rule change is so the Exchange may identify and track orders designated as such, which the Exchange believes will be useful for it in considering potential pricing modifications to such orders as it continues to evaluate its pricing structure. The Exchange further believes that the proposed rule change would enable the Exchange to have the appropriate mechanisms and processes in place to implement any differentiated pricing for Retail Orders if and when the Exchange proposes to do so in the future. The Exchange notes that, at some point following the adoption and implementation of proposed Rule 11.159 as described in this proposed rule change, the Exchange may separately propose to amend its fee schedule to adopt a specific fee code for Retail Orders to be provided on a RMO's execution reports and/or to provide differentiated pricing for Retail Orders, which the Exchange believes would attract additional retail order flow to the Exchange, thereby providing the benefits of exchange transparency, regulation, and oversight to more retail orders. The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change would allow it to be organized with the appropriate infrastructure (
i.e.,
mechanisms and processes) in advance of any such proposal, and as such, would allow the Exchange to more quickly implement any such differentiated pricing.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with the provisions of Section 6 of the Act
[
12
]
in general, and the proposed adoption of new Rule 11.159 furthers the objectives of Section 6(b)(5) of the Act
[
13
]
in particular in that it is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change is consistent with these principles because it would increase competition among execution venues by enabling the Exchange to implement future pricing changes to encourage the submission of additional Retail Orders to the Exchange. As the Commission is aware, a significant percentage of the orders of retail investors are executed over-the-counter.
[
14
]
The Exchange believes that it is appropriate to put in place the mechanisms and processes to enable the Exchange to subsequently offer any differentiated pricing for Retail Orders as the Exchange believes that such pricing could incentivize market participants to bring more retail order flow to the Exchange, thereby providing the benefits of exchange transparency, regulation, and oversight to more retail orders.
The Exchange also believes its proposed qualification standards and review process under proposed Rule 11.159 promote just and equitable principles and are not unfairly discriminatory because they are designed to ensure that Members are properly qualified as RMOs and only designate as Retail Orders those orders that meet the definition of Retail Orders under proposed Rule 11.159(a)(1). The qualification process proposed herein by the Exchange is not designed to permit unfair discrimination, but rather ensure that orders that are designated as Retail Orders are, in fact, orders submitted by a retail customer that satisfy the proposed definition of Retail Order. Lastly, the Exchange notes that, as discussed below, the proposed qualification provisions are identical to those included in MEMX Rule 11.21 and the review provisions are almost identical to those included in MEMX Rule 11.21. Additionally, the proposed qualification and review provisions are substantially similar to those included in the rules of Cboe BZX, Cboe EDGX, Cboe BYX, and Nasdaq Texas (defined below).
[
15
]
Distinguishing a RMO's routing services on behalf of another broker-dealer from services provided by a RMO that carries retail customer accounts on a fully disclosed basis in proposed Rule 11.159(b)(1) is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices because it highlights the parties for whom additional procedures are required because they do not maintain relationships with the end customer (
i.e.,
routing brokers) and still requires the RMO to follow such procedures to ensure that such orders qualify as Retail Orders. As proposed, however, a RMO would not be required to follow such procedures, including obtaining annual attestations, to the extent such RMO actually knows the end customer and carries the account of such customer and thus can itself confirm that the orders qualify as Retail Orders. The Exchange believes that this aspect of the proposed rule change will remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system because it will allow RMOs that carry retail customer accounts to designate Retail Orders as such without imposing additional attestation requirements that the Exchange believes are not necessary for such RMOs, as described above.
The proposed rule change does not raise any issues under the Exchange Act that have not been previously addressed by the Commission. As stated above, proposed Rule 11.159 is based on and is almost identical to MEMX Rule 11.21. The proposed rule differs from the MEMX rule in only one respect: proposed Rule 11.159(d)(1) provides that any request to appeal the Exchange's decision to disapprove or disqualify RMO status must be made
in writing.
Additionally, the proposed rule is substantially similar to Cboe BZX Exchange, Inc. (“Cboe BZX”) Rule 11.25.
[
16
]
Specifically, proposed Rule 11.159 is nearly identical to paragraphs (a)-(d) of Cboe BZX Rule 11.25, with the only differences being: (1) the name of the RMO Panel; (2) the deletion of a
(
printed page 75893)
defined term not otherwise used in the rule; (3) that the Exchange's Chief Executive Officer, rather than Chief Information Officer, designates two officers to serve on the RMO Panel; and (4) the Cboe BZX rule (like MEMX's rule) does not require that requests to appeal the exchange's decision to disapprove or disqualify RMO status be made in writing. Cboe BZX Rule 11.25 otherwise differs from the proposed rule in that Cboe BZX's rule contains a separate paragraph (e) that allows a RMO to designate a Retail Order to be identified as such on Cboe BZX's proprietary data feeds. As noted above, proposed Rule 11.159 would not allow a RMO to designate a Retail Order to be identified as such on the Exchange's market data feeds. Lastly, proposed Rule 11.159 is also substantially similar to the existing rules of several other equity exchanges.
[
17
]
Specifically, proposed Rule 11.159 contains identical definitions, standards and qualification procedures as the comparable retail order rules of Cboe BZX, Cboe EDGX, Cboe BYX, and Nasdaq Texas. However, unlike certain of those exchanges' rules, the proposed Rule 11.159 does not propose to attribute retail orders in the Exchange's market data feeds, adopt any special order handling for Retail Orders or orders intended to provide liquidity to Retail Orders, or to adopt any mechanics for price improvement for Retail Orders.
Additionally, the proposed express identification of Rules 11.156 through 11.158 as “Reserved” is consistent with Sections 6(b)(1) and 19(g)(1) of the Act,
[
18
]
which both require the Exchange to comply with its own rules, and the requirement of Section 6(b)(1) of the Act that requires a national securities exchange to be organized to follow its rules. This non-substantive change is designed to improve the organization of this section of its rules, which the Exchange expects will assist in following them as the rulebook expands.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The Exchange believes that the proposed amendment would not burden intramarket competition because the ability to designate Retail Orders to be identified as such to the Exchange would be open to all Members that wish to send Retail Orders to the Exchange. The Exchange believes the proposed rule change would not burden, but rather increase, intermarket competition by permitting RMOs to identify orders as Retail Orders when submitted to the Exchange, which would ultimately enable the Exchange to better compete with other exchanges that offer retail order programs.
[
19
]
As noted above, at this time the Exchange is not proposing to attribute retail orders in the Exchange's market data feeds, to adopt any special order handling for Retail Orders or orders intended to provide liquidity to Retail Orders, or to adopt any mechanics for price improvement for Retail Orders. Rather, adoption of the proposed rule will enable the Exchange to have the appropriate mechanisms and processes in place to implement differentiated pricing for Retail Orders if and when the Exchange proposes to do so in the future.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A)(iii) of the Act
[
20
]
and subparagraph (f)(6) of Rule 19b-4 thereunder.
[
21
]
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend the rule change if it appears to the Commission that the action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or would otherwise further the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-LTSE-2026-29  on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to File Number SR-LTSE-2026-29. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of LTSE and on its internet website at
https://longtermstockexchange.com/​
.
Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-LTSE-2026-29 and should be submitted on or before December 15, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
22
]
Vanessa A. Countryman,
Secretary.

Securities and Exchange Commission
[Release No. 34-106939; File No. SR-BOX-2026-24]
November 19, 2026.
Pursuant to Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”),
[
1
]
and Rule 19b-4 thereunder,
[
2
]
notice is hereby given that on November 9, 2026, BOX Exchange LLC (the “Exchange”) filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (“Commission”) the proposed rule change as described in Items I and II below, which Items have been prepared by the Exchange. The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to establish Rule 7600(a)(6) to provide a minimum eligible order size for single-leg Qualified Open Outcry Orders. The text of the proposed rule change is available from the principal office of the Exchange, and also on the Exchange's internet website at
https://rules.boxexchange.com/​rulefilings
.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, the self-regulatory organization included statements concerning the purpose of, and basis for, the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. The self-regulatory organization has prepared summaries, set forth in Sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The purpose of the proposed rule change is to amend Rule 7600 (Qualified Open Outcry Orders—Floor Crossing) to add a minimum eligible order size for Qualified Open Outcry (“QOO”) Orders.
[
3
]
Specifically, the Exchange is proposing to establish Rule 7600(a)(6) to provide a minimum eligible order size for single-leg QOO Orders of 20 contracts. Single-leg QOO Orders for less than 20 contracts shall be rejected by the system under the proposed rule.
Today, BOX Participants may submit orders for execution on the Trading Floor pursuant to the procedures outlined in Rule 7600. Under Rule 7600, orders on the Trading Floor, after being announced to the trading crowd, are submitted by the Floor Broker as part of a QOO Order for execution. QOO Orders may be submitted as single-leg, Complex, or multi-leg orders.
[
4
]
QOO Orders are limited solely to the Trading Floor and only Floor Brokers may submit QOO Orders.
[
5
]
Currently, there is no minimum eligible order size requirement for QOO Orders.
Now, the Exchange is proposing to amend Rule 7600 to include the concept of a minimum eligible order size for QOO Orders. Under the proposed change, the Exchange is establishing a minimum eligible order size for single-leg QOO Orders only. The minimum eligible order size for single-leg QOO Orders shall be 20 contracts. Single-leg QOO Orders for less than 20 contracts shall be rejected by the system. The Exchange notes that for orders under the minimum eligible order size, Floor Participants would still be able to submit these orders to the Exchange for execution via electronic methods (
e.g.,
BOX Book
[
6
]
or Price Improvement Period (“PIP”)
[
7
]
).
The Exchange believes that establishing the proposed minimum eligible order size will help to ensure that the Exchange continues to have the available resources to facilitate Trading Floor activity and oversee the Trading Floor, generally. The Exchange believes that setting a minimum eligible order size will curtail excessive smaller order activity on the Trading Floor that has the effect of disproportionately taxing the Exchange's resources, as no exchange has unlimited capacity. Additionally, the Exchange believes that, at times, excessive smaller order activity can become disruptive as the
(
printed page 75919)
scale of these orders in their totality may interfere with the orderly operations on the Trading Floor. Specifically, since all orders on the Trading Floor must be announced and certified by an Options Exchange Official,
[
8
]
all orders on the Trading Floor, regardless of their size, impose a comparable per-order burden on Exchange resources. When this is considered with the fact that these smaller sized orders are submitted with a higher frequency as compared to other orders on the Trading Floor, the Exchange believes these smaller sized orders in their totality can become overly burdensome to the Exchange's Trading Floor.
Therefore, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will assist the Exchange in the efficient allocation of resources applicable to overseeing and monitoring activity on the Trading Floor. The Exchange believes that setting a minimum order size for single-leg QOO Orders at 20 contracts is consistent with this goal given the Exchange's observations of past Trading Floor activity, which has shown that these smaller sized orders, when submitted with a high frequency, can disproportionately tax the Exchange's resources. Additionally, the Exchange believes that it is appropriate to only provide a minimum eligible order size for single-leg QOO Orders, but not multi-leg and Complex QOO Orders at this time, based on similar observations. Specifically, the Exchange has observed that the majority of smaller sized orders (orders under 20 contracts) on the Trading Floor are single-leg QOO Orders as compared to multi-leg and Complex QOO Orders.
The Exchange believes that it is appropriate to set a minimum order size for single-leg QOO Orders at 20 contracts to manage finite resources and accommodate overall demand on the Trading Floor by providing a means to efficiently deploy Exchange resources. Under Rule 7600, it is a requirement that an Options Exchange Official certify that each QOO Order is adequately announced to the trading crowd by the Floor Broker.
[
9
]
Therefore, the Exchange is required to manually certify that all QOO Orders executed on the Trading Floor are appropriately announced to the trading crowd. This certification is a manual process by the Floor Officials. Therefore, the Exchange believes that, at this time, it is appropriate to set a minimum eligible order size on the Trading Floor for single-leg QOO Orders to manage capacity and ensure that the Exchange is efficiently allocating its Trading Floor resources. The Exchange is ultimately looking to strike the right balance between curtailing certain smaller orders that disproportionally utilize Exchange resources without discouraging Floor Participants from utilizing the Trading Floor and the Exchange believes that setting a minimum eligible order size of 20 contracts for single-leg QOO Orders is a reasonable approach to satisfying this goal.
[
10
]
The Exchange is not proposing to implement a minimum eligible order size for multi-leg and Complex QOO Orders at this time, because, based on the observations of the Exchange, the Exchange believes it can achieve the goals stated above by only implementing the minimum eligible order size for single-leg QOO Orders. However, the Exchange will continue to monitor activity on the Trading Floor and, if the Exchange determines that excessive smaller size multi-leg and Complex QOO Orders on the Trading Floor are unreasonably taxing the Exchange's resources or leading to disruptive trading practices, the Exchange may propose implementing a minimum order size for multi-leg and Complex QOO Orders.
[
11
]
The Exchange will provide notice prior to implementing the proposed minimum eligible order size for single-leg QOO Orders. Such implementation date will be communicated by the Exchange to Participants via Regulatory Notice.
2. Statutory Basis
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act and the rules and regulations thereunder applicable to the Exchange and, in particular, the requirements of Section 6(b) of the Act.
[
12
]
Specifically, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
13
]
requirements that the rules of an exchange be designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, to promote just and equitable principles of trade, to foster cooperation and coordination with persons engaged in regulating, clearing, settling, processing information with respect to, and facilitating transactions in securities, to remove impediments to and perfect the mechanism of a free and open market and a national market system, and, in general, to protect investors and the public interest. The Exchange believes the proposed rule change is consistent with the Section 6(b)(5)
[
14
]
requirement that the rules of an exchange not be designed to permit unfair discrimination between customers, issuers, brokers, or dealers.
The Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will further the purposes of the Act by supporting the Exchange in regulating activity on the Trading Floor. The Exchange believes that allowing the Exchange to set a minimum eligible size for single-leg QOO Orders provides a means for balancing between providing a venue for orders to be executed while at the same time making sure that the Exchange continues to have the available resources to facilitate Trading Floor activity and oversee the Trading Floor, generally, which will assist with the maintenance of a fair and orderly market, promotes just and equitable principles of trade, and is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices.
Additionally, the Exchange believes that the proposed rule change will further the purposes of the Act by providing an additional means for the Exchange to manage finite resources on the Trading Floor. Specifically, the Exchange believes that setting a minimum eligible order size will curtail excessive smaller order activity on the Trading Floor that has the effect of disproportionately taxing the Exchange's resources, as no exchange has unlimited capacity. Additionally, the Exchange believes that, at times, excessive smaller order activity can become disruptive as the scale of the orders in their totality may interfere with the orderly operations on the Trading Floor. Given the manual nature of certain obligations on the Trading Floor, setting a minimum eligible order size allows the Exchange to better manage capacity and resources and, is designed to assist with the maintenance of a fair and orderly market, promotes just and equitable principles of trade, and is designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices, as it ensures that the Exchange is utilizing its Trading Floor resources in an effective and efficient manner.
As stated above, the Exchange has an obligation to certify the announcement of all orders on the Trading Floor and, therefore, it needs to ensure that the level of activity is manageable. The
(
printed page 75920)
proposed change is designed to provide the Exchange with the means to more efficiently manage this requirement. As such, ensuring that the Exchange can adequately certify the announcement of all orders on the Trading Floor furthers the objectives of such requirement, which is generally designed to prevent fraudulent and manipulative acts and practices.
The Exchange believes it is reasonable and appropriate to implement a minimum eligible order size for single-leg QOO Orders at 20 contracts, and not multi-leg and Complex QOO Orders at this time, because, based on the observations of the Exchange, the Exchange believes it will help manage capacity and ensure that the Exchange is efficiently allocating its Trading Floor resources. As noted above, the Exchange has observed that the majority of smaller sized orders (orders under 20 contracts) on the Trading Floor are single-leg QOO Orders as compared to multi-leg and Complex QOO Orders. The Exchange is ultimately looking to strike the right balance between curtailing certain smaller orders that disproportionally utilize Exchange resources without discouraging Floor Participants from utilizing the Trading Floor. As such, the Exchange believes the proposed change is designed to promote just and equitable principles of trade. The Exchange believes this proposed change will lead to a more efficient and effective use of Exchange resources and overall operation of the Trading Floor. In addition, it will help ensure the Exchange is appropriately overseeing activity on the Trading Floor. As such, the Exchange believes the proposed rule change is in the public interest, and therefore, consistent with the Act.
B. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Burden on Competition
The Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will result in any burden on competition that is not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. The proposed change is not intended to address competitive issues and instead is being proposed to assist with the maintenance of a fair and orderly market by providing the Exchange with support to efficiently manage the finite resources on the Trading Floor and assistance to prevent potentially disruptive trade practices.
Intramarket Competition.
The Exchange believes the proposed rule change to amend Rule 7600 to permit the Exchange to establish a minimum eligible order size for single-leg QOO Orders would not place an unfair burden on intramarket competition because it is designed to encourage the efficient and rational use of the Exchange's finite resources and to accommodate the overall demand on the Trading Floor. The Exchange also notes that the proposed rule change will apply equally to all Floor Participants. Additionally, as noted above, for orders under the minimum order size, Floor Participants would still be able to submit these orders to the Exchange for execution via electronic methods.
Intermarket Competition.
The Exchange believes the proposal would not place an unfair burden on intermarket competition as it is not intended to address any competitive issues but is instead designed solely to encourage the efficient use of the Exchange's resources on the Trading Floor. The Exchange believes that the proposal to permit the Exchange to establish a minimum eligible order size for single-leg QOO orders will help make sure that the Exchange continues to have the available resources to facilitate Trading Floor activity and oversee the Trading Floor, generally, which, in turn, will sustain the Exchange's overall competitiveness. The Exchange also notes that nothing prevents other options exchanges, as applicable, from proposing similar rules to allow for the adoption of a minimum eligible order size for open outcry orders.
For the foregoing reasons, the Exchange does not believe that the proposed rule change will impose any burden on competition not necessary or appropriate in furtherance of the purposes of the Act.
C. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement on Comments on the Proposed Rule Change Received From Members, Participants, or Others
The Exchange has neither solicited nor received comments on the proposed rule change.
III. Date of Effectiveness of the Proposed Rule Change and Timing for Commission Action
The Exchange has filed the proposed rule change pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
15
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
16
]
thereunder. Because the foregoing proposed rule change does not: (i) significantly affect the protection of investors or the public interest; (ii) impose any significant burden on competition; and (iii) become operative for 30 days from the date on which it was filed, or such shorter time as the Commission may designate, it has become effective pursuant to Section 19(b)(3)(A) of the Act
[
17
]
and Rule 19b-4(f)(6)
[
18
]
thereunder.
At any time within 60 days of the filing of the proposed rule change, the Commission summarily may temporarily suspend such rule change if it appears to the Commission that such action is necessary or appropriate in the public interest, for the protection of investors, or otherwise in furtherance of the purposes of the Act. If the Commission takes such action, the Commission shall institute proceedings under Section 19(b)(2)(B) of the Act
[
19
]
to determine whether the proposed rule should be approved or disapproved.
IV. Solicitation of Comments
Interested persons are invited to submit written data, views and arguments concerning the foregoing, including whether the proposed rule change is consistent with the Act. Comments may be submitted by any of the following methods:
Electronic Comments
Use the Commission's internet comment form (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
); or
Send an email to
rule-comments@sec.gov
.
Please include file number SR-BOX-2026-24 on the subject line.
Paper Comments
Send paper comments in triplicate to Secretary, Securities and Exchange Commission, 100 F Street NE, Washington, DC 20549-1090.
All submissions should refer to file number SR-BOX-2026-24. This file number should be included on the subject line if email is used. To help the Commission process and review your comments more efficiently, please use only one method. The Commission will post all comments on the Commission's internet website (
https://www.sec.gov/​rules/​sro.shtml
). Copies of the filing will be available for inspection and copying at the principal office of the Exchange. Do not include personal identifiable information in submissions; you should submit only information that you wish to make available publicly. We may redact in part or withhold entirely from publication submitted material that is obscene or subject to copyright
(
printed page 75921)
protection. All submissions should refer to file number SR-BOX-2026-24 and should be submitted on or before December 15, 2026.
For the Commission, by the Division of Trading and Markets, pursuant to delegated authority.
[
20
]
Vanessa A. Countryman,
Secretary.
